We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:11:32 GMT

Three women who have been told their abusive ex-partners will be released early from jail as part of controversial plans to free up prison space have said they fear for their safety.

Around 700 offenders will leave prison in England and Wales on Thursday under the government's early prisoner release plan - with a further 3,800 scheduled for release over the next year.

Ahead of the releases, victims have been sent letters informing them that their attackers will be let out early.

Claire Milne's ex-husband, Robert Dales, was convicted in March this year of coercive control and possessing offensive weapons, including samurai and ninja swords. He was sentenced to three years in prison.

"There was physical violence," said Milne. "There were threats to kill, there was punching of doors, punching of walls. I trod on egg shells throughout the entire relationship and it was almost like I had to coach myself into what to say just to ensure there wouldn't be an escalation."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) recently told her Dales, 36, would be released early.

"I am scared that he will come after me. I don't want to die," she said. "I am not a silly woman - I know that I've been in a very high-risk domestic abuse relationship and I know what he's capable of because I lived it."

She said she was "incredibly angry" with the government, who were "not listening to victims".

It comes as prison staff have told the BBC they are increasingly having to put inmates in cells that are unsuitable because of the lack of space. They argue there is no choice but to release more prisoners as room is urgently needed.

Prisons across England and Wales are at 98% capacity, with the latest government figures showing there are just 1,134 spaces remaining in the adult male prison estate. The lowest figure of vacant beds this year.

Under the new scheme, inmates serving sentences of up to 19 months will be released after completing a third of their jail term. Most will have expected to spend 40% of their sentence behind bars - with the remainder served in the community.

The MoJ said that while domestic abuse had a "profound and lasting" impact on victims, the government was committed to keeping the most dangerous prisoners behind bars.

It said offenders jailed for rape, child sex abuse offences and manslaughter would stay in prison, but going further than that would risk the prison system collapsing.

An MoJ spokesperson said the government was investing £1bn in support services, including placing domestic abuse specialists in 999 call centres.

In April, former primary school teacher Christopher Haynes was sentenced to 21 months in prison after admitting to coercive control against his now ex-wife, who has also been notified of his early release.

Karen Haynes told the BBC she was distraught and said it was "a punch in the gut".

"We have fought so hard and we have had to use every inch of the system to get justice," she continued. "I just find it devastating that somebody [who] can admit all of that can be released after only doing seven months of a custodial sentence."

She has been told her ex-husband will now be released in November.

"He always made Christmas so hard," said Karen. "We were constantly scared, we wanted one Christmas without him and without us being frightened he will turn up - but it looks like we won't even get that now."

Another victim, Alice - not her real name - was subjected to domestic abuse. Her perpetrator is due to be released later this month. She has asked that we do not name her or her ex-partner because she is frightened of what he might do.

"I am terrified," she said. "I had only just started to feel safe and to process what I had gone through."

She said she felt like "the rug had been pulled out from underneath me".

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. Inmates will be released in nine tranches until June next year.

Those serving longer sentences - including more dangerous criminals - will not become eligible for the scheme until next year. They had previously expected to spend two thirds of their sentence behind bars, but instead will complete half of their term in prison before spending the rest of their punishment in the community on licence.

Dame Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, called the scheme "shameful" and said she's had "no assurance that the danger perpetrators pose has been properly considered and assessed with meaningful input from victims".

"Ultimately, we cannot ignore the fact that the early release scheme has caused untold damage to victims' confidence in the justice system," Dame Nicole added.

She said Prime Minister Andy Burnham "must take urgent steps to address this" and called on the probation service to be given "the resources it needs to safely manage more offenders in the community". She also called for additional funding for domestic abuse services to support victims.

A recent report raised serious concerns about electronic tagging, which can be used to monitor offenders' movements in the community. It found almost half of tags were not fitted on time.

Alice told the BBC she had been looking to buy a doorbell with a camera fitted to help make her feel safer, but said she cannot afford one. "I don't feel prepared in the slightest and I don't feel safe," she added.

"I think the early release scheme is a joke to victims and survivors, who spent years preparing for trial, going through evidence and re-traumatising themselves to go to court, just for the perpetrator of their crimes to be released after just 33% of their sentence".

The MoJ said: "Anyone who is released faces the toughest-ever controls on their movements, including world-first restriction zones and the largest expansion of electronic tagging, with victims having a say in their perpetrators' licence conditions."

Singer Lola Young says vaping has made breathing feel like a 'chore'

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:11:21 GMT

Singer Lola Young has said her breathing feels like a "chore" due to the effects of vaping.

In a TikTok video, the Grammy winner told her followers her lungs feel "battery powered".

The 25-year-old has previously acknowledged in videos she "should quit", but suggested in her latest post that is unlikely to happen any time soon.

Vocal coach Lizzii Hills has told BBC Newsbeat vaping is "not advised" for artists and that difficulty breathing can affect a singer's voice and performance.

"Somebody once said to me, 'Lola there will be a day when you wake up, you'll be 25 or 26, from a deep sleep, and you'll start to feel the effects of vaping'," the Messy singer said in her post.

"You know what I said? I said 'nah' and rolled my eyes.

"But let me tell you something, the day has come."

Last month, The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) linked vaping to higher rates of breathing problems after reviewing more than 80 studies.

The review also found an association with wheezing, coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Describing her symptoms, Young said: "My lungs feel like they're battery powered, like they're just one big battery.

"Breathing feels like a chore, it feels like hard work, it feels like I should be paid for breathing. It feels like there will be no tomorrow."

The NHS says vaping is less harmful than smoking, but notes there are still risks - many of which are still not known.

The government is introducing measures to make vapes less attractive, including a ban on single-use vapes, introduced last year.

And from Thursday a new tax will be applied to e-cigarette liquid, with an additional £2.20 added per 10ml.

Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voice.

"Vaping may not affect the voice box just itself, it affects the lungs, the airways, the throat - it's all respiratory, it's all connected. So doing that can affect your vocal technique," she says.

"Breathing is really important. Singing requires controlled inhalation and sustained, efficient exhalation.

"You end up trying harder, putting in more effort for the same results you were getting beforehand."

She adds that when artists struggle with their voice, it can have significant psychological impacts on them too.

"They can feel like they've lost themselves," she says. "It can become quite a big deal emotionally."

Overall, she wouldn't recommend vaping to her clients.

"As a performer, as an artist, you want to stay in the best health you can for your voice to work at its best.

"We all know it's not the healthy choice and if you can avoid it - absolutely."

Young returned to the spotlight earlier this year following a five-month hiatus after she collapsed on stage.

She has been open in the past about her struggles with her health and addiction, previously telling The Guardian about dealing with cocaine dependency.

She has also struggled with her mental health and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and ADHD when she was a teenager.

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Young's representatives for comment.

Timeline of RAF Fairford incident and the investigation so far

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:08:02 GMT

The public is slowly getting more information about what happened near the RAF Fairford airbase at the weekend - but many questions remain unanswered.

We know that two early-morning calls were made to police about suspicious vehicles, and that five men, all British nationals in their 20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism offences.

We also know they were later released on bail, and the BBC understands that one of the men was the first 999 caller. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has now said the UK government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident.

Here is what we know about how the incident unfolded, and what has happened in the days since.

We now know that in the days leading up to the incident, security was increased around RAF Fairford, one of the UK's most important military sites, which is used by the US Air Force.

There were also reports of heightened police activity around the base on Saturday evening, hours before three suspicious vehicles were reported to police.

Gloucestershire police say they received a call just after midnight on Sunday 27 September about "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be travelling towards RAF Fairford.

The BBC now understands that one of the five men who was later arrested and then bailed had made the call himself.

Nearly an hour later, a farmer living close to the base called 999 after seeing three vans parked in a "weird formation".

There was "a large group of hooded and masked men" near the vans who started to "panic" when they saw her, she told Radio 4's Today programme.

The woman, who has remained anonymous, said she initially tried to contact the Ministry of Defence police at RAF Fairford, but no one picked up, so she dialled 999.

"Within 10 minutes the village was full of armed police," she said.

Shortly afterwards - although the exact time is unknown - Gloucestershire Constabulary arrested five men in the Whelford area, a village right next to the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act.

A grainy image purporting to show the moment of arrest shows five men sitting on the ground, shirtless and in handcuffs under guard by police officers.

The BBC has been unable to verify the original source, but BBC Verify has geolocated the image and confirmed it appeared to be authentic.

After sunrise, police declared a major incident in Whelford and set up a 400m (1,312ft) cordon around the three vehicles.

The Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit was brought in to examine them, and aerial pictures showed a remote-controlled robot approaching some white vans.

About 85 households in Whelford were evacuated to a local leisure centre.

Some residents said they had been "shaken by the incident" but that "community spirit and local support has been exceptional".

By Sunday afternoon, Counter Terrorism Policing had confirmed it was leading the investigation.

In a statement, it said the five men had been further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act.

The investigation was still in its early stages, Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said, and the public was asked "to follow official channels for updates" and not to speculate.

At about 16:00 BST, US President Donald Trump told reporters the arrest of the five suspects was "fantastic" and "an amazing job".

"We had them under investigation. They were looking to ‌do big ⁠damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great... We had them under view for a long time, and we got them."

The US is connected to this incident because its air force operates RAF Fairford, and has used the base to carry out strikes against Iran.

At about noon on Monday, counter-terror police released more information on the five men who had been arrested - they were all from London and aged between 23-25.

In a statement, Counter Terrorism Policing said they were being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (PACE) and that a custody extension has been secured.

A cordon remained in place in Whelford.

Within hours, however, counter-terror police announced that all five men would be released on police bail after "extensive interviews and enquiries".

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor stressed that the men were subject to "stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."

"They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said.

Speaking from the White House, Trump questioned the decision, saying he was "surprised that they released them", adding: "I wouldn't have done that."

Also on Monday afternoon, the prime minister chaired a Cobra meeting and urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts".

Taylor defends the decision, saying it was "grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers".

Later on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Fox News that the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", but did not provide evidence or further details.

Counter-terror police gave another update on Tuesday evening, saying properties in London had been searched as part of the investigation. No further details were given.

The three vehicles had also undergone an "extensive examination" with the support of military and forensic experts, Assistant Commissioner Taylor said.

The Counter Terrorism Policing boss said that no improvised explosive devices were found in the vans, but a "quantity of petrol" was recovered.

Three days on, the BBC has learned that one of the men who had been arrested had made the first 999 call.

It remains unclear why the man called police, or what he told them.

Also on Wednesday, Gloucestershire Police removed the cordon and reopened the scene.

A few hours later, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident.

"We will say more in due course but we can confirm... that we believe Iran to have played a part," he said, without providing further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:06:23 GMT

Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the European Union.

The prime minister told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now" but the UK needed to "consider the options" for its relationship with the EU as "where we are isn't good enough".

It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year.

The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing Burnham of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years".

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason, Burnham was challenged over whether he was reopening divisive arguments about rejoining the EU, despite promising not to in May.

In response, the PM said: "No, I'm not proposing that, am I? I am saying that in a context when we're looking at a 10-year plan for Britain, Britain needs to consider the options as to where we will be.

"That is way before you even get to anything that's put before the public, this is about now just looking at what are the broad options for our relationship."

He suggested these options could include staying "exactly as we are", a closer relationship similar to that being discussed by the EU and Canada or rejoining the EU customs union.

However, Burnham stressed that "to leap back to a proposal and a referendum on it wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

Pressed over whether including an in-out referendum in a future Labour manifesto was a possibility, Burnham said: "Yes, things are possible. I think where we are isn't good enough."

Asked earlier on BBC Radio 4's Today if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, Burnham replied that he wanted to "look at the options".

The PM added that he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now".

French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be "very good news" if the UK wanted to rejoin the EU, while Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said his country would welcome Britain back "with open arms".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said his party had put forward "concrete plans to boost our economy, strengthen our defences and cut people's taxes by joining the single market and a customs union".

He added: "Talk is cheap. Burnham must stop with all the 'maybes' and get negotiating that better deal for Britain today."

The party's Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said last week there is "no rejoin on the table", adding Britain would effectively be treated as a "fresh entrant state" if it wished to join the bloc again.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door".

Tice said: "He says Brexit has done more harm than good but what's done real harm is a Labour government that can't deliver growth, can't control migration and now wants to outsource the job to Brussels."

He added Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".

In his Labour conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham blamed Brexit for a loss of control over both immigration and the economy, telling delegates he did not believe the current relationship was "good enough".

He told activists he wanted to use the rescheduled summit later this year to lay out "different options" for the UK's long-term relationship with Europe.

He promised to "find consensus" on an option to clarify the UK's position, although did not offer further detail of how this would be measured.

In response to Burnham's conference speech, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "Labour cannot pin the blame for their disastrous economic decisions on a vote that happened over a decade ago.

"Besides, they are already dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "All Andy Burnham offers on repairing our relationship with our biggest trading partner is a promise to keep our options open.

"The Green Party is very clear that we should rejoin the customs union to start reversing the damage, and full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK."

Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:01:16 GMT

Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.

An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.

Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.

Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city".

He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.

Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.

Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports.

Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal.

Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process."

Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled.

"So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."

It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said.

He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself.

But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene.

City have said in a statement they are "both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission" and maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:01:16 GMT

Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.

An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".

The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.

The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.

Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted shortly before it was due to happen

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:29:11 GMT

The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour before it was due to happen.

Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last.

This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week.

Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child.

But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.

The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal.

It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this.

"We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement.

"It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay."

She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.

She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

A year later, Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence.

At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.

NHS trust admits 'failing families' over stillbirths

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:22:51 GMT

An NHS trust has apologised after an independent review found that eight babies might have survived with better maternity care, admitting it has "failed families".

The stillbirths all occurred at the East Kent Hospitals NHS Trust's hospitals between June 2025 and March 2026.

An independent review ordered by the trust found systemic issues lay at the heart of the failures. These included failures to manage high risk pregnancies, provide appropriate triage, identify foetal growth concerns, and make appropriate use of interpreter services.

Since the report, a further seven stillbirths have occurred, including three last month. A review into those deaths has now been ordered.

All the stillbirths occurred after 34 weeks gestation.

Three years ago, the Kirkup report found 45 babies might have survived at the trust's hospitals if they had received better care.

The East Kent NHS trust runs the William Harvey Hospital in Ashford and the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital (QEQM) in Margate.

Papers for a board meeting on Thursday contained a report by the acting CEO of the trust, Dr Des Holden, who apologised to the families involved.

Dr Holden wrote: "On behalf of the board, and personally, I am very sorry and apologise to the women and families, and their communities, where failings in our care are at the heart of these devastating outcomes."

The board papers contained a further report, headed Response to the Independent Stillbirth Review, which said four cases were assessed as having care deficiencies likely to have affected the outcome for the baby.

In a further four cases, care issues were identified that may have contributed to the outcome.

The review found "recurrent and systemic weaknesses in the management of high-risk pregnancy, foetal surveillance, maternity triage, escalation and organisational learning", documents said.

Documents also said since the review "there have, regrettably, been a further four term stillbirths from April 2026 and July 2026 and a further three in August 2026".

Helen Gittos, who lost her baby Harriett in 2014, has previously told the BBC how her baby was born at the QEQM, but sustained a brain injury and lived for a week.

After the latest review was published she said: "It's gut-wrenching, it really is, to be here again, reading a report of... a series of awful tragedies and so many failings in so many respects, and things that have been known about for so very long.

"Talking to other families involved, last night, our reactions are sort of a mixture of incredulity and rage. It's not acceptable that so little has changed in so long."

She added: "It's deeply distressing this trust have long-known that there were problems, but I think there are serious questions to answer for the national and regional NHS England support teams who have been intensively trying to help this trust and trying to help others elsewhere and it's not working.

"We have to try to do things differently."

After the board papers were published, Dr Holden said: "This review is clear that sadly, we have failed families. We are truly sorry."

He said the trust requested the review after increased safety monitoring introduced following Dr Bill Kirkup's investigation identified a rise in stillbirths.

Each stillbirth was investigated and an independent review commissioned into 11 cases.

"We are implementing the review's recommendations in full," he said, "including improving continuity of care for women with high-risk pregnancies, maternity triage, enhancing staff training and increasing the amount of translated information and access to interpreters.

"We are working with the national Maternity and Neonatal Intensive Support Team to ensure our services meet the standards women and families deserve."

Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:03:22 GMT

High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs.

It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lakes near Penrith, Cumbria, Pettigrews in Kelso, Scotland, Seaham in County Durham and Enfield, Greater London, though distribution operations would continue to run from the latter.

The proposals will also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will also continue as a distribution centre for the business.

The chain, which has headquarters in Newcastle, said its retail shops would not be affected by the proposed changes and like-for-like sales had grown across its managed stores.

It said the plans would save it about £20m across the 2028 and 2029 financial years.

The changes would take place over the next two and a half years, with parts of Greggs' manufacturing processes relocating, the firm said.

The range of products manufactured at its Clydesmill Glasgow and Manchester locations would be reduced and production of tinned bread at Gosforth would be stopped.

Some products would also be sourced from specialist suppliers.

The general secretary of the Bakers, Food and Allied Workers Union (BFAWU) Sarah Woolley said the union was "deeply concerned" about the announcement.

She said: "Our immediate priority is our members, their jobs, their families and the communities that could be affected by these proposals."

She added Greggs was clear in its own announcement the business continued to "perform strongly".

Greggs said positive trading and continued cost control means it expected a "modestly improved outcome" for 2026.

Like-for-like sales grew by 3.4% across its managed stores, with overall growth buoyed by the opening of new shops.

Woolley said Greggs' workers had played a "huge part" in getting the company where it is.

She said: "Against that backdrop, our members will understandably be asking why their jobs and livelihoods should now be put at risk in the name of efficiency and future progression."

But chief executive Roisin Currie said the company needed to "keep evolving alongside changing customer expectations".

She said: "Greggs manufacturing and logistics network remains a key strength of the business, and these proposals are intended to strengthen our manufacturing network, improve efficiency and ensure we remain well placed for the future while continuing to deliver the quality, value and service our customers expect."

The firm employs 33,000 people in the UK, the majority working in its stores.

A consultation with staff is expected to start soon and the company said "no final decisions" had been made yet.

Kelso and district councillor Euan Robson said the announcement regarding Pettigrews in the Scottish Borders had come as a "bit of a shock".

He said: "Greggs is a very good business and apparently doing well, but it will be a sad day if the factory does close because it's been here for a very long time.

"It's been a very valued business in the local community; it employs quite a number of people, and thoughts today are really with them because it's an uncertain future."

The shake-up is expected to cost the firm about £60m, including disruption costs and redundancy payments.

The retail business said its sales grew by 7.7% in the three months to September 26, compared with the same period a year earlier.

It said this represented progress in the face of "challenging market conditions", as consumer finances continued to come under pressure.

The company said positive trading and continued cost control meant it expected a "modestly improved outcome" for 2026.

Greggs opened 95 new shops and closed 38 in the year to date, taking its overall estate to 2,796 shops.

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 13:17:44 GMT

Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano (left) and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak have continued to insist that the club is innocent despite the guilty verdicts

The verdict that football fans around the world had been awaiting for years is in - Manchester City are guilty.

The club still insists it is innocent of the financial rule-breaking charges first brought against it by the Premier League in 2023, and can appeal, so the legal wrangling is far from over.

And the verdict has unleashed some huge questions for both the near and long-term future.

The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has said the independent commission's decision raises "serious issues".

BBC Sport has taken a look at the key questions in the case and what we know about each of them so far.

The deadline for Man City to make their appeal is Friday.

Precedent indicates that City's appeal will be considered and decided upon before punishments are declared.

Though that is not guaranteed. And a subsequent appeal against any sanctions could follow.

Exactly how long the process - which will be heard by a new three-person commission - will take is as yet unclear.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.

Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.

Man City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.

The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".

The phrasing may not offer any exact insight but the tone - of both the statement, and the strong language used in the independent commission's findings about the length of time the case has taken - is notable.

"It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision," the commission wrote. "That is regrettable."

It is clear that those in charge want the matter wrapped as quickly as can be done.

Erling Haaland's goals have powered Manchester City to the top of the Premier League, but whether they are truly in a title challenge is unclear until sanctions are known

And it is arguably to the benefit of both Manchester City and all of the other clubs in the Premier League and English Football League to know where they stand sooner rather than later.

City are top of the Premier League, having taken a maximum 15 points from their opening five matches, but whether they are genuinely in a title race will be unclear as long as players, fans, and club owners are in the dark about what their punishment will be.

Were the appeal and sanctions process to drag on beyond the end of the season, it would be possible that legal challenges could be brought by teams who finished below City in the table, or are relegated, or were knocked out by them in the domestic cups, which would be far less viable if the club's 'real' position is known before that point.

There are two key scenarios here.

The first is that one of the sanctions Manchester City are given is so significant a points deduction that they finish this season (or another future campaign, if the process takes longer) in the Premier League's bottom three and are automatically relegated to the Championship.

The second scenario is that they are expelled by the Premier League, which would require 15 of their rival clubs to vote in favour of a motion decreeing so.

Were that to happen, the club's future would be much less clear and would require them to apply to the Football Association for re-entry.

Because the EFL and National League are separate entities from the Premier League, neither would necessarily be obliged to accept an entry request from Manchester City.

And, even if a request were accepted by the EFL, its 72 clubs would have to vote whether or not to accept them.

That is where the possibility of City beginning a reascent in League Two - or potentially even lower - arises from.

There is a huge sporting and financial difference between dropping down to the Championship, with the high possibility of being promoted back to the Premier League after a single season, and starting again far lower down the pyramid.

When Juventus were relegated from Serie A to Serie B in Italy, after being found guilty of match-fixing charges in 2006, they were able to retain some of the world's best players, including Gianluigi Buffon, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet.

Players like Fabio Cannavaro, Patrick Vieira and Gianluca Zambrotta left Juventus after their enforced relegation, but Gianluigi Buffon stayed and captained the club to the title

They were willing to put up with a single season in a lower tier and, when the club returned to Serie A after winning the Serie B title, they immediately finished third and qualified for the Champions League.

If City faced only a single season outside the Premier League, players on long, lucrative contracts would likely be far more inclined to stay, and the economic damage of losing access to the top flight's TV rights income would be hugely reduced.

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson

The Fraud Act 2006 states that dishonestly making a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss can lead to individuals being imprisoned for 10 years and facing an unlimited fine, if charges are brought and proven.

"Surely the Man City findings are now a police matter," said Lord Cruddas, a banker and businessman.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled then it is potentially a criminal matter. The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

For the case to move from football wrongdoing to something more, there would first need to be an investigation by the relevant authorities.

The bodies who can investigate potential financial crimes in the UK include regional police forces, the National Crime Agency, HMRC and the Serious Fraud Office.

BBC Sport has contacted each of those bodies and been given no indication that any kind of investigation has begun, but some do not routinely confirm investigations owing to confidentiality.

Greater Manchester Police said: "No referral has been made by the relevant authorities in relation to any alleged criminal offences."

But former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein - who left the club five years before its current owners took control - raised the possibility during an interview on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"This is very serious and I wonder whether some of these issues might need to be referred to authorities outside of the league," Bernstein said.

"My immediate thoughts are - can the board of directors continue and should the people involved be suspended immediately?"

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire feels wider investigation may be unlikely.

"HMRC might consider it but there is not a lot for them to go on," he said. "There is certainly no corporation tax to recover. Football clubs lose money and City would have lost more money had it not been for the activities it undertook."

Fans and pundits have been making the point since news of Manchester City's guilt first broke - if they deliberately flounced the rules over the course of nine years, how can their owners possibly be trusted to run the club moving forward?

There is potentially a role to be played by the IFR, which was established in 2025 with the goals of protecting the heritage of English football, ensuring the financial soundness of clubs and promoting resilience in the ownership and spending of clubs.

The IFR awards licences to all 116 clubs in English football's top five tiers, which permits them to operate.

Club owners, directors and senior executives are subject to an enhanced suitability framework - a beefed-up version of the old-school 'fit-and-proper person's test'.

The Football Governance Act 2025 allows the IFR to suspend or revoke licences awarded to clubs as a last resort in cases of wrongdoing.

"The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals", IFR chairman David Kogan said in a statement.

"This includes taking account of findings made by the Leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.

"We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans."

And there is another possible scenario too - government intervention.

In 2022 Roman Abramovich was forced to sell Chelsea by the UK government, following the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Abramovich's background as an oligarch meant the government froze his assets and threatened to conduct a full seizure.

Within three months the club had new owners.

Abramovich had been in charge of Chelsea for almost two decades before he was forced to sell the club

The Manchester City owners are not subject to any action by the UK government, and all that has been formally declared is that the club broke football financial rules.

But the precedent exists that the government can be part of a process in which a football club owner is ousted.

Relations between the UK and UAE - whose royal family controls City's ownership group - were previously strong but have weakened to a degree in recent years.

Any form of ousting would prove a severe test of diplomacy.

Hidden habits that make your social anxiety worse - and how to break them

BBC News Wed, 30 Sep 2026 00:44:50 GMT

It was during her teenage years that Mary began to become anxious in social situations. It got so bad she developed depression and had to have time off school.

By the time she started university, she avoided group settings altogether.

"I didn't join clubs and societies like others did," says Mary (not her real name). "I just thought nobody would want to get to know me. I didn't really make a single friend during my whole degree."

Mary's social anxiety was so bad that she was diagnosed as having social anxiety disorder - something that affects up to 12% of people at some point in their lives.

But plenty more report struggling more generally. As students return to uni, we asked experts how to overcome these feelings whether in your first, or final year.

Research has suggested more than a fifth of university students face some kind of social anxiety during their studies – and it has been linked to lower grades, poorer relationships and isolation in a study by the University of Chichester.

For many, university marks the first time they have moved out of home – and the expectation is that they will quickly make friends.

Mary, who went to the University of Exeter, says she did try. "When I first got there I went to one society, but everybody was talking to each other and I had a sudden fear come over me. I felt I wouldn't fit in and I went home."

Mary, who is now 25, describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face and her hands would begin to tingle. "I'd almost feel myself separating from my body. I forgot how to form words," she says.

"After social situations I was often left with the sense that I'd done something awful. I had an all-consuming feel of shame. I kept thinking there was something fundamentally flawed in me."

Neil Greening, chair of the Social Anxiety Alliance UK, says this is a typical characteristic of people with social anxiety.

"People think they have a personality flaw. They internalise it rather than seeing it as a recognisable condition that they can get help for."

The key thing to remember: It's fairly normal to feel a little shy or anxious when meeting new people, being in new situations or going for a job interview. Social anxiety is when it actually stops people doing things, Greening says.

For those with a clinical diagnosis it can have a debilitating impact like it did for Mary.

"It can be hard to admit to any form of social anxiety in a world where extrovertism and social confidence is generally admired. Many people try to hide their social anxiety or use safety behaviours."

Signs someone may be socially anxious:

Greening says there is some evidence social anxiety is getting worse and that increased use of smartphones and remote working is contributing by "leading to less social interactions and increased levels of anxiety".

Mary, who has moved on to do a postgraduate course, is now managing her social anxiety better. After her undergraduate degree she got support from the NHS in the form of a talking therapy called CBT.

It is considered the gold standard treatment for social anxiety and encourages people to re-frame their thoughts and change their behaviours.

Prof David Clark, a psychologist at the University of Oxford, says he would like to see more people come forward for therapy but says people can also take steps to help themselves.

The first step, he says, is to stop obsessive self-focus. "People with social anxiety often monitor themselves constantly during social situations. Am I blushing? Do I sound stupid? Do I look nervous?

"Focus outwardly on the conversation, other person or your surroundings."

He says you also need to test your fears with behavioural experiments by asking a question in a meeting or saying something in a group and noticing what happens.

"People with social anxiety often assume negative outcomes – that they will embarrass themselves or think others will find them boring. Testing that can help people break that. It's frightening, but it can really help."

He also says they need to drop safety behaviours, such as rehearsing every sentence, avoiding eye contact or sticking close to one particular person.

And finally, Clark adds, try to avoid post-event rumination. "It's so easy to distort what actually happened."

This is something Mary can empathise with. "I used to play things over constantly in my mind. What I've learnt is that dealing with social anxiety is a gradual process. The therapy really helped me, but so did something a friend said to me a couple of years ago.

"When I said I didn't want to join her in meeting some of her friends, citing my poor social skills, she said she'd never thought that about me and that I shouldn't undersell myself. I was overcome with emotion.

"I'm now pushing myself to engage more. It helps that in my postgrad course we're in smaller groups, but I've also joined an astronomy group. It's still difficult and it doesn't always go how I want it to, but I'm learning to manage it."

A ‘unique opportunity’: is this the weirdest RightMove listing ever?

New Scientist September 30, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

There is a flourishing genre of content on YouTube and other video sites that can best be described as “gawping at real estate listings”. It can be beautiful, spacious houses that most of us can only dream of living in, or baroque explosions of horrific taste in interior decoration on par with whatever has happened to the White House lately.

So far, Feedback hasn’t been inclined to add to this content pile-up, but reporter Matthew Sparkes has lured us in with a listing on RightMove. It is for a building in Farnborough, England, on sale for £750,000. The listing has a link underneath the price that reads “Can you afford it?” Feedback didn’t click because we don’t need a website to tell us the answer.

Advertisement

The building is an upright white cylinder, with chunky extra bits on one side. The built area is about 1000 square metres. Feedback struggled to precisely count the rooms because the ground floor is partly open-plan, but there are at least 10 rooms on the ground floor and potentially around 20 on the floor above, though the top floor has a disappointingly scanty five.

Matt sarcastically described it as a “perfect family home”, and Feedback concurs with his sarcasm. Only a family whose members don’t enjoy each other’s company could use a building like this.

Readers wondering what this is doing in Feedback, wonder no longer. This building is the former Farnborough Centrifuge, which was used, starting in 1955, to train pilots to cope with the intense g-forces required for high-velocity flight and, later, space travel. The main cylindrical building houses the centrifuge, while the drive motor and bearings are in the basement. Helen Sharman, the first UK astronaut, used the centrifuge. No wonder the estate agents describe it as “a unique opportunity to purchase a piece of British aviation history”.

The Farnborough Centrifuge ceased operations in 2019, when a new and more modern centrifuge was built. It passed into the hands of a charity called the Farnborough Air Sciences Trust (FAST). However, in August 2024, FAST announced that it had been forced to close the centrifuge after the building’s owner asked for “a five-fold increase in rental payment”.

Two years later, it is up for sale. Does anyone have a spare £750,000 and fancy opening a museum? Feedback promises not to highlight it as unduly niche, because it actually sounds like somewhere we might go.

The ingenuity of the UK civil service truly knows no bounds. Not only can it outsource many of its functions to private companies, but it can also translate quantum phenomena into the macroscopic world.

How else to explain the sign spotted by reader Robert Milne outside the Twickenham job centre? It reads “Automated external defibrillator located inside”. Presumably the defibrillator is in superposition both inside and outside the building. Robert wonders if the same is now true of his job: “Am I now allowed to be both in full-time paid employment and on the dole at the same time?”

Feedback is further minded to inquire how much use the defibrillator is to cardiovascularly challenged members of the public during the many hours of the day when the job centre is closed and the defibrillator locked away.

We also want to know in what sense the defibrillator is “automated”. Does it have an internal AI and robotic arm, so it can snake out of its container and zap unwitting jobseekers?

Speaking of rogue AIs, readers may recall the actions of Anthropic’s Jacob Coxon, who on 9 September wrote: “I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.”

Feedback had a bit about this, but it was cut from a previous column because the editors said not enough people would get the reference. Feedback has reluctantly accepted the strong evidence, including book sales and talking to a normal person, that while many people have read J. R. R. Tolkien’s fantasy novels The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, far fewer have read his mythological epic The Silmarillion.

The Silmarillion is, we concede, pretty complicated. However, the essence is simple enough. There is a dark lord called Melkor. Melkor has a servant called Sauron, and they hang out in a fortress called Angband doing evil things. This includes creating the UrulÓki, more commonly known as dragons.

A lot of tech bros appear to have read this, although Feedback isn’t sure they have understood it fully. Famously, the surveillance company Palantir is named for the magical seeing-stones in The Lord of the Rings, a strong choice given that only two (speaking) characters make heavy use of the Palantir: one goes evil and the other sets himself on fire.

However, at least some readers of Tolkien do appear to have understood his works. Writing on Threads, a fan who goes simply by “bree” wrote the following, which seems to Feedback to cut to the heart of the matter: “I resigned from Angband today. I spent the last three centuries doing metaphysical research for both Sauron and Melkor. Neither dark lord is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to wingèd UrulÓki and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.”

Got a story for Feedback?

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist. com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.

Benjamin Labatut has written an utterly haunting novella about science

New Scientist September 30, 2026

There are two ends of science. At one end is a great lumbering machine where equations and numbers are fed in, and bullets, nerve gas and nuclear warheads come out. At the other end is an undeniable truth about the universe and our place within it.

Benjamín Labatut thinks we should be terrified of both.

When We Cease to Understand the World is a novella that explores what happens when science unravels its own core conceit: that we can understand reality. It combines the Lovecraftian terror of descending into the abyss of scientific truth and finding something utterly alien staring back with the absurd, Kurt Vonnegut-like possibility that the descent reveals nothing to hold onto at all – no meaning, no structure and no purpose.

Advertisement

The best new science-fiction books of September 2026

There could hardly be a better stage for Labatut’s masterpiece, translated by Adrian Nathan West, than the eerie calm that enveloped the planet after its two world wars. For decades, humans had tried to outcompete each other to come up with new and interesting brutalities they could inflict upon one another – with gas, with metal, with radiation. But for Labatut, science wreaks a different kind of violence. The huge revolutions in our understanding of space-time and the quantum world destabilise the logic with which we make sense of our brief lives.

Labatut’s characters are all real mathematicians and scientists. From Fritz Haber – the father of fertilisers and modern chemical warfare – to Werner Heisenberg, who pioneers quantum mechanics by abandoning ordinary human experience, the book weaves its plot across these biographical vignettes.

Again and again, Labatut returns to people who push discovery so far that it can only become dangerous to them. And the picture he paints is ghastly: science will bring people to the point of real enlightenment, but that enlightenment is something profoundly anti-human.

Quantum mechanics supplies his richest material. The theory does more than replace a clockwork universe with one governed by probabilities. In its more unsettling interpretations, it seems to deny any ordinary picture of what’s happening underneath our measurements. Quantum theory appears to suggest that physicists might instead be relegated to magicians: able to summon astonishing predictions from an arcane formalism while never quite grasping what, if anything, is really taking place underneath.

Labatut takes impressively few liberties with discussions of chemistry, mathematics, quantum mechanics and the “singularities” of general relativity. The book’s depth and rigour make it completely convincing to even the most seasoned physics enthusiast. He has done his research so well that fact and fiction become difficult to distinguish.

I know, for instance, that the mathematical visionary Alexander Grothendieck – one of Labatut’s key characters – revolutionised algebraic geometry before becoming a recluse. I don’t know whether his hermetic life was provoked when he glimpsed the “heart of the heart”, the object lying at the deepest centre of mathematics. Labatut imagines this revelation as something like confronting a beautiful, horrifying, many-eyed angel.

This book will haunt you.

Moonfish, a haunting animation, captures a tragedy in space

New Scientist September 30, 2026

FilmMoonfishDaniel Zvereff, Pending release

In the song Space Oddity, David Bowie’s Major Tom drifts beyond the reach of Ground Control, poised between tech and terror. The protagonist in Daniel Zvereff’s animation, Moonfish, occupies a similarly lonely orbit, but one that demolishes the fantasy of space travel, instead depicting work, radiation, quotas and the slow psychological erosion of being almost alone.

Cassius (Morgan Spector), a deep-space miner, is travelling with his companion Vesper (Lucy Liu) to an asteroid. Work is brutal: meet extraction quotas to earn passage home or stay, stranded. When Vesper dies in an accident, Cassius must complete the mission alone, with only her goldfish and the unreliable contents of his mind for company.

Advertisement

Moonfish premiered at the Venice Biennale last month, and cost a mere €200,000 to make. Zvereff turns that constraint into an aesthetic: drawing in stark black and white, building from simple lines, using a boxy frame and sparse environments that make Cassius’s universe feel both enormous and suffocating. What might have looked unfinished is the right visual language to express alienation, a man reduced to a few fragile marks against a void.

The scientific details of this world are left speculative; science ends up functioning as pressure. So, Cassius’s body is another system to fail before the machinery does – prolonged exposure to radiation in space has consequences requiring medication to function. Asteroid mining isn’t heroic exploration, but rather the economic logic of using vulnerable workers when tech costs more. This is one of the film’s bleakest tropes – and one of its most plausible.

But its most compelling element is the bond Cassius develops with the fish, which, as grief and isolation set in, speaks in Vesper’s voice. The exchanges become the film’s philosophical core, touching on consciousness, memory, mortality and what distinguishes life from non-life. This could have tipped into whimsy, but Liu endows the fish with an eerie tenderness, while Spector makes Cassius’s exhaustion feel physical.

Moonfish is ultimately less interested in whether humans mine asteroids than in who might, and under what terms. Its space setting amplifies existing concerns on Earth: precarious labour, dependence on tech, loneliness and the monetisation of endurance. Like Major Tom, Cassius drifts further from the systems supposed to keep him connected. The difference is that this Ground Control isn’t merely distant; it is his employer.

Davide Abbatescianni is a film critic based in Rome

Our verdict on Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s The Edge of Space-Time: a wild ride

New Scientist September 30, 2026

The New Scientist Book Club has been testing its collective brain power in September with Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s The Edge of Space-Time. Subtitled “particles, poetry and the cosmic dream boogie”, this sees the New Scientist columnist and theoretical physicist set out to explain our universe, from the quantum to the inner workings of black holes.

That’s a lot to get through, but as Chanda writes in her book, it is worth the effort: “We should bother with physics because it is, in part, how we as a species learn to use our minds.” She went further in an exclusive essay for book club members, challenging us to get to grips with the quantum nature of space-time. “Spending time with what feels strange about physics can help prepare us to better reckon with difficult political questions,” she wrote. “Given the crises we face – genocides, climate change, attacks on transgender people – we need our critical faculties now more than ever.”

Starting with a careful deconstruction of why we need to think hard about the metaphors we use in science writing to make sure they are helping rather than hindering readers in understanding non-intuitive concepts in science, Chanda goes on to take us through some of the most abstract areas of theoretical physics. It is, as member Dee55 put it, a “wild ride”, in terms of both the physics and the in-depth conversation that members have been having about the book over on our Discord channel.

Advertisement

I really enjoyed this book. I am someone who didn’t manage to finish Stephen Hawking’s A Brief History of Time, but who, thanks to Chanda’s friendly, encouraging and (most importantly) clear writing, emerged at the end of this book a little more knowledgeable about physics. I liked how Chanda slipped in multiple references to literature and popular culture to help make her points, as well as how she told us firmly: “This is supposed to be fun, and there is no test at the end.” She reiterated this in our interview: “[Part] of welcoming people into the material is saying, this isn’t something that only… a lone genius can think about. You’re entitled to this as well. This is your universe, too.”

Many book club members were similarly enamoured. “One of the earliest statements in this book which blew me away (there have been many) was ‘Humanity has only been aware of this cosmic light[from the beginnings of the universe]for sixty-two years’,” wrote Melissa on Discord. “Just the incomprehensible fact of cosmic light from the unimaginable ancientness of the beginning of the universe—which is just there but people have only found out about it in the space of less than one human lifetime ago.”

Jodie has been “enjoying it a lot, even if it does make my head ache at times!” – I think that’s fair, Jodie! – while Dee55 has also found Chanda’s explanations mind-expanding: “For years I have been making periodic attempts to understand Quantum Stuff and always come away fairly befuddled but also intrigued – and this time feels just a little different, as if I am not exactly grasping something but perhaps catching fleeting glimpses of it (we don’t get far without metaphors, I find).”

“The wonderful gift this book gives us is the opportunity to spend time in practicing feeling unsettled, sometimes even bewildered, as we experience the strangeness of quantum physics,” added Laura Akers. “It’s several hours, in my case over many days, of practicing the acceptance that science and reality are strange, bizarre… rather than simple and reassuring – and it’s really okay.”

Free newsletter

“I’ve really enjoyed The Edge of Space-time,” wrote DavidCl on Discord. “About half way through I realised what my perspective of reading it was like. It’s like sitting down and spending time with a good friend who is way cleverer and more intelligent than I am while she tries to explain what it is she does, why she does it and what drives her onwards.”

This book is packed with literary allusions, and with Chanda’s strongly expressed political perspectives – not everyone appreciated this. “I am not really enjoying this book, to be honest. I prefer straightforward scientific information and explanations,” wrote Lowenna, while Katita2026 found that Chanda’s politics and her subjective takes intruded on the physics a little too much. “Dr. Prescod-Weinstein is an incredible storyteller. I absolutely love how she brings the cold, intimidating world of astrophysics right down to earth. Explaining cosmic inflation through a TR-808 drum machine, or bringing Missy Elliott and Wu-Tang Clan into a physics book, is just brilliant science communication,” wrote Katita. But “as much as I’m enjoying the read, I find myself struggling when she tries to make the physics fit her politics”.

Chanda Prescod-Weinstein’s new book is a mind-expanding trip to space-time

This was a question picked over with great sensitivity by book club members. “I do agree that some of the connections are bit forced, but I think the author is trying to show not only how physics says that the universe is, but also how she from a particular background visualises that,” wrote Alan_P. “We all bring our own experiences and backgrounds to any field of knowledge and view things through that prism – she’s just giving us her prism. She many times explains the sheer wonder and joy that she experiences as a physicist, and that this is finding out about an objective reality.” DavidCl felt similarly: “The explanations are peppered with her personal viewpoints and politics but that’s ok because her passion and occasionally sweary outbursts are all part of painting a compelling picture.”

All in all, I think this was a (challenging) hit with book club members – on to the next one.

Unsettling images reveal stark impact of humans on the environment

New Scientist September 30, 2026

Do you have any idea what you’re looking at in the image above? It might look completely abstract at first glance, but this is, in fact, an aerial photo. The white cobwebby-looking bits are bubbles, the green is algae and the straight lines are the edges of tanks.

This is the Kasslerfeld sewage-treatment plant in Duisburg, Germany, next to the Rhine river, which treats wastewater from nearby businesses and homes.

“This is part of my series which illustrates environmental damage in a creative way to engage viewers,” says photographer and environmental activist J Henry Fair.

Advertisement

While wastewater plants help minimise human impact on rivers, Fair points out that they don’t remove all pollutants. For instance, they don’t filter out all microplastics. We all have microplastics in our bodies, Fair says, but the ramifications of that are not understood.

Fair has been using small aircraft to document the impact of human activity on the landscape, with the aerial view often revealing much that can’t be seen from the ground. The photograph above is one from a new exhibition at the Bruce Museum in Greenwich, Connecticut, A Great Breach in Nature: Aerial photography by J Henry Fair.

“I first photographed it in passing, then the curators became excited about it, so I went back to reshoot it. But then could not find it. So we flew all around Duisburg, and finally saw it as we were giving up the search,” said Fair.

Waste features in many of Fair’s photographs. The strange red landscape in the image below is made of the toxic mud left after aluminium is refined from bauxite in Gramercy, Louisiana. The two lines are vehicle tracks. The waste contains heavy metals such as lead and mercury, among other things.

Another alien-looking landscape in the image below is actually the waste treatment at a pulp mill in Ticonderoga, New York state. Trout in nearby Lake Chamberlain still have dangerous levels of dioxins as a result of historical pollution from factories including the original paper mill at Ticonderoga.

What looks like blood in the shot below is actually molten sulphur being added to large piles of solid yellow sulphur in Fort McMurray, Canada. The sulphur is a byproduct of the tar sands refining process and is stored on-site because there is little demand for it. Fair points out that the petrol (gasoline) made from tar sands results in much higher carbon emissions than that made from oil.

And does the image below show a peaceful Zen garden? No. This is actually earth from a lignite mine in Grefath, Germany. The earth is removed to reveal the lignite – a particularly dirty form of coal – around 100 metres down, and then transferred to areas where the coal has already been stripped.

Fair’s exhibition at the Bruce Museum runs until 7 February.

Why a modern approach to healthcare must consider more than illness

New Scientist September 30, 2026

When antidepressants were created nearly 40 years ago, they were expected to be a breakthrough in treating mental illness. Instead, rates of depression have kept rising. Why? Perhaps because we are missing the bigger picture.

There is tremendous evidence that lifestyle changes can treat depression. Exercise is effective, and dietary changes can be just as valuable as the most evidence-backed therapy. As psychologist Kimberley Wilson shows, proper nutrition makes it easier for people to control their emotions, and eating omega-3 is linked with a reduced risk of depression and suicidal ideation.

The antidepressant-backed mental health model was intended to be rigorous, mimicking methods in physical healthcare. But it was also political, with US mental health researchers receiving less funding to explore the social factors around mental health under President Richard Nixon. Decades on, practitioners like Wilson are finally challenging this approach and, this time, physical health can learn from holistic mental healthcare.

Advertisement

We need to engage with our whole body and mind to be well, not just rely on drugs

Indeed, nearly every aspect of health benefits hugely from engaging with lifestyle and community. Instead of seeing health problems as something to be fixed with drugs, we need to engage with our whole body and mind to be well.

That isn’t to say medication can’t play a role. GLP-1s are just a recent example of a medication that has had a dramatic impact in helping people grapple with diabetes and cardiovascular health, as well as depression and low self-esteem. Children are also increasingly being prescribed GLP-1s. But even cutting-edge medical research now recognises that our understanding of health needs to be less fragmented. Researchers are increasingly aware of the gut-brain axis, the heart-brain axis and other interconnected systems that affect our health.

No one cell, organ or person becomes ill in isolation. The more we start to understand our health as a reflection of our whole being, community and society, the healthier we will be.

Why do we have hair – on our heads and elsewhere? A new book explores

New Scientist September 30, 2026

Anxious and HairyJudy Wearing, Icon Books

Pick up Judy Wearing’s Anxious and Hairy, and you might well wonder at its length: how did she possibly fill 300 pages with… hair? It is a credit to her diligent research, infectious curiosity and personable voice that, on finishing this exhaustive exploration into what the subtitle calls the “evolution and culture of human hair”, I was struck by how much I’d taken for granted.

From the start, Wearing sets out to win over readers who might be sceptical, taking on the broad (and, arguably, often sexist) sidelining of hair to reveal a “biological wonder” touching “on virtually every aspect of humanity”. Her own fascination dates back to her postgraduate studies at the University of Oxford, and Anxious and Hairy builds on her research into mating behaviour, especially “adaptive benefits of human hair patches”.

Advertisement

Why did we evolve to have tufts in some places, but not others? Even now, research remains limited. As Wearing points out: “Oddly, humans have paid more attention to the traits involved in the mating of mites and birds than the plumage of our own species.”

The earliest fossil evidence of hair, she writes, dates back about 245 million years to cynodonts: warm-blooded, reptilian and the ancestors of mammals. They developed fur for insulation, but some hair follicles continued to evolve to produce milk and body odour. Homo sapiens shed their fur coats over time, but not as decisively as it seemed. The so-called naked ape, in fact, has the same number of follicles as our primate relatives, everywhere except on the soles of our feet and palms of our hands; but they produce mostly thin, fine “vellus” hairs.

The thicker, more mature hairs evolved, through sexual selection, to grow in specific locations for highly varied purposes. The hair on our head helps to regulate temperature while also offering sun protection, explaining the diversity in density, colour and curl. Curly hair, for example, blocks more solar radiation while keeping the head cooler. In men, this balance also involves facial hair, with Wearing exploring the links between bushy beards – which would have dissuaded sexual rivals – and balding.

At Oxford, Wearing ‘ambushed’ her peers with requests for samples from their ‘interesting bits’

The science behind our other furry patches is more speculative. Underarm hair might have evolved to broadcast our particular chemical blends, aiding social communication and helping to attract genetically suitable mates, she writes. As for pubic hair, Wearing’s preferred hypothesis is that it evolved as a “cheating detector”, trapping fluids and odour, informing mate choice and communicating about sexual activity, though she stresses this is untested.

Even with all the unknowns, Wearing’s evolutionary lens makes hair unexpectedly interesting. Culture adds an equally dense layer – and accounts for the titular “anxious”. Having too much hair in the wrong places, or not enough in the right ones, is associated with depression, anxiety and lower quality of life.

Hair styling has been a form of self-expression since the earliest societies, and across the classes. Rameses II, one of ancient Egypt’s most renowned pharaohs, used henna to hide greys. And the remains of a woman buried in the 14th century BC showed evidence of 70 coloured extensions.

Even deciding to wear hair up or down is socially mediated, and often political. Women’s flowing tresses convey feminine sexuality but may be covered, bound or shorn as a means of control. Hair has also literally been a matter of life and death, writes Wearing. Natural variations, a function of genetics and geography, were used to justify racialised prejudice, abuse and enslavement. Hair texture, an official classification criteria in apartheid South Africa, determined rights and freedoms.

Anxious and Hairy reflects Wearing’s careful, wide-ranging research, but the narrative is powered by her enthusiasm for hair and on-the-ground reporting. At Oxford, she made a name for herself, “ambushing” her peers with requests for samples from their “interesting bits”. Later, her quest takes her from a high-end Paris salon to Detroit for a beard and mustache convention.

She discovers that what is signified by our “patches of hair” continues to evolve. Botox, which limits eyebrow movement, may affect our ability to communicate and empathise. Overall, Wearing more than delivers on her promise to transform how we see hair.

Elle Hunt is a writer based in Norwich, UK
