Moa Point disaster: Greater Wellington lays charges against city council and Tiaki Wai

New Zealand Herald September 30, 2026

The Moa Point Wastewater Treatment Plant suffered a catastrophic failure in February where more than 14 billion litres of untreated sewage pumped into the sea off Wellington’s south coast. Photo / Supplied

Greater Wellington Regional Council has laid criminal charges against the city council and Tiaki Wai, formerly Wellington Water, over failures at Moa Point – with each facing potential $100 million fines.

In February, the Moa Point Wastewater Treatment Plant suffered a catastrophic failure where more than 14 billion litres of untreated sewage pumped into the sea off Wellington’s south coast.

Multiple reports have been released since, including a Crown Review which highlighted years of systemic and governance failures across organisations including Wellington Water and Wellington City Council.

Greater Wellington Regional Council has now filed charges under the Resource Management Act against the two organisations for alleged unlawful wastewater discharges.

The two entities face 10 charges each, and if convicted could face maximum fines of $10m per charge.

The charges cover two periods of alleged offending – between October 2025 and January 2026 and from the failure of the treatment plant in early February 2026 through to subsequent discharges connected to that failure.

Five charges cover unlawful discharges from the plant and five relate to alleged breaches of an abatement notice.

In a statement, Wellington City Council said that it “anticipated this was likely” due to the regional council’s responsibility as an independent regulatory body.

A spokesman said the city council will continue to co-operate and engage with the regional council throughout the court process.

Tiaki Wai chief executive Michael Brewster said that it was notified of the charges and acknowledged impact on the environment and mana whenua, as well as the community and local businesses.

“We remain resolutely focused on recovering the plant as quickly as possible.”

Moa Point is scheduled to be fully operational again by next February.

Grace Symmans is Wellington-based reporter who covers news in the capital. Grace joined NZME in 2025 as a producer for Wellington Mornings on Newstalk ZB.. She can be emailed at grace. symmans@nzme. co. nz.

All Blacks coach Dave Rennie says Springboks will play tests in Auckland and Christchurch in 2027

New Zealand Herald September 30, 2026

The All Blacks will host South Africa for two tests in 2027, according to coach Dave Rennie. Photo / Photosport

The All Blacks will host the Springboks in tests in Auckland and Christchurch next year before a potential quarter-final clash at the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia, according to head coach Dave Rennie.

Speaking to Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast this morning, Rennie let slip that a two-test series was scheduled for July.

Asked about the potential World Cup quarter-final showdown in just over 12 months’ time, Rennie revealed that they would meet twice before the World Cup.

“We play each other twice in July as well, straight after the Super Rugby final, like two weeks after that final. We play them again in Auckland and Christchurch,” Rennie said.

The fixtures are yet to be announced by New Zealand Rugby – and yet to be confirmed following a request from the Herald.

It would be the first time the Springboks have played at One NZ Stadium and their first test in Christchurch since 2016.

The Springboks beat the All Blacks 3-1 in the recently completed test series dubbed “Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry”.

“We’re going to play them a lot leading into the World Cup and I think their side may look a tad different, but I think the nucleus will be the same and how they play the game, I think it’ll still be pretty similar,” Rennie said.

“And likely to meet in a quarter-final if both teams won their pool, which is odd, but the way it is.”

The All Blacks played France in their first-ever fixture at Christchurch’s new covered stadium, which was a sell-out of 30,000 fans, in July.

One NZ Stadium also hosted the Warriors in a regular season NRL game this year.

Venues Ōtautahi, which runs the stadium, also said last month that tennis, ice hockey and even UFC could be coming to the city.

Chief executive Caroline Harvie-Teare said the stadium’s roof and infrastructure give it the flexibility to operate more like a large indoor arena.

“The likes of tennis, boxing, UFC, basketball, ice hockey, even eSports. All of those sporting genres are in the mix, which is really cool because not often can you have those types of events in a stadium,” she said.

The FIM World Supercross Championship is already confirmed for December, with competitors set to race on a track built inside the venue a week after British popstar Robbie Williams performs.

Labour wants to strengthen consumer protections with new rules the party believes will stop New Zealanders being hit by “hidden fees”.

These new rules include banning “junk” car insurance, like paint insurance or mechanical breakdown cover “that excludes almost everything”.

Retailers would be prohibited from “putting pressure on customers” to buy insurance or extended warranties at the checkout for new products, like whiteware and electronics. These would instead have to be “sold the following day or over the phone”.

If products are purchased on credit, retailers would be required to show the total cost over the life of the agreement before customers sign up.

Labour also wants to make it easier for people to cancel subscriptions, with online cancellations for services. It says “unclear automatic renewals, unfair exit fees, and excessive notice periods” would be banned.

This would also be the case for gym subscriptions, with Labour saying cancelling should be as easy as joining. Inflated penalty charges, such as for lost key tags, wouldn’t be allowed.

When New Zealanders purchase tickets for an event, the seller would be required to include all unavoidable booking, processing and other fees in the advertised price. Other mandatory charges could not be added on as the buyer goes through the checkout process.

Labour says it would implement these changes and more through a “Fair Go Law” that it believes would “stop businesses making money by tricking their customers”.

“People aren’t asking for much. Just tell them the real price upfront and make it as easy to leave a subscription or membership as it was to join,” said Labour’s commerce and consumer affairs spokeswoman Arena Williams.

“And those extended warranties? In many cases, what they cover is already your right under the Consumer Guarantees Act.”

Party leader Chris Hipkins said that, with the cost of living impacting Kiwis, Labour would put a stop to “hidden fees” people never see coming.

Election 2026: Act candidate Antonia Modkova heckled over te Tiriti comments at Auckland Central debate

New Zealand Herald September 30, 2026

Chlöe Swarbrick is the incumbent Auckland Central MP. Photo / Jamie Ensor

Act candidate Antonia Modkova faced repeated heckling over her answers at an Auckland Central candidates’ debate on Karangahape Rd, including during a heated exchange over te Tiriti o Waitangi which an audience member claimed was “racist bulls***”.

St Kevin’s Arcade basement venue Double Whammy had turned down the tunes for just over an hour last night to fill its stage with politicians for an animated debate on issues affecting the precinct and wider central city.

When an audience member asked candidates how their parties planned to honour te Tiriti, Labour’s Naisi Chen said her party backed restoring it to the school curriculum and retaining the Waitangi Tribunal, which both Act and New Zealand First have proposed to abolish.

Greens co-leader Chloe Swarbrick, also the electorate’s incumbent MP, criticised the Westminster parliamentary system’s perceived ineffectiveness and instead called for “constitutional transformation” with te Tiriti at its centre.

Modkova said Act was proud of how New Zealand “has redressed the wrongs of the past” through land settlements, but opposed continuing forward “with two sets of people having two sets of rights, based on when their ancestors arrived”.

“That’s racist bulls***,” an audience member shouted in response.

Swarbrick then jested: “Act Party said land back!”

Opportunity candidate Johan Chang said, in his view, New Zealand was technically in a legally “binding, contractual agreement” between the Crown and Māori under te Tiriti, and that constitutional reform needed both parties at the table.

“We pretend that we’re an independent country, but technically, by definition, we’re all British subjects,” he said.

“If we are to do, let’s say constitutional reform, it should not be a government-led exercise, because if it’s led by a party that got in at 8%, I think that’s pretty much the definition of authoritarianism.”

Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party candidate Christopher Manaia eased the tension with some humour before echoing the need for a two-party negotiation and supporting Māori self-governance.

The spat was the sharpest moment in a night otherwise heavily focused on the immediate problems facing central Auckland, including homelessness, housing and the survival of small businesses following years of disruption from the City Rail Link (CRL).

Modkova agreed with Labour that Auckland needs more homes, but not on “how we’re going to get there”, pointing to consenting and the recent Resource Management Act reform as key to increasing supply.

“Developers don’t want to build low-cost housing,” another audience member interjected.

“It’s not profitable.”

Swarbrick believed emergency housing was necessary but not sufficient, saying the state dually needed to build a pipeline of transitional and permanent housing.

There was more agreement on the need for a night shelter in central Auckland, with all five candidates backing one’s establishment.

All five also supported having more police on the beat.

The debate then turned to the future of K Rd’s small businesses, with one person asking how each party aimed to “raise the profile of all businesses rather than just the glamorous ones”.

Swarbrick pointed to the CRL hardship fund and the Greens’ proposal to change commercial rental rules and fill vacant storefronts, adding current tenants need an economy that allows them to “prosper and become more vibrant”.

Modkova focused on reducing regulatory barriers, while Chen proposed measures like lifting rebate thresholds and ensuring greater access to government procurement for small businesses.

Chang focused on reducing electricity costs, improving financial capability and addressing merchant surcharges, which he said couldn’t just fall back onto businesses themselves if banned.

Notably, National candidate Candace Kinser was absent from the debate, with a statement read on her behalf saying she was visiting Aotea Great Barrier for a prior commitment.

New Zealand First has not announced a candidate for Auckland Central, while Te Pāti Māori is pursuing a strategic “candidate vote only” campaign to take back all seven Māori seats.

New Zealand Herald September 30, 2026

Media personality Ganesh Raj is on a mission to help Kiwis put dinner on the table without it costing an arm and a leg.

It’s a passion that has seen Raj co-host TVNZ’s Eat Well for Less since the programme’s launch in 2020.

The restaurateur and food educator spoke to Real Life with John Cowan on Newstalk ZB on Sunday night about the show’s new season, what drives his love of cooking, and the journey that brought him to New Zealand.

Raj describes growing up in a Singapore that might be unrecognisable to many today. It was one with smaller villages, before it was transformed by mass development, where Raj and his friends could ride their BMX bikes around the island.

His love of food came at an early age. Raj was an only child, raised by a single mother, and he fondly remembers their time in the kitchen.

“She’d come home and be in the kitchen between four and six, and if I wanted her attention, that’s where I had to go,” he said.

“While she was cooking, I’d do these assessment sheets she’d put in front of me. All I had to do was finish the sheet, and then I could go and play football.”

He doesn’t remember studying much at school, but credits his mother’s emphasis on homework with giving him what he needed to become the school dux. From there, he went on to the prestigious Raffles Institution, one of the country’s oldest schools.

Raj told Cowan his upbringing and Indian heritage have given him a unique perspective on cooking.

“I have this global view of food, and I come from a part of the world where the street vendor is God. Street food is more delicious than anything else … the street vendor or grandma had a greater standing than any white-suited, white-hatted person,” he said.

Raj began working in television at 19, when Asia was experiencing a “golden period”.

However, after meeting his wife and deciding they wanted children, Singapore no longer felt right for them. He said a large proportion of families relied on maids, and that was not what he wanted.

“A lot of people have to work two jobs, both parents working to ‘keep up with the Joneses’ and pay for the cost of living, so maids raise children. I saw the effects … and it frightened me.”

His wife, who also works in television, was working on a Discovery Channel documentary called Kiwi Spirit when she floated the idea of moving to New Zealand.

Raj “loved rugby to death”, so they decided to go for it.

After making the move, they both worked in production before opening The Tasting Shed in Kumeū, which became a popular dining destination.

“The reason I think the restaurant did so well was … I understood how to put ingredients together on a plate to make them delicious, regardless of where they came from. No country of origin required.”

It wasn’t long before his friends working in television saw the potential in bringing together his cooking success and entertainment experience.

The producers of Eat Well for Less invited him to come into the studio for a day, and the rest is history.

Raj finds purpose in his television work, and believes the country needs the show.

“That’s why we’re on air, and it’s not for the right reasons. It’s because things are expensive. The cost of living is just out of control, and people need help.”

Raj says there are key issues making the situation worse, the first being the widespread effect of social media promoting ultra-processed products that claim to be healthy.

He gave examples such as the current “obsession with protein”.

“Nothing wrong with wanting to put as much protein in your body as possible, but marketers have found they can insert their products into this space, which will cause you to buy a one-kilo packet of something that’s $65 that apparently has nine things you have to have in it,” he explained to Cowan.

Raj also believes there is a lack of food education in New Zealand.

“We’re starting to see the effects now, where people are only used to two or three types of protein. That’s all they know what to do with, and there are one or two recipes in their toolkit.”

“Remember when mince went up, and everyone lost their mind? There are another 47 meat products in the supermarket that are much cheaper, but people aren’t so good at turning those into cheap dishes they can actually work on.”

Raj said his mission is to teach people how to cook for four people, using one pan, for under $20.

“I’m trying to show people it’s not the equipment. It’s knowledge. Knowing what to do will get you ahead, not how much gear you have.”

A new season of Eat Well for Less is out now, with episodes releasing weekly on TVNZ.

Real Life is a weekly interview show where John Cowan speaks with prominent guests about their life, upbringing, and the way they see the world. Tune in on Sundays from 7.30pm on Newstalk ZB or listen to the latest full interview here.

An Israeli official told Aviation Herald that the Kiwi was one of two off-duty pilots on the Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight who helped land the plane after the cockpit fight. The other was said to be of South African descent.

A Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson told the Herald its embassies in the region were responding to the incident.

“All passengers are reported safe and accounted for.

“We are aware of reports that a New Zealand citizen was among the 174 people on board, however we do not yet have formal confirmation of that.

Cabin crew, off-duty pilots and passengers managed to get through the cockpit door and overcome the knifeman, who was pinned against the floor, the website reported.

Passenger, Almog Itali, said in a video posted by the BBC that two relief pilots were on board, who were meant to fly the next flight.

The craft, with 174 passengers onboard, landed in Saudi Arabia.

Jerusalem Post reported a passenger claimed Israeli citizens “rushed to the cockpit and fought the attacker” while the plane was plummeting.

Gisborne rural rubbish sticker prices to rise for first time in six years despite public opposition

New Zealand Herald September 30, 2026

Councillor Rob Telfer said the existing charges were “1950s prices”. Photo / Imogen Brophy

It’s about to get more expensive to have your rubbish collected if you live in rural Gisborne, despite two-thirds of submitters opposing the change.

Residents face a 25% price increase on rural rubbish stickers after Gisborne District Council voted to increase their cost for the first time in six years, citing inflation and rising management costs.

The price of rural blue stickers will change from $2.80 to $3.50 for a 5kg bag, and rural pink stickers from $10 to $12.50 for about 0.5 cubic metres of waste, starting on November 11.

According to a report presented at Wednesday’s meeting, unchanged prices would result in a $1.6 million shortfall in recovering the cost of services at rural transfer stations.

Council staff operate the nine rural transfer stations and transport waste to Gisborne, where it is managed by an external contractor.

The price increase was expected to generate $6000 in additional revenue.

The proposal went to public consultation in June, after council fees, charges and rates changes this year.

Of the 77 submissions received, 66% opposed the increase, while 8% supported it outright.

About 22 submissions raised concerns about increased illegal dumping if prices rose.

Deputy Mayor Aubrey Ria moved an option to keep prices unchanged, saying councillors had already approved rates increases.

“After setting fees and charges, I feel like it’s moving the goalposts. After putting the rates up, it’s again moving the goalposts for a huge part of our rohe.

“And so that is at the heart of why I don’t want to impose another fine on any part of our community.”

She questioned why the decision was not being considered alongside work on the Waste Minimisation and Management Plan (WMMP) and the Long Term Plan, which would provide a broader view of the waste management system.

Council staff were working to identify further efficiencies across the waste management system as part of the WMMP, Knight said.

The increase was an interim measure to help reduce the shortfall before wider changes could be introduced.

Ria further criticised the move, saying she acknowledged concerns about increased fly-tipping, which would cause strain on staff and attract wild animals.

Councillor Anne Huriwai seconded Ria’s motion and questioned the purpose of public consultation if the decision goes against consultation results.

Councillor Rob Telfer moved a motion to increase prices, saying the existing charges were “1950s prices”.

“This is a classic example of a service that’s not paying its way. When a service is not paying its way, someone else is subsidising it.”

The council had hard decisions ahead in the Long Term Plan, but failing to make smaller savings now could mean larger cuts elsewhere, Telfer said.

“If people are really worried about it, they could dump and recycle a whole lot of stuff that’s actually going into the rubbish bags.”

Councillor Larry Foster agreed, and said households already received 52 stickers a year through their rates.

“The $2 extra is on the extra stickers that you buy after that; if you manage your waste enough, you shouldn’t need extra stickers.

He said the 70c increase for blue stickers was minimal and encouraged residents to manage their waste better. Councillor Rhonda Tibble said neither option adequately addressed the shortfall.

Telfer’s motion to increase prices was carried, with Ria and Huriwai voting against it. Tibble abstained.

Can’t afford to buy a house in Tuscany? These TV shows will let you dream about it

Sydney Morning Herald October 01, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Most reality shows rely on jeopardy or some kind of life-changing quest. They feature lucky contestants hoping to be recognised for their cooking or singing talents. Or average folk renovating a home or searching for a soulmate. The higher the stakes, the more relatable the challenge, the better.

But a spate of recent shows have upped the ante on a stalwart TV genre: the home renovation. They’ve set their sights on something more ambitious than plumping the cushions or installing the latest must-have kitchen gadget.

What if you could up sticks, leave the nine-to-five grind behind and start a new life on the other side of the world? Say, in a hilltop town in Tuscany; in a fairytale-worthy chateau in France; bottling your own wine in Spain; capping off a day on the tools with an Aperol spritz on a beach in Sicily?

Producers are always looking for a good hook and a bargain. So when a number of European nations introduced “one Euro schemes” several years ago, TV-makers were quick to see the possibilities.

These schemes, which have been flooded with interest, allow non-residents to purchase rundown and abandoned houses in remote villages that are at risk of becoming ghost towns. For a token sum, the houses can be purchased on the condition that they are renovated, to be used by foreigners looking for a life change, a holiday house or the chance to turn a tidy profit when the house is flipped.

Admittedly, the appealing proposition masks some sobering facts. Across Europe, traditional villages are dying because of declining birthrates and ageing populations, inheritance laws, poverty, unemployment and industrialisation.

The TV shows these initiatives have spawned don’t make too much mention of this. But as armchair adventures go, they have an irresistible appeal.

The Block judges Shaynna Blaze and Darren Palmer are getting their hands dirty. Blaze has purchased a €1 home, sight unseen, in a remote village in Sicily and enlisted Palmer to help make it habitable.

It begins with a small, abandoned stone terrace in Castronovo, a hilltop village with a population of 2800. With a budget of €210,000 ($342,000), they set to work with an ex-pat British builder (who also appears in Amanda and Alan’s Italian Job). A can-do spirit pervades this show, which doesn’t sugar-coat what’s in store for the intrepid and aspirational €1 renovator and sees the presenters finding thrifty solutions to design and decorating tasks rather than sponsored products.

It feels like a fun vacation job for the duo, though their tricks from The Block – such as a room reveal and confected shock when a building problem is uncovered – seem unnecessary.

British TV personalities Amanda Holden and Alan Carr have spent the past few European summers renovating rundown houses in Spain, Italy (twice) and most recently Greece. Their shows follow a familiar template as they inevitably realise they under-estimated the scope of the tasks they face, call in local trades, explore the local sights and visit compatriots who have made the big move, then eventually congratulate themselves on their achievements.

The main selling point of the hugely popular franchise is their easy camaraderie. Their on-screen chemistry is raucous and blue. Despite the dust and racket, Holden always looks like she just stepped out of hair and make-up, while Carr constantly reminds us that he has no practical skills and will never waste the chance for a snarky pun or campy innuendo. It’s naff as hell and forgets at times that it’s actually a renovation show, but that doesn’t seem to bother its legion of fans in the UK and Australia.

Banjo Beale and Rohan Christopher are a couple of Australians who ended up in Scotland’s remote Hebrides after years of backpacking adventures and travel. In this series, they are turning a dilapidated 27-room mansion with no running water or electricity into a hotel on the tiny island of Ulva. The island has been owned since 2018 by local residents who want to bring life back to the remote backwater, the building overseen by a charitable trust.

This isn’t a cookie-cutter makeover show. Beale, who looks after the decorating side of things while Christopher tends to the tools, has a taste for the esoteric and unconventional. And Ulva, with just 16 residents and accessible only by ferry from the island Mull, is as far off the beaten track as renovation porn has ever travelled. Their show is less an extended ad for the boutique hotel it is destined to become than a portrait of a remote farming community perched at the very edge of the world. When Australians are described as individualists with an adventurous streak, think of Beale and Christopher.

This sprawling lifestyle show falls outside €1 schemes, but it nails the escapist fantasy that those other series play with. Dick Strawbridge, an engineer and former lieutenant in the British army, and his flame-haired wife Angel purchased a derelict 45-room chateau in France. In between restoring the magnificent pile (which is partly used as a high-end wedding venue) and raising two children, the couple indulge in their various and many hobbies, from tinkering and practical building to crafting, dressmaking and cookery.

This 2024 episode of Foreign Correspondent looks at Italy’s €1 scheme, via a hilltop town in Sicily called Mussomeli. But it presents a far less telegenic vision of la dolce vita than what’s served up in Amanda and Alan. This is a village in decline, where houses are being bought not by cashed-up holiday-homeowners but by people priced out of more expensive European cities and the children of families who moved away.

*Nine owns this masthead.

Talks to end Garvaghy Road dispute in doubt after Orange Order criticises deal

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 21:31:18 GMT

Spokesperson says group will ‘not surrender’ to Drumcree parade proposal put forward by Northern Ireland secretary

Talks to end the Drumcree parade dispute are on a knife-edge after Jamie Bryson, the legal adviser of the Orange Order, said it would “not surrender” to a deal proposed by the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant.

With echoes of the former Democratic Unionist leader Ian Paisley’s “no surrender” mantra of the 1980s, Bryson told supporters in Portadown that Bryant could keep his deal.

He said he had the authority of the Orange Order’s district master to say: “The Portadown District will not surrender the fundamental principle, not now, not last week, not next week, not ever – ever.”

Bryson said the Portadown Orangemen would not “sell out” even if they were offered £20m.

Government sources said they expected talks to continue on Thursday and possibly into Friday.

Earlier today, Bryant said an end to the dispute was “tantalisingly close”, as the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition signalled it would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so.

Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the nationalist group, said on Wednesday afternoon that he had been through the document drawn up by Bryant and his team.

“Obviously, I can’t divulge what is in it,” he said after a meeting with Bryant. “But if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us.”

But after a second meeting with Bryant on Wednesday evening, Bryson rubbished the residents’ leader’s words.

“Do not be panicked by Breandán Mac Cionnaith coming out and saying there is a document on the table. The document can stay on the table because it won’t be accepted by the Portadown District.”

Earlier in the day, Bryant urged parties to “search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise” to break the deadlock, after meeting with both sides at Hillsborough Castle, just outside Belfast.

On Tuesday, Mac Cionnaith had described mediation over the dispute as “dead in the water”.

Bryant said on Wednesday: “I would just appeal to everybody – including the wider community, not just the people I have been meeting in the room – that people are going to have to search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise if we’re going to get to a successful long-term resolution of the situation.”

He added that he and his team were “working flat-out to try and get to a successful resolution, and I think that is tantalisingly close if everybody can just go that extra mile”.

Politicians and others had warned that any parade down Garvaghy Road risked returning Northern Ireland to the bleak days of the Troubles.

after newsletter promotion

But on Sunday a court of appeal overturned a high court injunction banning the Orange Order from processing through the mainly nationalist area, leading to a four-day standoff that has heightened sectarian tensions.

Attempts to march down Garvaghy Road were blocked by protesters, and a small group of Orange Order members has remained at Drumcree church, the starting point of the parade, vowing not to leave until the parade goes ahead.

Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of Northern Ireland’s police force, said the protest stopping the parade was unlawful, and that a major criminal investigation into the blockade was under way. He warned that mob rule must not be allowed to win, and that he would continue to seek a way to facilitate the Orange Order march.

The first minister of Northern Ireland, Michelle O’Neill, visited Garvaghy Road on Wednesday, despite accusations by unionist leaders that she had broken the law by supporting protesters when she went there on Sunday.

Asked if she had broken the law, O’Neill said: “I accept that I made a choice, a choice to stand with the residents of the Garvaghy Road. It is a choice I will continue to make.

“This is very clearly a community which feels under siege, a community that has been put in reverse and retraumatised in terms of what happened 28 years ago.”

The parade was given the go-ahead by the Northern Ireland Parades Commission on Friday, ending a 28-year ban on the Orange Order marching in Garvaghy Road. At a special sitting of the high court the next day, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, but that was overturned on appeal in the small hours of Sunday morning.

Critics of the Parades Commission’s decision included the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who called it “incomprehensible and wrong”, given that the march prompted some of the most serious violence seen in Northern Ireland in the late 1990s – including the murders of three children – and nearly derailed the 1998 peace process.

On Tuesday, the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition lodged a fresh legal challenge against the march, this time arguing the Parades Commission had “materially misdirected itself” by using historical police assessments over the risk of violence as opposed to a future-looking risk assessment.

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military.

Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates.

The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said.

Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration.

“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”

He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”

Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said.

Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, it emerged last week.

Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.

The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran.

During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”.

The Guardian previously reported on how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.

Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI-worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League.

Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values.

Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.

Hampton’s heroics preserve WCL point for Chelsea on Bompastor’s OL Lyonnes return

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 21:11:38 GMT

Chelsea claimed a valuable point in the Champions League on their head coach Sonia Bompastor’s return to face her former team, on a night where the English side’s controlled performance merited significant plaudits, even if the match itself was surprisingly low on goalmouth action.

The French side had scored eight times in their first fixture in the league phase, away against the Swiss side Servette, and had in fact scored at least seven times in all four matches they had played in all competitions this season. Given that formidable form and the confidence in the hosts’ frontline, Chelsea were grateful to Hannah Hampton for her sharp save from Salma Paralluelo on 20 minutes, and similarly glad to see Melchie Dumornay’s powerfully-struck effort fizz just wide of the base of the post a few minutes later.

Veerle Buurman also did well to produce a last-ditch challenge to block Marie-Antoinette Katoto’s effort from inside the area, as Jonatan Giráldez’s side continued to generate the better first-half chances. In fairness, though, Chelsea still matched their opponents in the midfield. It was a relatively even, albeit disappointingly dull, first 45 minutes.

Lexi Potter, buoyed by the receipt of her first senior England call-up on Tuesday, gave as good as she got in the physical battle in midfield and generally appeared at home on this stage, at the record eight-time European champions, which will have been pleasing for Sarina Wiegman. The 20-year-old, alongside her compatriot Keira Walsh, helped Chelsea maintain an element of control. It was the English side with the majority of the possession – they were just lacking a decisive edge in attack, although Melvine Malard – facing her former club – was demonstrating her quick feet and lively leading the attack.

Unlike in England, where Chelsea played – and won – a fiery derby against Arsenal on Sunday, the top French sides were able to rest at the weekend, in between the first two European fixtures, as the French league helps its sides stay fresh for the Champions League. Other French top-tier sides played in the League Cup instead. It was therefore reasonable to assume that Lyonnes might look the stronger as this contest went on.

Barcelona win big again, Bayern and Juventus bounce back

Barcelona continued their emphatic start to their title defence by brushing aside Roma 6-0 in the Italian capital. Caroline Graham Hansen got Barça off the mark in Rome inside 20 minutes. A Shukurat Oladipo own goal put them two up before the break and Claudia Pina made the points safe just after, before Graham Hansen and Pina both got their second goals and Ewa Pajor put the cherry on the cake late on.

Bayern Munich, who gave up a two goal lead last week to draw with Manchester City, were in danger of behind held again at Benfica, but won 3-0 thanks to three goals from in the last 16 minutes from Klara Bühl, Pernille Harder and Franziska Kett.

Juventus downed Häcken 3-0 in Sweden to make up for last Tuesday’s defeat against Benfica. The Spanish World Cup winner Alba Redondo scored again, making it three goals in as many games and seven in 12 in all competitions since joining from Real Madrid.

It was Chelsea, however, who started the second period the brighter. They thought they deserved a penalty when Tarciane took out Sjoeke Nüsken at the far post, just as the Chelsea midfielder looked certain to score, but after a check on the monitor, Lucy Bronze had been interfering with play from an offside position as the ball was crossed. Tarciane was booked for her challenge, nonetheless.

Bompastor, who won this competition as a player and a manager with Lyonnes and remains a popular figure in these parts, brought on Lauren James for Malard, to give her side a different forward dynamic with just over half an hour remaining, while Lyonnes introduced a former Ballon d’Or winner in Ada Hegerberg, but neither side was looking likely to break the deadlock, as the off-the-ball qualities of both teams appeared to be cancelling each other out. A cautious approach, from Chelsea in particular, was understandable; this was, by a significant distance, the toughest-looking fixture of their league phase matches, against last season’s runners-up.

Lyonnes, owned by the London City Lionesses and Washington Spirit owner Michele Kang, have high ambitions to try and win this title this term. They thought they had scored on 72 minutes, when Paralluelo struck a low shot into the bottom corner, but the offside flag was raised. Just a few minutes later, a moment of real controversy arose, as Chelsea were awarded a penalty for a foul by Damaris Egurrola on James.

Winter review – Richard Armitage’s new cop drama is as ferociously watchable as it is daft

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 21:00:18 GMT

Sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Armitage shouting in a cagoule

Dr Ethan Winter is a maverick, a wildcard, a lone wolf who won’t play by the rules. “Winter!” gasps DI Lauren Bell as the muscular outsider bursts into a police interrogation room and proceeds to subject a tremulous pensioner to the full force of his waxed cagoule. “You can’t do this!” But he can do this. And he will do this. Why? Because he’s Dr Ethan Winter, dammit, one of the greatest forensic pathologists of his generation; a bearded genius whose approach to obstacles is as uncompromising as his approach to tremulous pensioners.

And yet. Dr Ethan Winter is troubled. We know this because Winter – the new six-part ITV police procedural that shares his starkly unseasonable surname – keeps cutting to scenes in which our protagonist paces silently around his fashionably underlit Bristol flat while scowling into the middle distance. Has he misplaced the keys to his vintage sports car? No, they’re over there, next to the gruesome autopsy photos he keeps on the kitchen table in the hope they’ll prompt visitors to ask what made him want to be a forensic doctor (“I became a forensic doctor … to mend sores”). Could it be, then, that the source of his malaise is … complicated? That it could in fact have something to do with the murder, a decade ago, of his fiancee – a case which, though ostensibly closed, continues to raise enough questions to provide the series with its narrative backbone? While leaving sufficient time in each episode for the agitated hunk to solve a new, self-contained crime? It’s certainly possible!

Dr Ethan Winter is played by Richard Armitage, in accordance with the scriptures. His presence here (in his sixth – sixth! – TV thriller since 2021) serves as a seal of quality, or at least an assurance that the ensuing brooding will be accompanied by a) gratuitous demonstrations of upper-body strength, and b) a voice like a Twix melting in a bra fire.

Anyway, the body of a young woman has been found in a freezer lorry so it’s time for some plot. Prickly DI Bell (Annabel Scholey), who has recently moved to Bristol after a mysteriously self-curtailed career with the Met (“It’s a long story”), suspects a local recidivist. Bejumpered sidekick DS Ellis Daldry (a wonderfully rumpled turn from Jamie Kenna) knows better. Best leave the solving stuff to our perturbed hero, he tells her. “Ethan can,” after all, “read a body like other people read a book.” And he can. If by reading a body you mean slowly circling a cadaver while huskily whispering things like “hello, stranger” and “fly eggs”. Still, it seems to work, and soon we’re bounding after him as he tears excitedly through the woods, nostrils flapping at the prospect of another crime scene at which he can be a maverick.

“Can you smell that?” he gasps. We cannot. Tell us more, corpse man. “FAECES,” he bellows, hurtling towards a disused well like a cannonball in a Barbour. “ROTTING MEAT … IT’S A DEAD BODY!”

At this point, there is a strong chance you’re thinking, “This sounds like an absolutely terrible TV programme.” And you would be absolutely correct. But only partially. The script may be a thing of string and glue but the dead fiancee stuff is gripping and Winter’s production values are uncommonly high; the direction, soundtrack and lighting (so many burnished brass sconces!) conspiring to paint Bristol as a glowering storm cloud of polo-necked pain and longing. Based on long-running French thriller Balthazar, the aesthetic here shares a similar, ’ow you say, narked grandeur.

The upshot? It’s a potboiler in a belted trenchcoat. Silent Witness saying “bof” while eating an onion. And yet even the many, many ridiculous bits work, folded as they are into a soufflé that is as ferociously watchable as it is unnecessarily expensive.

The fact of the matter is this: sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Richard Armitage shouting, “FAECES!” while sprinting through Bristol in a cagoule. Let us give thanks.

Winter aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now

Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 20:00:17 GMT

What Guardiola knew at Manchester City relates to the true nature of the club and basic things like truth and human nature

“Do you know the question that you are asking me? Today, do you honestly think it is my job to make this kind of question happen …” Cut to the long, painful pause. Chuck in a deep, shaming stare, eyes that have suddenly become death rays of betrayal and disgust and Pep Guardiola himself transformed from a man cheerfully toasting his own FA Cup final victory to a grizzled chief detective addressing a room full of convicted perverts.

Guardiola had the wind entirely at his back at this point, sitting in the Wembley press room an hour after Manchester City’s 6-0 defeat of Watford in May 2019. Success drowns out every other noise in football. To be good is also to be good, noble, virtuous. History is written by the domestic treble winners. Right up until the moment it isn’t.

The question in question was asked by Rob Harris of the Associated Press. It was basically this: information is now in the public domain that suggests Roberto Mancini received a second salary from Abu Dhabi when he was City manager. Mancini was one of Guardiola’s immediate predecessors. So had he, Pep, ever received two salaries?

Even as Harris was asking this he was interrupted by City’s press officer, saying: “We’re not going here, we’re really just not going there.” A simple “no” would have done the job. Instead the exchange ended with another beautifully executed mad-dog stare from Guardiola; not angry, just sad and disappointed. But also, let’s be honest, really angry as well.

Fast forward to this week and a clip has been doing the rounds of the same Rob Harris, now of Sky News, and still the same perky, questing figure. Harris is approaching Ferran Soriano this time, Pep’s key man through that era, and asking the same entirely legitimate things, with a very different outcome. “The Premier League maintains you cheated for nearly a decade … is all this success, as the Premier League says, based on sham contracts?”

There is no glare in return now, no outrage, no flushed moral high ground. “Thank you, thank you,” Soriano mutters, with the look of a man caught shoplifting a Twix at the local primary school fete, followed by a mute, fumbling exit.

Sunlight. Scrutiny. Awkward questions from awkward people. It turns out these are still the best disinfectant. Just as it turns out “the question” was the only one worth asking in that room in 2019. Not that anyone agreed at the time. Predictably enough the comments on social media were about scum, bias, the press as a national embarrassment. Even other journalists held a perfumed kerchief to their noses, suggesting this was all a non-issue because, er, the club had just won a treble.

It turns out the exact opposite was true. It was entirely the right moment to ask this question. That Cup final win came at the end of the main period of shammery. It was in many ways its unholy coronation. There was an industrial-scale embarrassment in that room. But it wasn’t the person asking the questions.

There is an obvious problem with the City story at this stage. It’s just too big. There is too much to say, an entire Dickensian multiverse interlayered with oddities and moments of jaw-drop. This is not, repeat not, a media story. And yet it kind of is a media story. After all, it was media scrutiny and the efforts of the hacker Rui Pinto that first winkled it out. As such, Harris deserves his moment of grace, living proof that it’s culturally vital to keep on asking questions, the same Rob Harris I have seen grilling Vladimir Putin about corruption on the hoof in Zurich, and also walking into a pillar at the World Cup in São Paulo while running off with his laptop to ask someone else something else, a man so deeply locked into the news cycle even reinforced stadium infrastructure doesn’t register.

It is also worth mentioning at moments like this Nick Harris, AKA Sporting Intelligence, who has kept going at this story relentlessly despite an unusual degree of abuse, harassment and threats, and who has every right to feel vindicated, part of a world where we can still hold power to account, where a cat can look at a king. But for now the real object of interest in this exchange is, of course, the person on the other end of it. Welcome to the stage once again Pep Guardiola, the public face of the club for the past decade.

What did Pep know? This is more than just football legacy chat. It relates to pretty much everything here, the true nature of the club, of elite football itself, and more basic things like truth, spectacle and human nature. Is believing the assurances of others any kind of defence, given Guardiola was in the perfect position to ask questions of his own? Is any kind of deniability plausible here?

The other significant statement from Guardiola in that time came after City’s two-year ban from the Champions League for a serious breach of Uefa’s financial fair play rules was overturned by the court of arbitration for sport. “We didn’t break the rules. We played the same rules as all the clubs in the Premier League,” was Guardiola’s conclusion, which seemed pretty silly at the time, given time-barring of offences was key to that decision. How does it look now?

To this day Guardiola’s stance remains slavish adherence to the promises of his paymasters, as evidenced by his first statement on the matter on Wednesday. Guardiola says he will be getting through the current unpleasantness with the club and its fans, sticking together as always. But were you together, really? Because City’s fans have some urgent questions of their own now. The majority believed what they were told, and put their faith in the “irrefutable body of evidence” schtick. That ring binder of truth really is going to have to do a lot of instant high-speed kung fu when it finally comes screeching into the appeal room on its trail bike. Not to mention explaining where it’s been over the past three years of information exchange.

Guardiola will face his own questions too, and on a level that will hurt him. The coach who only stays for three or four years stretched this out to a full decade at a club where 80% of that time was spent under a cloud of sham contracts and casual hubris. Through all this he had a deeply personal relationship with his chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. The pair of them are seen whispering tenderly in the recent Prime documentary, in which Guardiola is presented as the most genuine and heartfelt of truth-seekers, a lone castaway on Integrity Island, Jedi-like in a tailored hoodie, eyes brimming with tears as he talks feelings and eternal truths, like a dad in the pub on Christmas Eve.

In his farewell hagiographies, Guardiola was routinely described as the greatest modern manager. He invented the Messi role for Messi. He reimagined the basic texture of the sport in this country. If this guy isn’t good, nobody’s good. On the other hand, the only logical conclusion on the facts as they stand is that all his City trophies were won with the benefit of concerted macro-cheating.

During the period embraced by the charges, City’s net spend on transfers was, according to Transfermarkt, almost £400m more than Manchester United in second place, and five times as much as Liverpool and Arsenal. From 2016 to 2018, the key period in building the Pep supremacy, they massively outspent every other team. After which they won the league on the final day or by a single point three times. There were little things throughout, like digging out an extra £25m for Kevin De Bruyne, stretching those fine details in your direction. How is it possible not to see that success as unrelated to stolen margins? This is an era that will now be defined by sham-ball, trophies hoisted with a hand behind your back and a thumb on the scale.

Pep can only double down now and ride this to the end. His life’s work, his vast and all-consuming reputation is at stake. “We will get through this together,” he says in Wednesday’s statement. Well, you have no choice now, Pep. Wherever that destination might be.

There are others who must now enter the matrix of who knew what. Soriano, subject of the second Harris grilling, is utterly bound up in this. He’s there right at the start, speaking to us in the leaked emails published by Der Spiegel. “We will need to fight this,” Soriano writes in one leaked memo, “and do it in a way that is not visible.” Hmm. How’s that part working out?

Soriano’s own pre-City past has already been sliced and diced by those who wish to see a pattern. For the record, and as a basic statement of fact, he was at Barcelona during the period when the alleged, unproved, time-barred refereeing scandal happened, but not implicated or punished. He was at Air Spain when it collapsed, but cleared of any wrongdoing. And now he’s been at City in the period of inflated income that has, in effect, left the club dangling over the edge of a cliff. It is certainly an unfortunate chain of coincidence.

Others who will be asked what they knew, or not asked because he’s not going to speak to you, include the owner, Sheikh Mansour. This has an added element. It speaks to the ultimate test, some way down the line, of fitness to run a football club. How is it possible to spend so much family money on this thing, to dole out what are in effect government contracts, and not know the actual process here?

But let’s face it, we all knew really. Weren’t the sham dealings obvious? It was there even in the absence of furious statements of support from the independent directors at First Abu Dhabi Bank, Etihad Airways, Experience Abu Dhabi, Emirates Palace Hotel in Abu Dhabi, Aldar Properties of Abu Dhabi, Masdar Energy of Abu Dhabi, e& telecoms of Abu Dhabi. Come on, chaps. Stand up for the investment. No word either from Dude Wipes, the club’s official male-oriented toilet-paper partner. Although who knows, we may now be entering full Dude Wipes territory.

We knew about the sportswashing aspect, knew that City was a soft-power vehicle for the state of Abu Dhabi, which has a record of alleged – and of course denied – human rights abuses and so on. And of course City’s fans must have known this too, or felt it on some level. It was there cooked into the blueprint, the sense of something brutally high-end but strangely cold.

JG Ballard coined the phrase “the death of affect” to describe the institutionalising of public feeling, rage and triumph commodified as a spectator event. Some champion teams have a strut. City’s basic vibe was always closer to an unceasing V-sign. Perhaps there was even a buried unease here. No one really enjoys being treated as a glove puppet, even when it is done gently and with a hand held discreetly under the desk. On which note, Pep? Any other questions now? Is this a good time?

Cristiano Ronaldo walks out on Portugal after being dropped from starting lineup

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:55:55 GMT

Jorge Jesus earlier said captain would again be a sub

The 41-year-old has trained alone in gym since weekend

The Portugal captain, Cristiano Ronaldo, announced on Wednesday that he had left the team’s training camp in Denmark after head coach Jorge Jesus told reporters that the iconic striker would not start their next match.

Ronaldo had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen on Wednesday but left abruptly after Jesus’s press conference. The veteran coach had said that Ronaldo, who spent the entire match on the bench against Norway on Sunday, would not start Thursday’s Nations League clash away to Denmark either.

“Following the national team coach’s press conference, and after having a conversation with the Portuguese Football Federation president, I decided to leave the national team’s training camp,” Ronaldo wrote on Instagram. “In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated.

“Now is time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception.”

Jesus had insisted earlier that there was no rift between him and Ronaldo, although the 72-year-old did acknowledge that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in the side’s Nations League win over Norway.

Following the 2-1 victory in Oslo, Ronaldo went straight to the changing rooms without joining his teammates in acknowledging the Portuguese supporters in the stands. “There was no incident whatsoever,” Jesus told reporters.

“Any player – and I was a player myself … when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don’t get on … no one is happy about that,” Jesus said on Wednesday.

The Portuguese coach added that he had told Ronaldo before the match that he would not be in the starting lineup, but that he might bring him on towards the end of the game.

“Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It’s nothing to make a fuss about,” Jesus insisted. The former Benfica manager also explained that Ronaldo had not refused to train on Tuesday, as some Portuguese media outlets had suggested, but that he had had to do individual exercises for physical “mobility” and “strengthening”.

Jesus had said that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would train as normal on Wednesday. However, despite arriving at the stadium in the team bus, Ronaldo did not join his teammates on the pitch. Portuguese media shared a video of him leaving Parken alongside two members of the backroom staff just after Jesus’s press conference. Reports also said that Ronaldo’s private jet was heading to Copenhagen. Just before Ronaldo’s social media post, the Portuguese federation had released a brief statement merely confirming that the former Real Madrid, Manchester United and Juventus player had not trained.

Catholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades, report finds

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:53:09 GMT

No new indictments from eight-year investigation as state attorney general says church knew about abuse

More than 270 Catholic clerics sexually abused nearly 1,000 children across three Massachusetts dioceses over several decades, according to a report released by the state’s attorney general’s office on Wednesday.

The eight-year-long investigation did not result in new indictments, the office said, claiming that some conduct identified was not a crime under Massachusetts law at the time it occurred, and that in other cases the applicable statute of limitations had expired.

However, three cases were referred to different district attorney’s offices and one of those resulted in criminal charges. The majority of the abuse occurred before 2002.

“The evidence gathered during this investigation also shows that, for decades, and especially before 2002, church officials in all three dioceses knew about the sexual abuse of children yet did not take effective action to prevent it or to examine the institutional failures of leadership that led to scores of children being victimized at the hands of abusive priests,” the report stated.

The attorney general’s office said the report was “the first comparable public accounting of the institutional failures within the Fall River, Springfield and Worcester dioceses”.

The abuses in the archdiocese of Boston drew international attention after the Boston Globe published its Pulitzer-winning coverage in 2002, and prompted other investigations around the world that found similar cases of sexual abuse.

“I strongly urge the dioceses and the broader church to take these recommendations seriously and implement greater, meaningful changes to strengthen child protection and improve responses to allegations of abuse,” the Massachusetts attorney general, Andrea Joy Campbell, said at a press conference.

“Behind every one of those numbers is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed forever and a survivor who carried that abuse for years, and in many cases decades. They continue to carry this trauma even today,” Campbell said.

“I know many survivors have been waiting a long time to see these findings made public. I understand the frustration that comes with that wait. It is my hope that today is a meaningful step forward toward truth, accountability and healing that survivors deserve,” she added.

Only one of the three dioceses responded to the report in a statement. “We will study the attorney general’s report to identify any additional improvements that can be made to respond to victims of past abuse and to continue to strengthen efforts to keep children safe,” said the diocese of Worcester in a statement.

The diocese of Worcester did not apologise on Wednesday for its clerics’ behavior, but pointed to an apology by Bishop Robert J McManus, who wrote in 2022 that he was “profoundly sorry for the abuse of minors by priests” within his diocese.

“I continue in my commitment with the help of many collaborators to do everything we can to ensure such abuse does not happen again,” he said at the time. The diocese of Worcester also highlighted that no charges were filed.

Many of the individuals identified in the report are also deceased, the report said. “Any legal limitations do not diminish the seriousness of what this investigation found. The office believes that while criminal law cannot provide justice for all survivors today, the office still has a responsibility to tell the truth of what happened.”

Leah Williamson blunder gifts Paris FC a point as Arsenal’s struggles continue

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:31:37 GMT

Renée Slegers did not attend the post‑match press conference, the manager understood to have been too furious after Arsenal threw away a two-goal lead in their draw with Paris FC on Wednesday night.

The assistant coach Aaron D’Antino stepped in to speak to the media instead of Slegers, after a disastrous mix-up between the goalkeeper Misa Rodríguez and the centre-back Leah Williamson gifted Paris FC a penalty that Maeline Mendy converted to deny Arsenal all three points in the Champions League.

“The most frustrating part is how much we are working behind the scenes to try and turn this around, and it is just not going our way at the moment,” D’Antino said.

Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway had given the Gunners a two-goal lead but Clara Mateo pulled one back before Williamson handled the ball after the referee deemed play to have restarted from a goal-kick when Rodríguez passed it to her.

D’Antino said: “If we’re looking at what we can control, it’s just passing the ball to Leah. From what I remember seeing, the ball was still rolling and she was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal-kicks as we normally do. So maybe the learning in that is how we get the ball to Leah, so we don’t put ourselves in that situation. But as far as we’re concerned, that’s not a penalty … we haven’t taken a goal-kick, there’s no advantage gained by Leah stopping the ball.”

It has been a tough start to the season for Arsenal, who are up against it in the title race with only five points from their opening four games, and the closing stages of the match in Paris delivered another gut punch.

Barcelona win big again, Bayern and Juventus bounce back

Barcelona continued their emphatic start to their title defence by brushing aside Roma 6-0 in the Italian capital. Caroline Graham Hansen got Barça off the mark in Rome inside 20 minutes. A Shukurat Oladipo own goal put them two up before the break and Claudia Pina made the points safe just after, before Graham Hansen and Pina both got their second goals and Ewa Pajor put the cherry on the cake late on.

Bayern Munich, who gave up a two goal lead last week to draw with Manchester City, were in danger of behind held again at Benfica, but won 3-0 thanks to three goals from in the last 16 minutes from Klara Bühl, Pernille Harder and Franziska Kett.

Juventus downed Häcken 3-0 in Sweden to make up for last Tuesday’s defeat against Benfica. The Spanish World Cup winner Alba Redondo scored again, making it three goals in as many games and seven in 12 in all competitions since joining from Real Madrid.

Paris FC had promised another tricky test, with teams that are happy to concede possession frustrating an Arsenal side that just cannot seem to find their way through low blocks. Chelsea had read that script on Sunday: they were organised at the back and punished Arsenal’s profligacy and failure to make their early dominance count.

At the Stade Jean-Bouin, which sits in the shadow of Paris Saint-Germain’s Parc des Princes, the story was familiar. As a result, it was less a wave of relief that swept through the pocket of travelling Arsenal fans and the players when their first goal went in and more a tsunami. It had looked as if Arsenal’s hesitancy had cost them a possible opening again when Stanway prodded the ball towards Russo but the England forward took several touches to create the space to shoot before firing her low effort in.

With the home team forced to come out more, that it took only five minutes after the restart for Arsenal to double their lead was no surprise. It was a stylish finish from Stanway that gave Arsenal breathing space, the midfielder pushed Emily Fox’s cross forward a little with her chest before lashing a volley in from close range.

However, only 22 minutes of comfort followed, before the team that inflicted a shock win on penalties to knock Arsenal out of qualifying in 2023 pulled the goal back that would test the Gunners’ resolve.

It was a mix-up between the centre-backs Lotte Wubben-Moy and Williamson that delivered the goal. The pair both moved to close down Evelyne Viens and the Canadian forward slipped the ball wide to Clara Mateo who raced free, rounded Rodríguez and slotted into the empty net.

It was tense as the clock ticked down. Paris posed a threat throughout, but the leveller followed the most calamitous of mistakes by Arsenal. Rodríguez collected the ball for a goal-kick, rolled it on to the pitch and then passed it to Williamson who bent and stopped the ball with her hand. The referee’s whistle went and she pointed to the spot, with Rodríguez deemed to have taken the goal-kick while Williamson clearly assumed she was being given the ball to take it. VAR did not intervene and Mendy converted from the spot, driving powerfully into the bottom corner.

It was a bruising end to another bruising game for Arsenal, who really need some luck to go their way to lift the increasing pressure. Meanwhile, Slegers’s decision to avoid talking after the game will have only ramped that pressure up further ahead of a must-win game against league leaders Manchester City on Sunday.

Quips, slights and a surprise twist: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury come face to face

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:15:37 GMT

Joshua reveals he is speaking to Peter Fury on training

Fury vows to ‘blast him out’ at London press conference

Anthony Joshua has revealed that he is in contact with Tyson Fury’s uncle Peter, in a surprise twist to the buildup between the two former world champion heavyweights who will finally meet in the ring in Cardiff in December.

Peter Fury trained Tyson when he shocked Wladimir Klitschko to win his first world heavyweight title, in 2015. The uncle and nephew fell out soon afterwards, apparently over a financial dispute, and have not spoken in many years.

“I speak to Peter Fury,” Joshua said before the fight’s first press conference on Wednesday evening in London. “He’s willing to help me as well. Yeah, I’ll speak to him [before I fight Tyson Fury].”

Asked if he can learn more about Fury from his uncle, Joshua said: “Not about Fury but about our training and how I can approach the fight. This is where I can improve. Everybody’s going to tell me how to win. But the most important person to listen to is myself at this point in my career.”

Joshua said he last spoke to Peter Fury about a month ago. “I speak to Matty Harris [the British heavyweight whom Fury Sr trains] quite a lot. Matty Harris comes down for some sparring. That’s how it all comes about. Through Matty and Peter.”

Ben Davison will train Joshua for the fight and he, too, has also worked previously with Fury. Davison helped Fury to return to boxing in 2018, after the fighter had been out of the ring with drink and drug problems for three years following his defeat of Klitschko.

Fury seemed initially taken aback when he was told that Davison will be in Joshua’s corner. In seemingly genuine surprise, Fury asked: “Is it confirmed? Is he gonna have him?” He paused and then turned to Frank Warren, who has promoted him for years and said, in deadpan style: “That’s deflating, isn’t it, Frank? It is deflating.”

Fury soon made clear that his last comment was a joke: “Don’t forget I left Ben Davison to go with SugarHill [Steward] because he wasn’t good enough and this is the same Ben Davison who Anthony Joshua left because he wasn’t good enough.”

After Joshua was dropped numerous times and then stopped by Daniel Dubois in September 2024, he switched from Davison to work with Oleksandr Usyk’s team. Fury, who was in a cheerful mood, said: “When he got knocked out by Dubois it was the same Ben Davison who everyone said: ‘Oh, he’s this, he’s that …’ Now they’re going back to him?

“So that gives me encouragement. That gives me happiness. [Joshua] will probably go out there, get told to throw a jab and throw an uppercut and get himself chinned.”

Joshua stressed that “it wasn’t so much going to Ben and Peter because they have worked with Fury before”, saying: “The reason why I went with Ben is because he and his team pinpoint things. [Against Dubois] there are things I could have done better so I won’t put all that blame on Ben.

“What I’ve got to do is take control of my fight with Fury, but also add their touch. And with these two powerhouses coming together, I think it will be a match made in heaven. Ben and his team are very good at pinpointing certain things leading up to a fight that I can execute and exploit. I believe that they will get me that one step closer to landing the perfect punch to pin Fury to the ground.”

At the press conference Joshua called for a minute’s silence, which was impeccably observed, when he remembered the close friends he had lost over the past 10 months. Unexpectedly, Fury then spoke respectfully about Joshua as they shared the stage. But Fury did insist that: “I’m going to blast him out. I’m going to catch him and when I do it’s going to be curtains.”

Joshua smiled, saying: “I don’t expect anything else from this man than him saying he’s going to render me unconscious.” He then laughed when Fury quipped: “This man is built like an Adonis, I’m built like a blancmange.”

Fury turned to Joshua and said: “I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together.” Joshua paused and then said: “I don’t know if I can trust you.”

But the traditional face-off between the two men passed peacefully and calmly, for both fighters know that none of the intrigue and wisecracks will matter when the first bell rings and they leave their corners to face each other and fight.

From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary life

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:01:13 GMT

Be it her pioneering approach to consumer injustice or her extraordinary tackling of systemic social issues, the broadcaster was at the forefront of what television could be

Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86

Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in pictures

Esther Rantzen’s early CV reads like a chronicle of the world working as the 1960s thought it should. A smart young woman, privately educated in north London from the age of 10 (the Rantzens had previously lived in New York), then at Somerville College, Oxford, she started on the bottom rung and had exactly the right mixture of graft and luck. Having trained as a radio studio manager, she got her first TV production job as a researcher for BBC-3, Ned Sherrin’s satirical show in the mid-60s. From there, she went to Braden’s Week, a magazine show hosted by Bernard Braden, a serendipitous connection for two reasons – first, he put his researchers on screen, then he decided to return to his native Canada. From there, That’s Life! was born, with Rantzen as the main presenter. It was 1973, and it was conceived as a new, revamped Braden’s Week. In reality, it was nothing like it.

That’s Life! ebbed and flowed over its 21 years, but at its various peaks, it would draw in audiences of more than 22 million. It definitely became more searching and serious as it went on, but even from the start, it would have bizarre and audacious gear changes, from an item about funny-shaped vegetables to another on lethal patio doors without skipping a beat. That is not to cast shade on the lighter material: there was a dog called Prince that could say “sausages”, and a generation of us have not been able to eat sausages without saying “sausages” in Prince’s voice at least once since. It was delightful to watch partly because there was so much texture to the studio audience’s laughter: there’s one part affection for the dog, one part affection for the owner, five parts, dude, your dog is not saying “Anthony”, and then this wild overflow of excitement when the Yorkie says something that definitely sounds like “sausages”. Then, wham, the next story would be a toddler with life-changing injuries from a poorly surfaced playground, then Victoria Wood would come on and be funny.

It shouldn’t have worked, since surely audiences either wanted to be amused or have their heartstrings tugged, or be mobilised in outrage: how could they cope with the emotional maelstrom of all those things at once? Yet it did work, partly because it was a different era: mainstream culture was extremely macabre in the 1970s and 1980s. Kids were always being electrocuted in public information videos, there was a kind of glee to it.

These huge audiences, bombarded with consumer injustices, large and small, forced change at incredible speed. Seatbelts were made mandatory for children as a result of That’s Life!; schools nationwide brought in anti-bullying policies after Rantzen’s campaign inspired by the tragic death of Katharine Bamber, who took her own life as a teenager in the early 1990s.

As the impact of her investigations became more and more extraordinary, Rantzen’s focus turned to issues that were more serious and systemic; fewer dodgy door-to-door salesmen and kitchen appliances that might give you an electric shock, more stark and in-depth stories on organ donation, maternity care and stillbirth, mental health problems or the dark side of food manufacturing. She became the person who lifted the lid on the tragedies nobody talked about, and it was in that spirit that Childwatch was conceived: a one-off special in 1986, in which survivors of childhood abuse talked of their experiences. The immediate consequence was Childline, Britain’s first anonymous helpline for children who were being abused.

The BBC didn’t have a clue about what it was about to unleash. This show was heartbreaking, as people in their 20s and 30s shared, often for the first time, their accounts of what they had endured in childhood. But it also revealed that the country simply didn’t know how to have this conversation. The Childwatch set was dominated by a gigantic cake, as if the stark subject matter could be leavened by the trappings of light entertainment. What do people want when they have just said a terribly sad thing? Well, cake, obviously. For 48 hours after the show, the professionally staffed phone lines weren’t operational, and calls were being taken by the production team, who were overwhelmed, not just by the numbers but by the urgency and gravity of what they were hearing – young kids in mortal fear, asking for help. Quite soon, better news stories began to surface, as the project was professionalised and the police and other agencies began to get involved, but at the outset it was necessary and stunningly naive, in the way that pioneering work probably is by definition.

More than 30 years on, far too little progress has been made on child abuse, but two things stand out: first, that nothing will change until victims of abuse have someone to tell who won’t stonewall them; second, that Rantzen understood that instinctively, at a time when so many relevant institutions were making it their business not to.

It was as a result of a call to Childline that Rantzen subsequently uncovered the “nest of paedophiles” at Crookham Court boarding school. It resulted in three criminal convictions and a growing awareness of the predatory nature of abusers – that it was the result of active strategy, not tragic happenstance, to find them concentrated in boarding schools and children’s homes. Again, this is taking decades to resolve, but once more Rantzen was at the frontier.

Widowed in 2000 when her husband, Desmond Wilcox, died, she also campaigned on palliative care and spoke movingly about the pain of bereavement. In 2013, The Silver Line was launched nationally, to address loneliness and isolation in old age. Having been awarded a CBE for services to children in 2006, Rantzen was made a dame in 2015, in recognition of both Childline and the Silver Line. Her legacy is complicated by the fact that our approach has changed; so many of the subjects she broached seem glaringly ill-suited to the breezy magazine TV format she favoured. But her groundbreaking approach to making television raises a question: without her interventions, would that change have come about?
