Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 19:01:03 GMT

Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.

More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.

The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.

Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.

Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.

“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”

The ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. .

“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”

A bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans for even broader controls on trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.

On Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was narrowly defeated after winning backing from all but one Democrat.

“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.

A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.

More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.

The Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.

Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.

“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.

Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.

The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.

Earlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmert called for the international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.

Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.

A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.

An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.

“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”

On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”

Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 18:55:31 GMT

Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary life Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in pictures

Esther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86.

In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”, whose “legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her”.

“We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things,” said her three children.

Rantzen announced a diagnosis of stage four lung cancer in 2023, and became a vocal campaigner to change the law around assisted dying. In September 2026, she announced she had to abandon plans to end her life in Swiss clinic Dignitas, due to being too physically frail.

“Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful; indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest,” she said in a statement. “And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.”

“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Very sad to hear that Dame Esther Rantzen has died. Through her decades of campaigning, including founding Childline and The Silver Line, she changed countless lives and gave a voice to people who often went unheard.

“And I will always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life. My thoughts are with her family and all who loved her.”

Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced a bill to legalise assisted dying, said: “Esther was a strong, warm and compassionate woman and a fighter to the end.

“Her positivity and determination never to give in gave me strength, but more importantly helped all those others like her who were confronting a terminal illness to keep going in the knowledge that they were not alone.”

Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, in 1940 and began her career in 1963 as a BBC radio studio manager. Having moved into television as a researcher, she became a presenter in 1968, as part of the consumer affairs show Braden’s Week, before being appointed as the main host of its replacement programme, That’s Life!, in 1973.

Part magazine, part consumer show, with hard-hitting investigations and jokes, That’s Life! drew more than 20 million viewers at its peak – and ran for 21 years with Rantzen as anchor. After she successfully pitched an episode about child abuse to the then BBC controller Michael Grade, a set of phone lines was opened for 48 hours, which enabled children to call in and speak to social workers. The volume of responses led her to turn the service into a permanent fixture, launching the children’s charity Childline in 1986.

In 1988, Rantzen created Hearts of Gold, a series focusing on people responsible for outstanding acts of kindness, and hosted her own BBC Two chatshow, Esther, from 1994, when That’s Life! came to an end, until 2002. Further TV projects included the consumer affairs show Old Dogs New Tricks, as well as competing in Strictly Come Dancing’s second series and the 2008 edition of the ITV reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! She received an OBE for services to broadcasting, Bafta’s Richard Dimbleby award for factual programming and a lifetime achievement prize at the Women in Film and Television awards.

Her wide-ranging charity work saw her act as a patron or vice-president of numerous organisations. In 2010, she launched the Silver Line – a free confidential helpline for older people, which led to her being made a dame for services to children and older people.

In 2010, she stood as an independent candidate for Luton South in that year’s general election, coming fourth after winning 4.4% of the vote. She wrote numerous books, including a murder-mystery novel. In later years, she was a regular contributor to the One Show and hosted a podcast with her former That’s Life! colleague Adrian Mills.

On Instagram, the television presenter Anna Williamson described Rantzen as “somebody truly iconic, who really cared, and who has left behind one hell of a legacy”.

Fellow presenter Lorraine Kelly also paid tribute to Rantzen on social media for being a “pioneer and a force of nature – [who] helped so many people – funny, forthright and fabulous”.

One of Rantzen’s former co-hosts of That’s Life!, Howard Leader, said: “Over the time that I was with her, through her fantastic generosity, she taught me how to be a journalist.

“I think Esther’s skill was that she really understood how to use the platform she had to create an effect for, we hope ... the improvement of people in our country.”

Her husband, Desmond Wilcox, whom she married in 1977, died in 2000. Rantzen is survived by their three children, Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua – as well as five grandchildren.

FTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in July

The US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation ⁠into Anthropic, OpenAI and other ⁠AI labs ​to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers.

The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day ⁠harm humans.

The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top ​AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research ‌group Metr, according to multiple reports.

Anthropic and ‌OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology.

Anthropic, OpenAI and ‌Metr did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The New York Post first reported the news.

Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue.

Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any ​harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin.

The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to ⁠take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data.

Donald Trump met with top ​AI executives on Tuesday, where the ​companies agreed to establish voluntary standards.

No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 18:33:20 GMT

Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit

Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.

Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.

Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.

The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”

On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.

Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”

Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.

Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”

The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.

Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.

Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.

On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.

Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.

Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.

The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.

In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.

No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.

Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.

But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.

He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”

An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.

No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.

Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.

One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.

A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.

Passengers heard screams from the front of the plane, and the wounded pilot managed to open the latch on the cockpit door, leaving it ajar.

The plane also began to abruptly descend, falling about 17,000ft in two minutes. As the plane began to dive, passengers and a crew member pushed their way into the cockpit, subduing the attacker. Other crew members then stabilised the descent of the plane and began to land it safely in north-western Saudi Arabia.

A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office then said the incident was not a hijacking, as media reports circulated of a fight between the two pilots.

As more information emerged about the violent nature of the attack, Israeli and international media began to report officials anonymously saying an investigation had been opened into whether this was an attack on Israelis.

The head of the Israeli military, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, has postponed a visit to the US over the incident, where he was meant to have a meeting with US joint chiefs of staff and the head of US Central Command.

The incident came just days after Netanyahu had warned there were indications an attack would be carried out during Israel’s October elections. Israel’s military, quoted by Israeli media, said it had no intelligence that an attack was being planned.

Yair Lapid, the opposition figure and former prime minister, cast doubt on the connection between the alleged attack and Netanyahu’s warning, saying a security briefing on Tuesday night gave no information about any potential incident similar to what happened on Wednesday.

Israel experienced a series of hijackings and attacks on planes by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s, but has not experienced anything similar in decades. Israeli media reported that a later flydubai flight heading to Tel Aviv turned around in mid-air and headed back towards Dubai after the incident.

The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 17:37:06 GMT

Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him

Sunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, is neck and neck in the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.

Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his father, but he is no less extreme. For many on both sides, this is a vote against a man they detest more than an endorsement of their own candidate. Most voters disapprove of both men.

Initially, pundits predicted victory for the leftwing incumbent. Some feel that at 80 he is too old to begin a fourth term, though he remains energetic. His social programmes are extensive, but frustration at Brazil’s enduring failure to match its economic record to its potential may hobble him, especially with growth slowing. Violent crime remains a top issue.

Then came the Banco Master financial scandal, which has snowballed into a corruption case spanning Brazilian politics and the judiciary. First, Flávio Bolsonaro was caught on tape asking the failed bank’s playboy owner, Daniel Vorcaro, for almost $27m to make a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.

Then compromising messages between Mr Vorcaro and the supreme court judge who led the prosecution of the ex-president were revealed. The allegations fed the perception that politicians are all dirty, and bolstered the unfounded far-right claim that Mr Bolsonaro Sr was stitched up. His son has also papered over a damaging public rift with his stepmother Michelle – an influential figure, key to the evangelical support he needs.

Mr Bolsonaro Jr has said he will abide by the election’s result. But the Bolsonaros have spent years working to undermine trust in internationally respected Brazil’s electronic voting system. A narrow first-round victory for Lula would probably be contested. With other candidates on the right, Mr Bolsonaro Jr would also have an advantage in a second-round vote. He has talked up the prospect of privatisation and cuts to public spending and taxes if he wins. He has pledged to pack the supreme court with anti‑abortion conservative judges, who would also be critical to future election disputes. He has vowed to introduce the kind of aggressive anti-crime drive that has trampled human rights elsewhere.

President Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, will be further emboldened in their “Donroe doctrine” of aggressive intervention in the western hemisphere if Mr Bolsonaro Jr is victorious. US meddling in this election has often backfired – high tariffs on Brazil have allowed Lula to run as the patriot defending the country against foreign interference. But it is no less disturbing.

Mr Trump’s more ruthless and reckless second term also offers an alarming vision of how another Bolsonaro presidency might look. The first showed historic levels of deforestation in the Amazon as well as a surge in illegal resource extraction and the invasion of Indigenous people’s lands. Those fell sharply once Lula returned to power. A Bolsonaro presidency would be bad for women, the poor and minorities. Democracy would probably be its first, local victim. But the climate would surely be another – with consequences for us all.

The Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young people

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 17:36:26 GMT

Empty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young people

School closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are having fewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for an ageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.

The fall has been most acute in inner London, where 90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born each year has dropped by more than a third since 2010, eight primary schools have closed in the past six years. As London’s councils have observed, high living costs are pricing families out of the centre and dissuading people from having children. It is no surprise that Islington and Westminster, two of the most expensive places to live in Britain, also have among the lowest fertility rates in England and Wales.

Declining enrolment shapes the quality of education that schools can provide. They receive funding for each child they enrol, which is currently £7,000 per primary-age pupil in England. Schools with fewer pupils are forced to make their funding stretch further, cutting teachers, merging classes, and losing extracurricular activities. Official forecasts have previously overestimated the future number of young people, making it harder for local authorities to plan. They have not been helped by the promotion of free schools, which have created a surplus of school places, or the expansion of academies, which decide their own admissions and can entice pupils away to neighbouring areas. The government has recently given local authorities greater powers to object to academy expansion, which should help them plan more effectively.

The Treasury may be tempted to recycle savings from falling pupil numbers towards rising demand for health and social care. Over the past seven years, for example, as primary school pupil numbers in England fell by 5%, the number of teachers and classes shrank by 4%. But treating this development as a justification for cutting spending on education would be a mistake. Lucy Powell, the education secretary, has promised expanded enrichment activities and earlier intervention for children with special educational needs. Falling pupil numbers offer an opportunity to deliver these ambitions, provided the government retains the resources to do so. The gap between private school fees and state school spending per pupil has more than doubled over the past decade, and spending more on state school pupils would help narrow this inequality.

The closure of a school shapes an area. “Without this school it’s all just tourists, isn’t it?” one parent recently said of Soho’s last remaining primary school, which is at risk of imminent closure. Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away. Yet if people continue having fewer children, more schools will probably have to close. In some cases, this may be unavoidable.

Schools that have large numbers of unfilled places tend to perform worse on average, but closing them won’t necessarily improve results. Local authorities, which have excelled at selling off public assets, should be required to keep hold of shuttered schools. Empty classrooms could be repurposed as youth clubs, turned over to nurseries, or transformed into Sure Start centres. The focus should be on managing resources to improve education and opportunities for young people in an increasingly old society.

Exposed bras and unitards: why are people wearing underwear on the outside?

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 17:15:38 GMT

From crystal balconettes on the catwalk to mankinis on the parkrun, showing off your undies seems to be all the rage

Name: Underwear.

Age: The first loincloths date from about 7,000 years ago.

Appearance: Increasing.

You mean people are increasingly wearing underwear? No, they’re increasingly wearing it on the outside.

This is what happens when you let educational standards slip. They’re wearing it on the outside on purpose.

Why? Fashion. In recent shows Fendi had models striding the catwalk wearing skirts with matching bras.

What about their tops? Did they match as well? The bras were the tops.

I don’t know much about designer fashion, but this is a category mistake: the bra is a foundation garment. Nevertheless, the bra-as-top has become an established trend. It’s been creeping up on us for some time, with glimpses of bra beneath unbuttoned shirts.

And the shirt has finally been removed from the equation? Not always: at Erdem’s London fashion show, crystal bras were worn over the top of shirts.

I suppose if I had a bra made of jewels, I’d want to wear it on the outside. All kinds of bras are being reimagined as outerwear: tube bras, bandage bras, bralettes …

Bras for women who don’t need bras, you mean. Meanwhile, unitards are becoming popular for men.

They are not. They are: the single-piece “speedsuit” favoured by some elite athletes has started to work its way down to the amateur runner.

If wearing a mankini can help you win a race, it’s probably worth cramming yourself into one. The thing is, while speedsuits may enhance performance to some degree at a professional level, they’re not going to do much to improve your parkrun time.

So men are just wearing them because they like the way they feel? Or the way they look. “You have to have some level of audacity to wear one,” an amateur marathon runner told the Wall Street Journal. “And I think I have that audacity.”

The audacity to wear underwear in the street. He probably doesn’t see it that way.

If walking around in their smalls makes people feel modern, who am I to judge? Actually the underwear as outerwear idea has been with us for quite a while – corsetry was a popular fashion trope in the 1990s, as were slip dresses.

I suppose we have superheroes to thank for all this. While it’s true that Superman and others wore their pants on the outside, there is no evidence to suggest it ever caught on with the wider public.

Do say: “There is nothing new in fashion – let’s not forget that the ubiquitous T-shirt was once considered underwear.”

Don’t say: “It’s eight o’clock and the Uber is here! Why aren’t you dressed yet?”

Government must stop dithering over energy bill support for the vulnerable

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 17:04:09 GMT

Ministers should introduce a properly targeted social tariff rather than tinker with the warm homes discount

Energy bills forecast to jump by £276 a year from January

What to do as prices head for £2,000 a year

After the hopeful good vibes in Liverpool, here comes a reminder of what is coming this winter: a mighty new year shock in energy bills, hitting the poorest hardest, that the government looks unprepared for.

From the quarterly price cap level of £1,723 that will apply from Thursday for an average dual-fuel household, take your pick from a range of forecasts for the first three months of 2027. The energy consultancy Cornwall Insight says £1,999. The big supplier EDF thinks £2,076. Split the difference and we’re talking about an 18% quarter-on-quarter rise in the unit rate at the worst time of the year, the months of peak consumption.

Everybody knows the immediate reason – soaring gas prices – but the government cannot claim to be surprised by events. The threat of a prolonged price spike has been present ever since Donald Trump’s Middle East misadventure became more than a one-week affair.

The government, it’s true, has fiddled at the margin. Rachel Reeves, when chancellor, took a chunk of green levies into general taxation from April. Andy Burnham cut VAT on electricity from 5% to zero for six months, starting on Thursday, in one of his “breathing space” measures. But what is missing from the government’s response is properly targeted help for the most vulnerable.

There is the warm homes discount scheme – worth £150, used by 5.5m low-income households last year and paid for by all bill payers – but virtually everybody agrees it is inadequate for the bills on the way and misses swathes of households who would fall within a better definition of “vulnerable”, such as those with high energy needs for health reasons.

The consensus answer, promoted by various thinktanks, charities, regulators and energy companies for years, is a well-designed flexible social tariff or discount scheme.

Here, for example, was the chief executive of Ofgem as long ago as February 2023 after the gas price spike caused by Russia’s war on Ukraine: “We think that, with bills continuing to be so high, there is a case for examining with urgency the feasibility of a social tariff for customers in the most vulnerable situations.”

Three winters later, it is hard to spot signs of urgency on the part of successive governments. Nobody pretends a social tariff is easy to design. At heart, it’s a data exercise that would have to take in household income (as opposed to information on individual incomes held by HMRC), health records and energy consumption. Cliff-edge judgments would have to be made. Perfection would be impossible.

But the result would surely be better than what will come this winter, which will probably be John Healey upping the level of the warm homes discount in next month’s budget because it’s the only lever available to him.

In addition, Healey could conceivably remove VAT from gas as well as electricity (though that would run against the national electrification agenda). Or, as urged by 120 organisations a fortnight ago, he could take more of the “hidden taxes” of energy transition into taxation (there are excellent reasons to do so, though all will look expensive from his point of view).

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, seems to recognise the mess she has inherited. She could hardly miss it now that unpaid consumer debts in the energy system are projected to reach a colossal £7bn by the end of this year. “There is a question that needs to be answered … we have to think about the costs and how we recover it in the most fair way,” she told this site’s Politics Weekly podcast this week.

Yes, that is indeed the question, and it’s encouraging that Fahnbulleh is not parroting her predecessor’s dreamy line about “£300 off bills by 2030”, because everybody can also see that “stubbornly high” – EDF’s projection for bills for the end of the decade – is more realistic. Higher “non-commodity” costs are coming down the track even when the gas price falls.

But it does not sound as if the government is even close to settling on a joined-up model for bill support for the most vulnerable that could serve for this winter and future winters. It’ll be the usual last-minute scramble for ideas and higher levels of fuel poverty than needs to be the case. The multi-year dithering is inexcusable.

Kevin’s ultramarathon challenge ends in time for kick-off at Old Trafford as son Jack vies for first title with Wakefield

There are few families with more stories to tell when it comes to the Super League Grand Final than the Sinfields but, even by their lofty standards, this week will take some beating.

Leeds has been the epicentre of that story for more than 20 years but this week the focus has moved 10 miles down the road to Wakefield.

Jack will fulfil a childhood dream by playing at Old Trafford for the first time on Saturday, when Wakefield Trinity attempt to win their maiden Super League title. Unsurprisingly his father, Kevin, will be there – but in circumstances that make this story all the more remarkable.

Sinfield Sr is in the midst of his seventh and final fundraising challenge to support those living with motor neurone disease, which will conclude at Old Trafford on Saturday and passed through Wakefield on Wednesday.

He will finish the last leg of his seventh ultramarathon in seven days at the Grand Final and will carry the match ball into the stadium for Wakefield’s showdown with Warrington Wolves. Waiting for him on the pitch will be his son, who first attended the event shortly after he was born, when Kevin played in the 2004 final for Leeds Rhinos.

Jack has been in the stands for all eight of his father’s Grand Final appearances but, this weekend, the roles will be reversed. “When he planned this last challenge and for it to finish at Old Trafford, I don’t think even he could have imagined that I would be playing in it,” the 22-year-old says with a smile. “So it’s worked out pretty well, right?”

Just as Kevin will no doubt be beaming with pride at his son’s upcoming debut in a Grand Final, Jack unsurprisingly possesses similar emotions when asked about his dad’s incredible fundraising efforts, which continued from Wakefield’s stadium on Wednesday morning, with a message of good luck delivered to the Trinity squad.

“It was really nice to see him this morning before he set off,” the half‑back said on Wednesday. “I’ve missed him a lot when he’s been away because I’m still living at home, so it’s really weird around the house without him! I’m hoping I’ll see him on Thursday when he goes past home and he runs up near our neck of the woods. But I’m so proud of him.”

Jack holds as his favourite rugby memory the 2015 Grand Final, Kevin’s final match as a player which ended with victory and Leeds winning the treble. “I’ve got that picture on my phone still,” he says when reflecting on a family photo from that game. “It was a pretty special moment – hopefully there’s a chance to have another picture this weekend.”

His exposure to the biggest game of the season began much earlier than that, though. “My first ever rugby league game was the 2004 final when I was three weeks old. I have been to every single one of the Grand Finals my dad has played in but the last one really stands out in 2015 for all the right reasons.”

But this is where their respective stories begin to diverge. While Kevin won everything there was to win as a Leeds player, Jack’s career has taken a different path. Unable to force his way into the first-team picture at the Rhinos after coming through the academy, he made the decision to look elsewhere last winter.

His lifelong affiliation with the Rhinos over, Sinfield Jr made the decision to move across West Yorkshire and sign with Wakefield. Sold by their vision of a club determined to step out of the significant shadows of their past, Jack may have been forgiven for wanting to do the same, with the pressure of being Sir Kevin Sinfield’s son at Headingley ominous.

But he has blossomed away from that pressure and has played a key role in taking Wakefield to within one win of a first league title in almost 60 years. Just as his father helped deliver a first league title to Leeds in over 30 years in 2004 and begin an era of success, Jack now has the chance to do the same in his own way.

“It’s been a dream of mine to go there one day and emulate him and win one. As soon as I spoke to the club, I knew I wanted to come here. They’re growing, they’re hungry to go and win things and so am I.”

And as they both head for their most memorable venue, albeit in very differing ways, on Saturday, will there be too much contact between father and son? “I’ve spoken to him a little bit but obviously he’s just been really tired,” Jack says. “Hopefully we can celebrate together after … I just hope he gets a shower first.”

Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:53:27 GMT

Readers respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lock

In the aftermath of Andy Burnham’s speech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September).

Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers.

The reality is that many of the services needed by elderly and incapacitated people – such as cleaning, meal preparation, transport to medical appointments, household repairs and personal services such as podiatry, hair care, physiotherapy, counselling or therapeutic massage – are also required by others and are already freely available in local markets.

The trouble is that they are most often supplied by online platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo or Housekeep with no commercial incentive to address social need.

One solution would be to set up local platforms that supply these services to anyone, regardless of age or disability. If these platforms made sure that all staff were suitably trained, qualified and security-checked, and their vehicles suitably adapted, they could be attractive to all local residents, whose commercial use of them would help subsidise their costs. Social care recipients could be provided with access to them using a voucher system that would be much cheaper than setting up such services from scratch or bundling them in with huge outsourcing contracts.

With suitable public oversight, using platform technology for public good would also bring other benefits to the local economy. Services would be better for all. Workers could upgrade their skills and gain job security. And, instead of being siphoned off to tax havens, any profits could remain, as Burnham might put it, “in every postcode”. Ursula HuwsLondon

Andy Burnham’s commitment to a national care service brings welcome clarity to a debate that has too often avoided difficult choices. But before deciding how to pay for care, we must answer a prior question: what should people be able to count on?

Reports that the proposed service may follow Scotland’s model of free personal care raise an important distinction. Removing charges for help with washing, dressing and eating could make a substantial difference. But social care is about much more than these tasks. When we in the coalition government developed the Care Act, we placed wellbeing at its heart. Its purpose extends to dignity, independence, relationships, participation and people’s control over their own lives.

There is a risk that defining a national care service primarily through free personal care narrows our understanding of what social care is for. The two need not be in conflict. Free personal care could form part of a wider national guarantee, grounded in the Care Act’s wellbeing principle and applying to people across adulthood.

The Casey commission has an important opportunity to help establish that wider promise. The question is whether the new service will simply change what people pay, or also strengthen the care and support that they can rely on to live their lives. Paul BurstowFormer minister of state for care services, 2010-12

Andy Burnham’s decision that proposals for social care reform will not happen until after the next election is the latest instalment in almost two-decade saga of delays.

Since a Labour government first committed to social care reform in 2007, we have seen a succession of unfulfilled promises: the discarded Personal Care at Home Act 2010, David Cameron’s part-implemented Care Act 2014, Theresa May’s failed 2017 proposals, and Boris Johnson’s 2019 pledge on the steps of Downing Street to fix social care – delayed under Rishi Sunak, then scrapped by Rachel Reeves in 2024.

In the years since this saga of broken promises began, both of my parents were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. One of them survives, and our family continues to wait for any meaningful help.

Families living through the reality of the social care crisis do not have the luxury of waiting for another election cycle. Mr Burnham needs to get a move on. Dr Ruth CharlesSwavesey, Cambridgeshire

As a 69-year-old in receipt of 20 years’ teacher’s pension and a full state pension, I say by all means take money from pensioners. Scrap national insurance (a retrogressive tax) and increase income tax. Scrap all age-related tax benefits/exemptions. But please don’t hit the triple lock until the state pension reaches parity with most European states (Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?, 29 September). It is mainly women who rely solely on this inadequate pension, and many of them live alone in rented accommodation. They are the last people who should be asked to make sacrifices. Sarah JamesMonmouth

As an 86-year-old, I’m sure I am not alone in having anxiety about paying for a care home if the need arises, and am delighted that Andy Burnham is determined to sort out the system at last. While the triple-lock pension increases are very welcome, I’d happily accept their change into simply keeping up with prices as a trade-off for never having to worry about paying for social care. Michael MillerSheffield

A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:53:18 GMT

Gian Lorenzo Spisso says his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evils

Reading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen.

I come from Italy, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented.

Having lived in the UK since 2014 and watched its parties with an outsider’s eyes, I still see first past the post as the lesser of two evils.

Brexit exposed a complete lack of leadership in David Cameron’s Conservative party, and it was an act of unprecedented self-harm that we are all still paying for, quite literally. But it also showed that parties outside the big two can exert enough pressure to force the party in power to adapt and, alas, to listen to voters.

Labour, meanwhile, has reinvented itself remarkably: from Ed Miliband’s soft left to Jeremy Corbyn’s more radical programme, and back again when that proved ineffective. Would a major party put itself through so much self-scrutiny without the incentives of first past the post? Or would it have split into several streams, perhaps more representative but far less effective, squandering its history as so many parties of the Italian left have done?

As a settled-status resident who expects to become a citizen this year, and is hoping to vote for Labour at the next general election, I can only say: please don’t do this. Gian Lorenzo SpissoBristol

Unfair method of splitting pensions can add to the pain of divorce

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:53:09 GMT

Richard Nobbs draws attention to fundamental flaw in way pension assets are split on divorce and calls on Labour to act

Your article on the impact of the escalating cost of living on divorce settlements (Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers, 23 September) provides a timely reminder of the financial inequities facing many separating couples.

As a pensions expert, I have regularly encountered a particular imbalance in the splitting of pension assets on divorce. Although the last Labour government enabled pension savings to be taken into account in divorce settlements, there remains, 25 years on, an inherent unfairness in the way many such arrangements are implemented.

Where one partner (usually the husband) has built up valuable pension entitlements through a defined benefit pension, the allocation of those assets on divorce is often based on an equivalent cash value at the point of divorce, known as “external sharing”.

In thousands of such cases, especially those involving private sector pensions, this leads to the undervaluing of pension assets transferred – usually to the wife and, in some cases, by many thousands of pounds.

Divorce is a traumatic enough experience. This fundamental flaw in the legal process compounds unfairness and is both unnecessary and easily rectified. The government should address this urgently to avoid sleepwalking into another pensions scandal. Richard NobbsExcalibur Actuaries

I have a new favourite medical drama – and now I want to have a nasty accident in Pittsburgh

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:20:36 GMT

The Pitt is on a different level – it’s not so much like watching drama as being in one

I do like a TV doctor. I’m not talking about proper doctors who sit on studio sofas dispensing wisdom. I’ve nothing against them – why, I worked with Dr Hilary Jones on ITV and he was a very nice chap – but it’s to fictional doctors I want to entrust my care.

I’ve not always felt this way. Either the standard of fictional TV medics has improved or, more likely, I’m losing the plot. It’s a relatively recent thing. I never watched ER, for some reason, and I find Casualty to be quite entertaining without ever fantasising about being rushed into Holby City hospital for emergency treatment. As for being treated by the staff of Grey’s Anatomy, that would be fine, but the constant playing of pop songs at key moments would get on my nerves. Nurse Jackie? Jackie Peyton and Dr O’Hara are a compelling nurse-doctor pairing, but too unhinged for me to take the risk with them. Shame, but I’ve got to be sensible.

There’s only one place I want to take my accident-and-emergency requirements. Be it a mere ankle sprain or a full-on life-threatener, to Pittsburgh is where I’ll be heading. The Pitt, on HBO, is on a different level.

It’s not so much like watching drama as being in one. I feel so close to the doctors, from the trainees to the top dog, that first and foremost I want to be friends with them. Although, understanding the need to keep our doctor-patient relationships professional, I appreciate this won’t be possible.

It’s in their capacity as doctors I want to engage with them. If I had a nasty accident in Pittsburgh – I haven’t ruled out going there to try to make this happen – and I woke up in that emergency room, I’d be absolutely made up. Seriously, even knowing they are actors and not doctors, I’d be very happy to have their medical attention. Perhaps not for actual surgery – that would be silly – but for general diagnosis and a bit of stitching or some such, bring it on.

I’ve given some thought as to my top picks. Naturally, it depends on the nature of my emergency, but at my bedside I’d go for Frank Langdon. Not everyone’s cup of tea, but he has bags of experience and he’s dealing very bravely with his drug-dependency problem. Alongside him I’d want Cassie McKay: no nonsense, but compassionate with it. And I would, of course, be hoping against hope that my case was complex or nasty enough to warrant them calling out for Dr Robbie to come over and have a look. No further intervention would be necessary. Two minutes with him would see me rise from my bed and walk away, right as rain.

As for my primary-care needs, geographically challenging though it would be, as it’s 3,600 miles away, my GP would be on the Cornish coast. There’s no one for me but Doc Martin’s Dr Martin Ellingham. I’ve only recently come across this classic, thanks to my mum, whom I gently mocked when I found her watching it. One episode and I was hooked.

I had it down as chocolate-box fluff, but there’s more to it than that. The doctor is engagingly misanthropic and some of the storylines and themes are decidedly dark. I went back to the beginning and I am binge-watching all 79 episodes. I love it so much that I interviewed its creator, Dominic Minghella. While he was naturally pleased at my enthusiasm, I got the sense that even he thought I might be going a little over the top.

But Martin Clunes’ Dr Ellingham is exactly what I want from a GP. Enough of the kindly, understanding family doctor guff; I want someone skilled, but also impatient, abrupt, direct and unpardonably rude. Just give it to me straight. And if Doc Martin can’t help, he can pack me off to Pittsburgh to do the rest.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

‘Strong indications’ that Iran played role in RAF Fairford incident, says Burnham

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:00:12 GMT

PM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security services

There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said.

Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved.

On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Washington believed “a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran.

In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.

“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”

Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.”

He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”

Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”

In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.”

The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police.

They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London.

On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events.

The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it.

Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions.

He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”

It emerged on Tuesday that one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident.

The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed.

However, UK officials and Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, have indicated that security services were aware in advance of what was happening.

A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”

French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:58:30 GMT

Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing

A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel.

Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.

Five years on, another four people are still missing.

The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”.

Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.

Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”.

Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.

The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.

Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four ​years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. One man was found innocent.

According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.

Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived.

For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel.

A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.

Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found.

He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ”

The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region.

Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.

‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:56:09 GMT

Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.

As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”

The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.

Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.

Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.

Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.

Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.

This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.

Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.

While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.

“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”

Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.

“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”

Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.

Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.

She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”

The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.

“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”

Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.

Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”

Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.

“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:44:17 GMT

The price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save

Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill forecast to jump by £276 to the equivalent of nearly £2,000 year.

It is a worrying outlook but there are practical steps you can take to mitigate the predicted price shock.

“Switching energy tariff to a well-priced fixed deal is the biggest lever households on the price cap can pull to bring their costs down right now,” says Richard Neudegg, the director of regulation at Uswitch.

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable tariffs set by Ofgem’s price cap, which increases by 4% from Thursday, equivalent to taking the typical annual dual-fuel bill up by £60 to £1,723.

The cap is due to rise 16% further to £1,999 in January, according to the latest forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight. “The cheapest deal on the market is currently £324 less than this,” says Neudegg.

The number of cap-beating deals has been steadily declining in recent weeks but there are still 34 deals below the January forecast, with some cheaper than October’s rates. At the moment the cheapest is Fuse Energy’s 12-month fix at £1,675, beating the October price cap by £48, and potentially January’s by as much as £324.

Combi boilers work best when they heat radiators to 60C or below. But in many homes the “flow temperature” is often set much too high at 70C- 80C. It only takes a few minutes to turn it down and this alone could save you about £60 a year. With some people reluctant to fiddle with their boiler settings, the charity Nesta has a step-by-step guide on its website.

Combi boilers allow users also to control the temperature of hot water supplied to taps and showers. Reducing the hot water temperature to 42C reduces the amount of fuel needed to heat the water and doing this could shave 2% off your gas bill, it suggests.

Installing inexpensive draught-proofing strips around windows and doors is a quick and easy DIY job that could shave £25 a year off your energy bill.

You can buy foam, metal or plastic draught strips, or brush seals for sash windows, cut them to size and attach around opening casements. Use a thicker option for doors. Flues can be plugged easily with a chimney balloon or a draught excluder.

Curtains are another easy way of reducing draughts and retaining heat. You could invest in some heavy-duty thermal-lined curtains, or alternatively buy a thermal lining for your existing ones.

According to the World Health Organization, the lowest comfortable temperature for most people is between 18C and 21C so if you’re warm enough, try turning your thermostat down by 1C – this could save you about £120 a year, according to the Energy Saving Trust.

If you have thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs), the dial that controls how much hot water enters the radiator it is attached to, you will be able to adjust the temperature separately in each room. TRVs usually have a scale from 0 to 6, where 0 is off and 6 is fully open.

The Energy Saving Trust recommends putting it on the lowest setting that keeps the room at a comfortable temperature, which could be 3 or 4 for rooms you use the most and 2 or 3 for others. Managing the temperature this way can save a household about £40 a year.

Most modern hot water tanks have plenty of insulation, but an older tank might have only a small amount. Adding an 80mm jacket to a tank with 25mm foam built-in can save homeowners in Great Britain about £45 a year, it says. The jackets cost about £20 and are widely available from DIY retailers.

Insulating (or lagging) pipes helps keep in the heat and prevent damage during cold winter months. There are several different types of material used for lagging but the most popular is polyethylene foam mainly because of how affordable and easy it is to install.

Homes can lose about 25% of their heat through an uninsulated roof. Many already have some loft insulation but topping it up can help retain more heat. If your current setup is about 120mm thick, increasing it to the 270mm (the minimum recommendation for new builds) could save you in the region of £20 a year.

There are plenty of online tutorials showing you how to do this yourself. DIY stores sell rolls of mineral wool insulation, with a roll of standard “top-up” insulation £27 at Wickes, for example.

Most homes built between 1920 and 1990 were constructed with uninsulated cavity walls, and the Energy Saving Trust estimates adding cavity wall insulation (where an installer injects insulation material from the outside) could save £200 a year.

If your boiler needs replacing it might be time to explore a green alternative. The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to help homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water heat pump system.

Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000. If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get an interest-free loan or a grant to make your home more energy efficient.

When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.

The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits. Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can save about £330 a year compared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.

‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 15:28:45 GMT

Prime minister’s pure political argument marks new era for party as he sets out his plans and priorities

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history.

There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough.

Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases.

The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed.

When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears.

But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy.

After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them.

In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said.

The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument.

And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence.

“I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.”

Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one.

Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said.
