after newsletter promotion

On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines.

“There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.”

Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.”

Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted.

Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.”

Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality.

But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:55:28 GMT

Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics

A number of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour party conference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission on electoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tell you to when (definitely not the 1990s).

Burnham’s support for proportional representation has always been extremely unusual for a Labour politician. To this day, he ascribes that to his experience of winning an election as mayor of Greater Manchester on a supplementary votes system, where people get to choose a first- and second-preference candidate. He said that campaigning under that system “finally aligned the conversation on the door with what people want from politics, which is about problem-solving first and foremost, not about point-scoring”. He went a bit further this morning, asking Nick Robinson on the Today programme: “Can we really watch a party with less than 30% walk into Downing Street?”

Plainly, he was talking about the spectre of a Reform government, and it’s that very context that makes this already difficult constitutional conversation even more vexed. Back in May, the all-party parliamentary group for fair elections held a meeting to discuss the aftermath of the local elections. It feels like a long time ago, and furthermore, so different in atmosphere as to be irrelevant to the prime minister, but 2020s politics are defined by their switchblade turns. In the matter of constitutional reform, the overriding priority has to be to build a system that’s fair across a range of imaginable scenarios, not just the one in front of you.

The locals delivered great results for Reform, and satisfactory ones for the Liberal Democrats, which reflected the realities of a first-past-the-post (FPTP) system – first, it rewards the winner, and second, it rewards geographical concentration. Labour walked away from the 2024 general election with 63% of the seats on 34% of the votes, the largest overrepresentation ever. The Greens have spent years commanding the fervent support of a geographically diffuse but not insignificant minority, with almost nothing to show for it in parliamentary terms.

The distortions of FPTP have been well-known for years, but historically they were only ever discussed in terms of the barrier to entry they presented to insurgent parties, and the democratic deficit they constituted to any voter who didn’t live in a marginal seat, which is to say the majority of voters. So the counter-arguments were that, for all its flaws, by keeping out insurgents, the traditional voting system kept out extremists: and who wouldn’t sacrifice a little bit (or a huge amount) of democracy, for the sake of steadiness?

Stability was the first myth to fall, when it transpired, over the past 10 years, that you can keep on returning one of two main parties as reliably as you like, and they will have no problem confecting so much intra-party turmoil that you might as well have voted for the Monster Raving Loony party. The efficacy of FPTP in keeping out extremists, meanwhile, was – like a stock market bubble – true until it wasn’t. Once politics has fragmented, the system rewards short bursts of popularity with potentially very long periods of power. That has a toxic effect on the supposedly sober heads of the political centre who, once they see extreme, often bigoted, positions pay off in the polls, steer straight towards them. The best prophylactic against extremism is not a gamified voting system but some political backbone. Undoubtedly in response to all that, public attitudes to proportional representation have changed enormously, hitting an all-time high of 60% support last year. In 2011 it was 27%.

To return to that meeting in May, there was one more finding from the local elections: once you start to lose, under FPTP, you lose calamitously. So the obvious solution, to a room full of already fully committed constitutional reformer MPs, was for the next prime minister to change the system, right? Psephologists John Curtice and Prof Tim Bale sounded the warning: you can’t change the rules just because you’re losing. The point was so self-evident, from such trusted sources, that all the air seemed to leave the room. But four months on, Labour is ahead in the polls, Reform’s support is tailing off and seems to have further to fall. Far more importantly, this week Burnham showed himself prepared to have a thorny, inconvenient debate that wouldn’t necessarily even serve his political interests, and even if it did, would certainly disperse his power, because he believes in his cause and does so persuasively. So he doesn’t look like he’s losing.

How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:45:43 GMT

As soaring rents and house prices across Europe​ feed into the political discourse, campaigners believe they have a rare opportunity to force housing to the top of the agenda

Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It was billed as one of the largest real-estate events in Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset.

Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair, was being evicted from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. As anger over the eviction gave way to days of protests and an encampment in the heart of Madrid, the presence of campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis.

The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit. “Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.”

The Guardian has long reported on the depth of the housing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period.

Not all countries have been hit equally; while Vienna remains a bright spot for its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rents surge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%.

Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim White noted last year, as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.”

Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected by the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona, told me last year.

Voters in Berlin, however, recently opted for another path. In a city where rents had climbed nearly 70% in the past decade, a quarter of voters backed the leftwing party Die Linke in this month’s state elections, making it Berlin’s strongest party. The strategy behind their success was far from rocket science, said Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir. “Because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue [of housing] unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.”

‘This is just getting started’

Some have sought shared solutions to the shared crisis. At the Madrid counter-summit, campaigners launched a pan-European alliance to demand indefinite rental contracts and rent control across the continent.

Earlier this month, dozens of organisations launched the European Citizens’ Initiative, calling on people to sign their petition for EU-level measures to protect tenants, curb speculation and convert empty buildings into homes. “In every European country, in every major survey, and across all age groups, housing emerges as the number one concern of citizens,” the initiative notes. “We see and feel it every day: workers who can no longer afford the city they build, young people who cannot leave their parents’ home, tenants pushed out of their neighbourhoods after renovation, empty buildings while people sleep on the street.”

In Spain, where the days-long encampment in Madrid has led to similar camps in cities such as Barcelona, Seville and Palma de Mallorca, the protests have already begun to have an impact.

after newsletter promotion

Maricarmen, the evicted octogenarian, will be allowed to return to her apartment, it was confirmed on Tuesday. Her rent will remain around the €500 a month she had paid for years – significantly less than the €2,650 the investment firm that owns her apartment had initially demanded.

This week the Spanish government also said it had approved two housing decrees that include reforms such as a ban on evictions until 2030, and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. But these measures will now have to win approval in the country’s fractured parliament.

What exactly comes next for the housing movement that has gripped Spain in recent days is anyone’s guess. With the spectre of general elections looming and the Socialist-led coalition scrambling to shore up its base of progressive voters, campaigners have spotted a singular opportunity to tackle an issue that Spaniards have long ranked as one of the country’s biggest problems.

“The coming days will be crucial,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said on Tuesday as it called for further protests this weekend. “A historic window of opportunity has opened to reverse decades of the commodification of housing. That is why we need to step up the pressure.”

Or, as the Málaga Tenants’ Union put it in an online post: “This is just getting started.”

BBC removes article linking bare nails trend to ‘white supremacist standards of beauty’

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:38:43 GMT

Corporation says story did not meet editorial standards after it attracts criticism from US and UK media

A BBC article that included a claim that a trend for bare nails was linked to “white supremacist standards of beauty” has been permanently removed from its website, after editors concluded it did not meet the corporation’s editorial standards.

The article, which first ran on the BBC’s website on 27 September, examined an apparent “viral craze” for bare rather than decorated nails. It said the trend had been flooding social media and fashion catwalks.

It also covered criticisms of the trend, which suggested it could “stigmatise bold manicures”. The article noted that nail art had its roots in black, Latino and Asian communities.

In an early section of the article, it quoted the beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo as saying: “That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities.

“They are often called elegant or tasteful and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty.”

Later in the piece, Rodulfo was quoted again as saying: “The examples are almost always white women or celebrities … [and] they’ll often conflate class and taste with that bareness.”

The BBC initially removed the article from its website on Tuesday after the piece had attracted criticism from media outlets in the US, particularly on the political right. The corporation stated it had been removed “pending an editorial review”.

However, the BBC has since confirmed that the article had been permanently removed. Bosses concluded there was no challenge in the piece to the quotes linking bare nails to white supremacy, or any context that such opinions would be seen as extreme.

A Wall Street Journal piece stated the BBC article was “embarrassingly retrograde – displaying outdated intellectual fashion – in its attempt to locate offences against social justice in the decisions of individual women whether or not to paint their nails”.

It stated: “When you see someone dressed for a costume party, you notice how conspicuous that person is. So it is with the BBC’s attempt to gin up outrage over the semiotics of nail polish.”

The New York Post, part of Rupert Murdoch’s media stable, also ran an article criticising the piece, as did Fox News.

An opinion piece in the Telegraph also attacked it. “I’ve had some rude awakenings in my time, but being told I’m a white supremacist before I’ve had my coffee? That’s got to be up there,” wrote Celia Walden, a feature writer.

On its corrections and clarifications register, the BBC stated: “This article examined the trend of bare nails and what might be motivating it, hearing from a range of contributors as well as looking at the cultural significance of manicures. It was removed on 29 September pending an editorial review.

“Following this review the article was permanently removed on the same day because it reported criticism of the bare nails trend without sufficient context or challenge and so did not meet our editorial standards.”

The BBC has not revealed who made the decision to remove the article. However, the corporation’s deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, was appointed to the new role in order to catch potential editorial rows that plagued the leadership of the former director general, Tim Davie.

Matt Brittin, who replaced Davie, was also keen to have a deputy for support on editorial matters, given his lack of television and editorial experience.

The BBC is still the subject of legal action from Donald Trump over the way an episode of Panorama edited together two parts of a Trump speech. While the BBC apologised for the edit, it has always maintained the documentary did not defame the president.

‘Of course I’m the underdog’: the British former spin doctor trying to turn California red

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:00:42 GMT

Steve Hilton’s long-shot campaign for governor is courting Golden state voters with unapologetically populist message

Steve Hilton stands almost no chance of becoming California’s next governor, but that isn’t stopping him from campaigning as though he was just one step away from pulling off the impossible.

The former Downing Street political adviser and Fox News host refuses to be daunted by the rancid political environment for Republican candidates this year, or by opinion polls that tell him he is lagging 20 percentage points or more behind his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra.

Instead, as he barnstorms the state in an effort to rally the Republican faithful and win over as many Democrats and independents as he can find, he is following a full-throated people-versus-the-powerful script and pumping out what he hopes will be crowd-pleasing policy proposals as fast as he can come up with them.

Abolish the department of motor vehicles, he suggested a couple of weeks ago. Cut the price of gas to $3 a gallon. Start a new business school in working-class East Los Angeles. Set up a competition among California’s 58 counties to build 10 brand-new cities from the ground up.

Many of these ideas dovetail with the argument Hilton has made from the day he started running, that California has been driven to the brink of ruin by 16 years of Democratic party control over every statewide office. “Enough is enough,” as his campaign slogan says.

But they also mark a return to his roots as a prolific and occasionally unpredictable political ideas man, known during his time working for the British Conservative party for spitting out proposals while wandering barefoot through the corridors of power.

Policy has been one of the few throughlines in Hilton’s unconventional political journey from one side of the Atlantic to the other. He’s been a restaurant owner and business consultant as well as a senior adviser in the coalition government led by David Cameron in the 2010s. He came to California largely because his wife, Rachel Whetstone, established herself as a big tech public relations guru in Silicon Valley.

For many years, Whetstone was considered the power in the couple, while he wrote a couple of policy books – about “positive populism” and putting a human face on government – and used his connections in the conservative movement to land his Fox News show. Seizing the chance to try to resuscitate a largely moribund California Republican party came only much later.

Hilton prides himself on being “un-pigeonhole-able” and thinks of his campaign style as some combination of three startlingly different recent presidential candidates – Bernie Sanders, for his unwavering commitment to lift up struggling people; the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, for his fondness for libertarian free-market solutions; and John Kasich, the former governor of Ohio, for his “happy warrior” campaigning style.

Many of his ideas come straight out of the Republican playbook, accounting for the mistrust he inspires in many Democratic voters. He wants to set up a California version of Doge, Elon Musk’s so-called department of government efficiency that took a hatchet to federal agencies in the opening months of Trump’s second presidency. He wants to kill several environmental regulations, including a plan to introduce more energy-efficient vehicle tires over the next decade. (Hilton calls the energy commissioner who came up with the idea a “tire-rant”).

He also wants to cancel big, expensive public works projects starting with the long-delayed high-speed train from San Francisco to Los Angeles, which Hilton, in common with other Republicans, calls “the bullshit train to nowhere”.

Many of his other proposals, though, are harder to define: a plan to eliminate state taxes on the first $150,000 of income, which echoes similar proposals from some of Becerra’s more progressive Democratic primary challengers; the business school plan, which would offer free tuition to lower-income students; or a plan to turn the highway patrol into a full-fledged statewide police investigation force “liberated” from the DMV that currently finances it.

Still, Hilton is a savvy and appealing communicator, with a keen understanding of what frustrates and infuriates ordinary Californians. He acknowledges that his more outlandish ideas are unlikely to win this or any other election. But he believes they tell voters he is a pragmatic, independent thinker who, in an age of extremes and polarized political discourse, can talk to anyone, negotiate with anyone, and can entertain any good idea as long as it makes people’s lives easier and lifts the burden of government inefficiency and bloat.

He knows that California voters of all political persuasions are frustrated by the daily struggle of keeping up with soaring food and gas prices and looking for solutions to an array of social ills from homelessness to dwindling access to healthcare. It’s a big part of the reason why he led the polls for much of the primary campaign and ended up a close second behind Becerra in a crowded field.

“I’m not ideological,” he likes to say. “I’m not tribal.”

A major problem for him, though, is that he belongs to a party in thrall to “the president whose name begins with T”, as Hilton calls him – a leader whose name is particularly toxic in California, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a two-to-one margin, and, this year, is dragging down Republican candidates across the country.

That has greatly complicated his quest to convince Californians that, by shrinking the size of the state government and slashing what he sees as over-burdensome regulations on small businesses, he can make the state more affordable for ordinary people. However encouraging it was to win close to 25% of the primary vote in June, building up another 25% of the vote in the general election has proven daunting.

And Hilton knows it. “Of course I’m the underdog,” he said. “Of course it’s an uphill battle. People are out of the habit of voting Republican. Still, I see a narrow but real path to victory. I see winning.”

Often, Hilton finds himself walking a fine line between indulging California’s Trump diehards, a vital part of his base, and broadening his appeal. He has made clear he doesn’t want Donald Trump or any other national Republican figure to campaign for him. He has distanced himself from Trump’s complaints of a “rigged system” and sees no need to restrict mail-in voting. But he has talked in the past of being friends with half of Trump’s cabinet and earned Trump’s endorsement during the primary, making it difficult to put much distance between himself and the man in the Oval Office.

When facing crowds of the Republican faithful, as he did during the primaries and continues to do at town halls up and down the state, his non-tribal bona fides are quickly tested by supporters eager to talk about Democrats stealing elections, conspiring to take away gun rights, and unjustly prosecuting insurrectionists who attacked the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.

At a recent event in San Gabriel, in the eastern Los Angeles suburbs, Hilton did nothing to discourage such talk. Rather, he milked several applause lines by promising to be a champion for such supporters once he was in office. “I’ve never said anything I don’t believe,” he explained in an interview shortly before the event. “I just don’t say everything that I believe.”

Away from the Maga faithful, Hilton has made the case that California’s problems have far more to do with the Democrats than with the occupant of the Oval Office. “You don’t have to like Trump. You don’t have to become a Republican,” he wrote in an unusual full-page advertisement that ran in the Los Angeles Times and the San Francisco Chronicle in July. “You just have to ask yourself: does it make sense to vote the same way and expect a different result?”

On the campaign trail, Hilton likes to point out that California sees more people moving to other states each year than it receives in new residents. This trend goes back to Schwarzenegger’s governorship, and has not, in most years, led to an overall decline in the state population because international migrants have made up the shortfall. Still, Hilton has woven it into his stump speech. “In the time Gavin Newsom has been governor, millions have moved out of the greatest state in the greatest nation on earth. That’s a terrible indictment,” he says. “Are they fleeing Trump? I don’t think so. Most of them are fleeing to states run by Republicans.”

The voters Hilton hopes will be most open to such lines of argument are those he sees suffering most acutely from California’s affordability crisis – working-class, non-college educated, many of them Latino. From the early days of his primary campaign, he has sat down with small groups and listened to them talking about the tax and regulatory burdens on their businesses, or the high cost of running a car or truck, or the struggle to find high-quality public schools in non-affluent parts of the state.

Such small-scale campaigning goes against received wisdom in California, where consultants of both parties have traditionally relied on television and internet advertising in the belief that a state of 39 million people is too big to reach any other way. Still, Hilton is betting that by talking to voters who don’t normally get to interact with candidates, he can spread the word that he is personable, willing to listen, and eager to help improve people’s lives.

Hilton knows his idiosyncratic mix of styles exposes him to mockery, if not actual satire – his shoot-from-the-hip policy ideas were memorably parodied on the British TV show The Thick of It. He recalled, for example, an episode of his Fox News show when he insisted on promoting the distinctly un-Republican virtues of home nursing visits to promote perinatal health. “It was a low-rated segment,” he said.

But Hilton also has faith in his ability to connect to voters – the British accent probably helps – and his talent for a pithy phrase. He can be devastating, for example, when talking about Becerra, who he calls an “empty suit” embodying the very worst of Democratic party complacency.

“The level of disrespect for the process is actually shocking,” Hilton said. “Clearly he assumes he’s just going to coast to victory on the back of the Democratic machine … We keep inviting him to engage with us in different ways, but he keeps citing schedule conflicts. What are these conflicts? He’s not scheduling anything.”

Becerra did eventually agree to one debate with Hilton, set for Wednesday. In response to Hilton’s criticisms, Becerra spokesperson Jonathan Underland said: “Steve is desperate to land his dream job as a talking head on the Fox propaganda network. That’s why he can’t stop saying Xavier Becerra’s name.”

It remains to be seen if the debate can shake some of the Becerra camp’s confidence, but for now Hilton is on track to do worse than Gavin Newsom’s barely remembered Republican challenger from 2022, Brian Dahle, who lost by 18 points. A recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showed even independents favoring Becerra by close to a 20-point margin.

Hilton, though, is refusing to let these numbers bother him as the race enters its final frenetic stretch and his campaign stops become shorter and more intense. On a recent Saturday, Hilton dropped into an Orthodox synagogue in Beverly Hills, where he sported a tallit and a kipa to address a congregation of Iranian Jews for a brisk 10 minutes. On his next stop, 35 miles to the east, he poured exactly one beer and served up one table’s worth of taco plates at a family-owned Mexican restaurant in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains.

He has learned to spit out his message in small bites, asking a group of tattooed truckers at the Mexican restaurant how they would like it if their annual vehicle registration fee was capped at $73 (part of his DMV abolition plan), then telling a gaggle of Republican women in stars-and-stripes shirts that they needed to copy Democratic get-out-the-vote techniques instead of complaining about the other side cheating.

“This election is not about who you hate in Washington,” Hilton pleaded in his Trump-distancing ad in July, “it’s about what you love here.” His supporters keep telling him he has to win because their livelihoods depend on it. But, so far, the wider California electorate believes the race is indeed about who they hate in Washington – and nothing Hilton does or says seems to be changing their minds.

Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:00:28 GMT

Dad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lens

Is this the sketch my father would have wanted? Not something I have previously given much thought to. He died 15 years before I even started this job. But my guess is that it is. He was the loveliest of men who only ever wanted for me what I wanted for me. He was stupidly proud of even my most forgettable successes. I still see him in my dreams, cheering me on. He’d almost certainly be embarrassed, but secretly pleased, to find himself in the first paragraph.

But that’s enough about my father issues. Time now to talk about Andy Burnham’s. In his emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech on Tuesday – I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to have a politician other than Nigel Farage say exactly what he thinks and believes – Andy told us he wanted to build the country his father would have wanted. It was almost a debt of honour. Burnham was very precise. This was not his vision. This wasn’t the country he wanted to build. It was the one his dad had wanted. Andy was merely a conduit, channelling Roy, who died earlier this month.

So come Wednesday morning, on the traditional post-speech media round, the BBC’s Nick Robinson had clearly designated himself a latter-day Sigmund Freud for Burnham’s Today programme interview. You get the picture: Andy on the couch, Nick sitting just behind his right shoulder, firmly out of view. Never let the therapist get in the way of the subconscious. Only Robinson can’t take the silences. Some analysts pride themselves on a 50-minute session where nothing is said. That’s when the real psychotherapeutic work gets done. Apparently. A nice earner if you can get it.

There was no time to bother with the niceties. Nick specialises more in speed therapy. Done and dusted inside 20 minutes. From nought to catharsis. There was no “How are you feeling? Is there anything you need to talk about today?” Instead, he cut straight to the chase. And why not? Everyone knows that all patients are merely mainlining their parents. Everything can be traced back to childhood.

Andy clearly doesn’t hold with the Philip Larkin “They fuck you up” doctrine. He only got good stuff from his dad. Or maybe the good stuff is all that he cares to remember. Siggy Robbo missed a trick there. Surely your father would be telling you not to be so nostalgic, he said, but Burnham was adamant. Roy would have stuck to his roots of quiet patriotism. Nick tried another tack. The funeral was taking place on Friday. Was he on an emotional rollercoaster? Andy conceded that he could be. But rollercoasters were his happy place.

This could be habit-forming. Maybe it’s an approach we should take with all our party leaders. Rather than seeing them as players on a global stage with the capacity to make our lives infinitely worse, we should be more understanding. Treat them as patients in need of treatment. After all, you’ve surely got to be a dangerously unbalanced narcissist to even imagine you can run a country. Desire for office should act as a disqualification on health grounds. Some politicians would probably get an automatic upgrade from narcissist to sociopath. Donald Trump and Boris Johnson come immediately to mind.

Think also of Keir Starmer, Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch. Keir clearly had a tricky relationship with his dad. One where there was a lot that went unsaid. So maybe we shouldn’t blame him for never being able to articulate what he felt. Then there’s Nige. Has he inherited a hatred for all immigrants, or is he reacting against his parents? Maybe they took in refugees and forced the seven-year-old Nige to play with them against his will. And where did he get his pathological need for money, no matter how questionable the source? Did his parents squander his inheritance on gifts to charity? As for Kemi, where to start? I’ve never seen a politician so full of loathing. Could that be down to a Larkin-like childhood?

With the therapy over, Siggy briefly turned to the substance of the speech. All the big-ticket policies were for after the next election. What was going to happen in the next three years? Andy shrugged. He was a straight-talking guy. There wasn’t much he could do. Energy bills were going up faster than he could offer rebates. He couldn’t stop the wars around the world. The cost of debt was out of his hands. The Tories could say they would cut welfare, but nothing much would change. We needed to be patient. Things would get better. Just so long as Labour won in 2029.

Social care, the triple lock, Brexit and electoral reform. These were the real engines that would transform the country and reconnect voters with politics. Instruments of trust. How that would happen would be for others to decide. Single market, customs union, rejoin. All were on the table. Let’s just hope the far right haven’t taken over the EU by the time it happens. A national care service. Not ideal – some people would still lose their homes – but better than what was currently on offer. Just don’t forget: Andy was merely a channel of peace. In a rare turnabout, Nick thanked Burnham for the therapy session. The bank transfer would follow.

Over in the main hall, the conference proper was dying on its arse. You could hear the exhibition stands being dismantled as Yvette Cooper, Lucy Powell and others made the last few speeches to polite applause. We ended as all Labour conferences ended – with renditions of The Red Flag and Jerusalem – and then it was a dash for the exits. Not that there was a scrum. Most people had already left.

But it was always going to be this way when the main event had taken place the previous afternoon. This had been the Andy Burnham show. And delegates couldn’t have been happier. The Labour party had rediscovered its soul. Its belief. A leader who could go toe-to-toe with the other parties. Maybe this was also the sketch that Andy Burnham’s father would have wanted.

Two million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of flooding

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 13:50:05 GMT

Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead

More than two million people in England are unaware their properties are at risk of flooding, as the UK braces for a wet and stormy start to the winter, according to the Environment Agency.

Experts say the next three months are more likely than usual to be wet and windy – due to a combination of large-scale weather patterns and the “subtle” impact of a supercharged El Niño – increasing the risk of flooding.

However, the EA warned on Wednesday that people in a third of the six million properties most at risk of flooding are unaware of the threat they face.

Caroline Douglass, the director for flood and coastal risk management at the Environment Agency, said: “We know with the 6m properties at risk [in England] … we know that one-third of people who are at risk don’t think they are at risk.”

She urged people to check on the government website whether their properties were at risk, and to take measures to prepare.

“We want the public to make sure they know what their risk is, so check on gov. uk. We need them to sign up for flood warnings … and if they are at risk, to have a flood plan so they know what they need to do.”

Flooding caused havoc across the UK last year and the Met Office said that, after a summer of droughts, extreme heat and wildfires, the UK was facing a wet and stormy start to winter.

Will Lang, the chief meteorologist with the Met Office, said its three-month outlook indicated there was an increased likelihood that October, November and December would be wet and windy, adding there were early indications of drier, colder and calmer conditions later in the winter.

“There is an increasing likelihood of it being wet overall, windier than normal and milder than usual as well,” said Lang.

He said El Niño – which is bringing devastation to other parts of the world – increased the likelihood of wetter and windier conditions in the UK but was only one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather. “This is just a subtle shift in the odds of it being wetter and windier,” he said. But he added that would lead to “a heightened potential for flooding”.

The Met Office said that although flooding was likely in the months ahead, drought conditions would remain in large parts of the UK until reservoirs returned to their normal water levels, adding that would require above-average rainfall over the winter.

Who’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone call

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 13:19:33 GMT

For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life

Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy.

When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues.

For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery. They are talking to us; their siblings, parents, cousins and friends. Sometimes the person on the end of the line is back home, other times they are in a western city also navigating the dislocations of immigrant life. The long phone call is a regular feature of diaspora lives, and even more so for those employed in long, solitary work such as cab driving. These conversations are about nothing and everything.

What are they talking about?

This is not an exhaustive list, but based on the calls I constantly field from friends and family, the content I receive in a follow-up call, and familiar themes from chats with drivers in Arabic (which I sometimes get drawn into), the subjects are remarkably consistent. The range includes family gossip, wedding updates, complaints about the cost of living in the west, advice on navigating complex immigration systems, extremely detailed health updates, and political analysis of whatever crisis is unfolding. These conversations can broadly be sorted into one of two categories: “serious technical resolution of a problem” or “shooting the breeze”.

In my experience, these beast mode long phone calls are between someone on a long shift, commute or drive, and a mother cooking in the kitchen. There is a languorous quality to the call. Time and conversational convention shift to accommodate long silences without explanation, as one person or the other breaks away to get on with something – dismount or park or blitz something in the food processor. Because the point is not the actual chat. It is a broadly phatic – that is to say language used for bonding – form of communication, an exercise in yearning and homesickness. It helps us bridge a gap between long distances and absences, and simulate a proximity that is so deeply longed for.

Why talk all through the working day?

The interminable phone call is an immigrant’s lifeline, now made cheap and stable by voice over IP (the ability to make calls on an internet connection). But it is also a feature of broader cultural and economic patterns. Western time is personal, individual, literally “me time”, something that is violated if demanded without permission. This time is parcelled out necessarily for decompression, for work, for leisure. In other cultures, time is social and public.

In Sudan, for example, there is no such thing as calling ahead before a visit. Your home is a drop-in destination from about 11am onwards. A neighbour will pop in for a chat, a relative will be driving home and swing by, and if there are children in the household, their own social lives mean you just never know how many people you are cooking for. The corner shop is a lifeline of last minute provision as numbers swell unexpectedly. If you are an introvert, good luck.

When that physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work. Certain conditions make the visit and the call possible. Homes where there is often a homemaker to receive, or work that does not require strict, in-office professional deportment and execution. Highly structured working environments and fast-paced modern lives mean that entire societies are firmly post-casual-phone-call. In these contexts, I find myself so wary of ambushing or alarming people with a call that I send a clear warning beforehand. No, there is nothing to worry about, and are you sure this is a good time to speak? Absolutely no worries if not.

But it is also a mindset, which you can lose over time. I find myself becoming increasingly post-phone call outside work, constantly thinking to myself that I will ring a relative back when I have the time. Generally, I prefer to message or voice note, conscious that when I return the call, it absolutely will not be a quick and efficient catch up. But, in truth, I do have the time, I have just assimilated the same rigid notions of downtime and non-urgent phone calls as an incursion. Fundamentally, this is an extremely capitalist notion of time as purely a function of work, where even if you are not working, you are “re-charging” in anticipation of more work.

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

Reclaiming the lost art of the ambling phone call

The fact that the long driver call is such a bewildering anomaly is a meeting of those two worlds. In one, a passenger cannot fathom that you might have so much to say to someone over the phone, because everyone you love or want to see is generally within your immediate social reach, and because it is unfathomable to dedicate so much of your precious bandwidth to seemingly aimless conversation. In another, loved ones are in a different country or sprawl all over the world, and without their constant companionship life is just alienation and monotonous work.

But I suspect there is more to the lost art of the phone call in certain societies than just the pressures of modernity. In contemporary life, there are so many ways to feel like you are in touch and in conversation when you are not. So many ways to feel part of some slipstream of humanity, when in fact we are scrolling, meme-ing, seeing news from friends and strangers alike via story updates, while not exchanging anything meaningful or even uttering a single word. Those in exile are acutely aware of alienation, and reach out to remedy it. But for those in their home countries, loneliness still lurks in ways harder to recognise. A phone call is honestly less time consuming and more replenishing than anything else we use our devices for.

Do you have long, aimless phone calls? How do you think your preferred mode of communication connects to your culture? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us at thelongwave@theguardian. com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Last week, we explored Britain’s fraught relationship with its historical role in enslavement. You shared your thoughts on the publication of the Register of British Slave Traders and the records of enslaved people, and mounting calls for recognition and reparations.

double quotation markI started to search online for my enslaved ancestors for the first time and discovered that decades of British secrecy means I have no written records of my ancestors to start with. No names no approximate births or death dates. This legacy means I have a family left not literate enough to document their history. Ancient family members that don’t speak English. People who make up their new own names because their family names derived from the slavers. It’s great that we have this info but I wish there was more help in finding the people we want to know about.

Former colonial powers would do well to teach history accurately – otherwise they risk forgetting the past rather than learning from it, and helping to correct the damage that was done while they enriched themselves for generations.

David P. A. Mullings, based in the US and Jamaica

Heavy metal is about uplifting the downtrodden. So why is alleged abuse by Marilyn Manson so easily forgotten?

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:53:08 GMT

Slipknot sharing their stage with a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women is the antithesis of everything the genre should stand for, even if he denies it

I have so many fond memories of my first heavy metal festival. It was Download 2012, and I was 15 years old. Metallica headlined, playing their landmark Black album in full for its 30th anniversary, and it was my first exposure to one of my future favourite bands, Trivium. But just as important as the music I heard that day was the sense of acceptance I felt when I was there. Outside of that field, my shaggy hair and my penchant for noisy riffs were looked down upon; inside, everybody looked like me. It seemed like some kind of paradise, and I went home feeling empowered. I’m far from the only person who’s had an experience like this. It’s easy to dig up interviews with everyone from Metallica’s James Hetfield to Judas Priest singer and gay icon Rob Halford about how heavy music champions the misfit – or at least it’s supposed to. This week, Marilyn Manson was confirmed to support Slipknot in front of 90,000 people at Wembley Stadium next July. He was booked despite the wave of sexual misconduct allegations levelled against him, plus a lawsuit from his former assistant alleging physical, emotional and psychological abuse that’s set to go to trial in November 2027. (The singer denies any wrongdoing, and in 2025 a four-year investigation into his alleged crimes was dropped with no charges filed.) If metal is supposed to uplift the downtrodden, then putting a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women on one of Europe’s biggest stages feels like the antithesis of everything the genre stands for.

Manson, whose real name is Brian Hugh Warner, retreated from the public eye after the start of the allegations against him in 2021, but he returned in 2024 with a new record deal and a string of high-profile tour dates. He’s far from the only allegedly problematic figure to have recently made a successful musical comeback. Chris Brown, who in 2009 pleaded guilty to felony assault of his ex-girlfriend Rihanna, and Ye (formerly Kanye West), who made a string of antisemitic statements in 2022, are playing massive venues. Earlier this month, the Guardian published an op-ed about Queen of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme’s cosy image rehabilitation after he kicked a female photographer and his ex-wife accused him of domestic abuse. Metal, with its long-established identity as a dangerous and anti-mainstream force, appears to be particularly lenient with this kind of figure. The news of Manson touring with Slipknot came three months after Pantera supported Metallica on their second night at the 62,500-capacity London Stadium. In 2016, Pantera singer Phil Anselmo faced widespread backlash for raising his hand and screaming “white power!” onstage at a charity concert. He eventually apologised, but in 2017 gave an interview where he called some of his detractors “phonies”. None of it stopped his band from reuniting to much celebration in 2022. In November, Nuclear Blast Records, the same label to which Manson signed in 2024, will release a new album by Anselmo’s other group, Down. In February, As I Lay Dying are poised to release a new album. The band split in 2014 after its sole constant member, singer Tim Lambesis, was sentenced to six years in prison for soliciting the murder of his ex-wife. Then, in 2024, everyone bar Lambesis quit the band, and some disturbing video surfaced online where he’s seen flipping a table that another ex-wife was sitting at. (The former couple have each accused the other of abuse.) As I Lay Dying’s latest single, aptly entitled Polarized, has amassed 560,000 YouTube views in two weeks regardless. Those figures are wildly outdone by US metalcore band Falling in Reverse’s track Joseph: currently one of the hottest songs in metal, boasting 20m YouTube views in two weeks, boosted by guest spots from Slipknot’s Corey Taylor and System of a Down’s Serj Tankian. This is after frontman Ronnie Radke became a lightning rod for controversy, having made a number of transphobic comments on social media, and contorted the backlash into part of his image: the cover of the band’s 2024 album Popular Monster bears his mugshot after a 2012 arrest for domestic assault. (The charge was dismissed in court in 2014.)

As far as pushback against these artists goes, the most consistent voices have been the disappointed fans on social media, who have dominated the announcement of the Slipknot/Manson tour to the point that the BBC and NME have reported on it. However, in previous instances, these disaffected cries have been drowned out by ticket sales: Manson’s tour of the UK in February 2025 completely sold out. Even more disheartening has been seeing other artists play along. Arena-fillers Five Finger Death Punch attempted to launch a Manson rehabilitation narrative ahead of their summer 2024 tour together, guitarist Zoltan Bathory saying it was OK because Manson is now “clean and sober”. Lamb of God toured with Pantera in 2023 and 2024: singer Randy Blythe apparently didn’t see any irony in doing this, then in 2025 called Elon Musk a “fucking asshole” for raising his hand in a similar manner to Anselmo’s gesture.

Of course, metal has never entirely been the post-judgmental utopia I experienced at 15: there has long been a drought of female representation and hate has found pockets in underground subcultures such as the Nationalist Socialist Black Metal scene. But in 2026 – with some of its biggest artists being accused of heinous acts against vulnerable people, only to return as popular as before, possibly more – the genre has never felt more fractured or unwelcoming, its inclusive messaging never more hollow. If I were to walk into my first metal festival today, see Falling in Reverse or Marilyn Manson play to thousands of fans, then go home and look at their histories, there’s a very strong chance I’d never go to a second.

How could Great Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your area

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:45:42 GMT

These visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systems

New analysis produced exclusively for the Guardian reveals how different voting systems would return significantly different seat totals in the UK parliament, based on recent polling.

While the current first past the post (FPTP) system could leave Labour short of a majority with 250 seats, the modelling shows how proportional systems would be likely to reduce the number of seats given to the leading party – and give the UK a more finely balanced parliament that better represents the votes people cast.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new national commission on electoral reform aimed at changing the electoral system, a plan supported by more than 100 Labour MPs as well as parties such as the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, the SNP and Plaid Cymru. Electoral reform has enjoyed increased public support in recent years.

The research conducted by More in Common suggests that, under proportional systems such as single transferable vote or regional party list, the UK could end up being governed by a minority government – or a progressive alliance of parties.

Under the current system, Labour would be the largest party, winning 39% of seats with only 26% of the vote. Labour would be 76 seats short of a majority, and would need to enter a coalition to form a government.

Lab 250

Reform 147

Con 125

Lib Dem 63

SNP 27

PC 6

Green 3

Restore 1

Others 9

How it works: Voters elect a local constituency representative. Because they elect a single MP in each constituency, parties can secure a parliamentary majority without winning a majority of votes nationwide, leading to disproportionate results between vote share and seats.

Labour would be the largest party in a fractured parliament, and would be well short of a majority. A coalition would be inevitable, but either a leftwing or rightwing coalition would struggle to claim 50% of the seats.

Lab 166

Reform 138

Con 125

Lib Dem 67

Green 59

Restore 45

SNP 20

PC 9

Others 2

How it works: Voters choose a party and seats are allocated in proportion to each party's vote share. Used widely across Europe and for Senedd elections in Wales, party list systems can use larger or smaller constituencies, balancing local representation against overall proportionality.

No single party would win a majority, and a coalition would be needed. Any realistic coalition would have to include at least three parties, and might still have to govern as a minority.

Lab 178

Reform 139

Con 127

Lib Dem 63

Green 56

Restore 37

SNP 23

PC 7

Others 1

How it works: Voters rank candidates by preference, with votes redistributed as candidates are elected or eliminated until all seats are filled. Used in Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland and Malta, it aims to balance local representation with proportionality through multi-member constituencies.

Labour would win the largest share of the seats, with almost a third, but it would not be enough to form a government. A three-way coalition would be almost certainly needed – and might still struggle to form an absolute majority.

Lab 301

Reform 223

Con 201

Lib Dem 111

Green 91

Restore 71

SNP 32

PC 13

Others 9

How it works: Voters cast one vote for a local representative and one for a party. This gives a local constituency MP. Additional seats are then allocated regionally or nationally to make the overall result more proportional. Used in Scotland, Germany and New Zealand, the balance between constituency and list seats determines how proportional the outcome is.

Proportional representation (PR) aims to produce a parliament that more closely reflects how people voted, allowing voters to back their preferred party without worrying about tactical voting. It often makes it harder for a single party to win a majority and is more likely to result in coalition governments.

Alongside the current first past the post system, More in Common modelled three different PR systems for the Guardian: regional party list, single transferable vote (STV) and additional member system (AMS).

Under the current electoral system, Labour would win a plurality of the vote in England, while the SNP would confirm its traditional dominance in Scotland.

In a party list system, voters would be choosing a party – rather than a single candidate – in large regional constituencies. The higher proportionality produced by larger constituencies would result in a scaled-down SNP presence in Scotland, and a lower Labour seat share, closer to their national polling figures.

STV systems aim to produce proportional results while maintaining strong local representation. Voters would be ranking their favourite candidates in a number of subregional constituencies. STV would reduce the dominance of any one party in a region – for example the SNP in Scotland, Reform in the north-east or Labour in London – in favour of smaller parties.

AMS is a compromise solution that combines single-member, first past the post constituencies with several regional top-up seats aimed at making the outcome of the FPTP vote more proportional. Strong local representation would be maintained, while ensuring that smaller parties such as the Greens get their fair share of seats even outside their traditional south-eastern strongholds.

The More in Common research shows that no single party would achieve a majority according to their projected polling, regardless of which system is used.

The current FPTP system would come the closest, giving Labour 39% of the seats off just 26% of the vote – still short of a majority. The party would most likely need the support of the Lib Dems and the SNP to form a majority government.

The proportional systems would not give Labour such a boost: regional party list is estimated to give the party 26% of seats off 26% of the vote; AMS would give it 26% of the seats off 29% of the vote; and STV would give it 27% of the seats off 28% of the vote.

Under each of these systems, either a progressive coalition of parties – a combination of Labour, the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP or Plaid Cymru – or a Reform-Conservative-Restore coalition would be the only paths to forming a government. Even then, several scenarios would lead to a minority government in a finely balanced parliament.

While the leading Labour party would lose the largest proportion of seats under the proportional systems, smaller parties would be the biggest winners.

The Green party would win only three seats under FPTP under current polling, but more than 50 seats in all three PR systems that we’re modelling – 9% of the seats on offer, more closely matching their vote share. Likewise, the far-right Restore Britain party would surge above 30 seats in each of the PR systems, compared with winning just one seat under FPTP.

Charlie Buckley, a senior research associate at More in Common, said: “With [Nigel] Farage’s [Reform UK] party having lost some momentum and Andy Burnham being – for now – a more popular prime minister, it’s Labour who would reap the benefits from our current electoral system.

“Despite only being four points ahead of the Tories, our model shows Labour winning double the number of seats under first past the post, while a proportional system would give us a parliament which better reflects the close three-horse race we now have between Labour, Reform and the Conservatives.”

Burnham said in his conference speech that Labour shouldn’t “open the door” to a “divisive government” that could win power on “less than 30% of the vote”.

The proportional systems were more likely to remove the regional dominance of any one party. In London, Labour is estimated to gain 69% of seats under FPTP. This number would drop dramatically under PR, to 37% in the party list system and 42% under AMS.

Reform and the Greens would be the biggest beneficiaries in the capital: while Reform would win one seat and the Greens nothing under FPTP, they’d collectively win 18 seats – nearly a quarter of London’s seats on offer – under the party list system.

The same disparity can be seen in the east of England, with the poll-leaders there, Reform, gaining 43% of the seats under FPTP but falling to 29% under both the party list and AMS systems.

Use the postcode search below to see how your local representation would change under each system. Under systems that use regional vote counts to produce more proportional results, you would have regional representatives in place of – or in addition to – constituency ones.

The most recent polling in Britain, as well as recent elections, show an unprecedented fragmentation of the political system. Labour leads on an average of 26%, with Reform second on 23% and the Conservatives third on 20%. The Greens and the Lib Dems are each polling at 10%.

This is based on an average of the last 10 polls, with Labour enjoying a slim lead in the national polls since the party chose Burnham as its new leader and prime minister.

With three parties clustered closely together in the polls, the FPTP system means small shifts in vote share could produce highly volatile and sometimes counterintuitive seat projections, as marginal changes in local contests are amplified into large swings in parliamentary representation.

In the last general election, Labour won 411 of 650 seats with just 34% of the vote.

A report from the Electoral Reform Society modelled the 2024 vote under different voting systems. Only first past the post gave Labour a majority, with all proportional systems giving smaller parties more representation and leading to a hung parliament.

There have been renewed calls for proportional representation. In his conference speech, Burnham said: “We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard.”

Farage has also previously called for electoral reform, calling the current system “outdated” and “not fit for purpose”, but has gone quiet on the subject since Reform went on to lead the polls – until Burnham’s Labour retook a slim lead.

Experts say any attempt to introduce proportional representation for Westminster elections would be likely to face strong pressure for a referendum, given its significance as a constitutional change and the precedent set by the 2011 referendum on the alternative vote system (AV).

The referendum saw voters decisively reject AV, showing the difficulty of winning public support for electoral reform. Experts warn that any future move to proportional representation could face similar challenges, as voters are familiar with first past the post and may be reluctant to replace a system they already understand.

Buckley said: “The real winners with a PR system would be on the edges of the political spectrum. The Greens would go from a handful of MPs to a sizeable bloc, while Restore Britain would arrive in parliament in numbers, potentially giving these smaller parties a kingmaker role in the formation of coalitions.

“So the prospect of forming a workable majority – already a dubious one in our current electoral system – looks even more complicated under a proportional one. Regardless of the system in place, our fragmented politics would make any election in Britain a challenge for those seeking to enter and control government, and the idea of a ‘commanding majority’ is out of reach for all the major parties right now.”

When More in Common conducted similar modelling in July, Reform was leading in the polls, and they found the proportional systems would equally not give Reform the same seats boost that FPTP would. The researchers said then that it was difficult to predict how voters might adjust their own behaviour under a new system.

Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, told the Guardian: “The prime minister’s pledge for a new commission to look at electoral reform is an important step in the right direction. This needs to be an independent and trusted process that focuses on making sure parliament properly reflects the way the country voted.

“There is a growing problem with our democracy in that parliament is looking less and less like the way people voted. The last general election saw the biggest mismatch in British history between the votes people cast and the seats parties won.

“This is largely due to the fact that our outdated two-party voting system can’t cope with the multiparty politics we now have, and is throwing up increasingly distorted and unstable results.

“Simply put, bringing in a system of proportional representation would mean parliament better reflects how the country voted by making sure seats match votes.”

Latest polling and seat distribution figures were provided by More In Common (MIC). Alternative electoral system modelling is based on MIC and Guardian assumptions about constituency boundaries.

Party list uses 11 regions – the nine official English regions plus Scotland and Wales – with variable seat totals. AMS uses a combination of the eleven regions and 631 existing first past the post constituencies. STV uses 52 subregional constituencies – composed of the current FPTP constituencies – of variable size depending on aggregate population.

Northern Ireland and the Commons speaker’s seat of Chorley are excluded from the modelling. This results in 631 total modelled seats for FPTP, STV and party list systems, and in 1,052 seats for AMS.

The exact details, shown as seat totals, boundaries and regional groupings, are based on assumptions on how the new proportional systems could work, and in reality, these totals and exact workings would vary should another voting system be adopted.

Udder madness: why are highland cows suddenly everywhere?

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:24:27 GMT

This shaggy beast is now plastered across everything from mugs to hot water bottles. Or you can sit on her, wrap yourself in her, wipe your feet on her …

Picture this: you get home from work, wipe your feet on your doormat, which has a picture of a highland cow on it, sniff the flowers growing from your highland cow-shaped plant pot, then step inside, hang your coat on one of your highland-cow-themed hooks and put some water on to boil in your highland cow kettle. When the tea is ready, you drink it from one of your highland cow mugs, plucked from a highland cow mug tree, discarding the teabag in a highland cow-emblazoned pedal bin. Oops, you’ve spilled a drop, but not to worry – there’s a fresh roll of kitchen roll waiting for you in between the resin cow-butt and cow-head of its highland cow-shaped holder.

You then carry the tea to your living room, and place it (atop a highland cow coaster, of course) on your coffee table, which has been carved into the shape of a highland cow, before taking a seat in an accent chair made to resemble a highland cow’s head. If you get cold, you can always wrap yourself in a hooded throw, designed to make the wearer look like a highland cow, or reach for your dressing gown-wearing highland cow hot-water bottle.

Every one of these products is available from Next, which stocks so many highland-cow-themed products that it has created its own character, Hamish the Highland Cow, who is apparently “here to bring a smile to every season” and “make everyday moments special”. A search for “highland cow” on the clothes and homeware shop’s website yields 589 results, including Hamish pyjamas, toothbrush holders and wall art.

Next certainly isn’t the only shop to have gone all-in on Scottish-cattle-themed products: from Asda’s highland cow in a pumpkin ornament to Wilko’s highland cow-printed washing-up brush, they seem to be everywhere. On a recent visit to Pets at Home I even spotted a highland cow dog toy.

Clearly there’s a demand for such products: “I love anything highland cow,” writes one reviewer of Next’s highland cow glass chopping board, thanking the retailer for introducing a wider range of highland-cow-themed products. “How gorgeous is this?” comments another highland cow fan on TikTok, showing off Next’s highland cow crockery.

Home and garden shop the Range, which sells highland-cow-themed products such as bedding, lamps and kitchenware, saw an 88% increase in searches for highland cow products in August. “There’s a rise in the number of customers looking for decor that feels personal and the highland cow offers just that,” says a spokesperson for the company. “Instantly recognisable,” they add, it has “a strong connection to British heritage and countryside living, bringing a sense of warmth and calm into a space”.

Kate Hewitt, DIY content creator and former contestant on Interior Design Masters, first noticed the highland cow trend last autumn, and says it’s now “appearing more and more”. She thinks its popularity is part of a wider shift towards a “cosy, country, vintage-style look,” with lots of people wanting “an antique-y, cosy cottage home”.

She thinks the appeal of highland cattle in particular is largely “because they are cute” and, unless you live in Scotland, something a bit unusual: “You don’t see them every day.” The brown and orange hues and the general “cosiness” of highland cattle decor fit the “autumnal” interior design that has become more popular in recent years – it is not uncommon to see influencers on Instagram changing elements of their home design to match the seasons.

While the aesthetic doesn’t necessarily match Hewitt’s taste, she says: “Some of the prints I’ve seen are actually quite beautiful.” She could see herself incorporating the odd highland cow cushion into a space – though she “wouldn’t decorate a whole room in it”.

That said, Hewitt says her mother has bought “loads” of highland cow items for her house. “She loves it and it makes her smile,” she says. “That’s what it’s all about, isn’t it?”

“I would never buy it but my mum loves it” is a common response when I chat to friends and colleagues about the trend. It strikes me as hun-culture adjacent (most directly reflected in Next’s ornament of a highland cow ironing while drinking prosecco), a kind of live, laugh, love sign for the 2020s.

Chances are, even if you are too cool for highland cow decor, you’ll have someone in your life who loves it. So best to beat the Christmas shopping rush and get your hands on a highland cow nativity scene now.

Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 route

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 12:00:43 GMT

The trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railway

The air is scented with the sweet tang of ladies bedstraw and made musical by skylark and blackcap song. An abundance of marbled white butterflies, small skippers and common blue damselflies dart over the flowering knapweed, yarrow and wild carrot.

That the largest chalk grassland in the Chilterns is full of wildlife may not surprise you. But the fact that it is completely artificial, only four years old and has been built by the much-maligned HS2, may do.

The Western Slopes “rewilding” project is due to open to the public next year on land beside the high-speed railway as it dives under the M25 and into a 10-mile tunnel beneath the Chilterns. The trains may be running late, but the wildlife has already arrived.

A decade ago, this area was a vast wheatfield with precious little biodiversity. Today, as the construction effort winds down, more and more of the 127-hectare site is being turned into wildlife-rich grasslands, wet meadows, ponds and small woods.

It is now one of the largest wildlife habitat creation projects in south-east England, and has already witnessed the arrival of hedgehog clover, which hasn’t been recorded in Hertfordshire since 1878, alongside water voles, lesser emperor dragonflies and pyramidal orchids.

The transformation began when Matt Hobbs, lead ecologist at Jacobs, was invited to take a look at the huge planned HS2 works around the south entrance to the Chilterns tunnel.

“I asked the engineer: ‘What’s coming out of the tunnel?’ When he said ‘chalk’, it was like a lightbulb moment. I thought, I know what I’d like to do with that chalk,” said Hobbs, who has designed and overseen the Western Slopes project for HS2.

Chalk grassland is one of the most wildlife-rich habitats in southern England because a wide range of wildflowers flourish on its thin, nutrient-poor alkaline soils, alongside an array of associated invertebrates, including rare moths and bees.

According to Hobbs, the valley slopes could have been expensively restored to arable land by HS2, as much of the land temporarily taken for the huge construction effort will be. “We saw the opportunity to do something different,” he said. “This project is unique. The whole landscape was predicated on what’s the best thing to do with the earthworks and soils. We’re not moving any soils or material off site. Any concrete waste from this site is crushed and used as aggregate under the grasslands.”

Reusing 10m cubic metres of chalk, topsoil and subsoils from the construction effort in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel mouth has also drastically reduced CO2 emissions, and the construction traffic that dumping it elsewhere would have entailed.

According to HS2’s calculations, the wildlife grasslands here could sequester 7% of the carbon impact of the whole high-speed line’s construction, because grassland is much better at storing carbon than regularly-ploughed arable land, which releases carbon every time it is ploughed.

Over the past four years, all the chalk excavated from the tunnel has been sculpted into rolling “downs” on the land above the Colne Valley, creating varying topsoils and a future mosaic of grassland, scrub, woodland and ponds and wet areas.

It took the ecologists a bit of effort to retrain the digger drivers who were spreading the chalk over the site. Groundworks teams are trained to leave everything beautifully smooth and neat, whereas the ecologists were seeking topographical variation, with dips, hollows and “untidy” rough areas.

The future vision is a “wood pasture” landscape, inspired by rewilding sites such as Knepp in West Sussex, where a mixture of scrub and wildflower glades are grazed by herbivores.

Four cattle-grids have been installed on roads – believed to be the first in Hertfordshire – to enable free-roaming cattle to graze within four separate compartments.

“They were really key to the project. We wanted to have that Knepp rewilding technique where you have cattle that can move anywhere they want within the site – it’s brilliant for soil health, soil carbon and dung beetles,” said Hobbs.

Luke Craner, a senior landscape clerk of works for the HS2 contractor Align, said: “I’m really keen to get livestock grazing sooner rather than later so we can kickstart biological processes. We’ve already got a really good grassy sward establishing. We want natural regeneration to occur, because it’s always much more beneficial for wildlife. We’ve already got loads of hawthorn and quite a few oaks coming up. It’s already going out nicely.”

Later this summer, green hay from other calcareous grassland in the local area will be spread on the Western Slopes to bring in more invertebrates. As ant populations develop, rare butterflies including the Adonis, chalkhill and small blue are likely to arrive, with these species interacting with ant colonies. There is also a mammal shelf built into a culvert beneath the railway, enabling badgers, stoats and other mammals to safely cross the high-speed line.

Some footpaths through the site are set to be opened up in the next 18 months, although the western portion of the site is likely to remain protected from public access to boost the ground-nesting birds – from skylarks to little ringed plover – that have quickly colonised the land.

While HS2 is still under construction, the forthcoming track-building and electrics phase will require a much smaller construction footprint, enabling the nature areas to be expanded.

At the bottom of the slopes, beside the River Colne, nearly five hectares of new wetlands have been established. These pretty ponds have been rapidly colonised by club-rush, water mint and sneezewort, as well as breeding reed warbler and lesser emperor dragonfly.

“We’ve definitely extended the population of kingfishers,” said Craner, who has also recorded new sightings of water vole on a tributary of the Colne. “Water voles are a massively declining species because of habitat loss – we’ve put in habitat that’s good for water voles. They’ve colonised it immediately.”

What Craner has noticed is the changing soundscape. While the roar of the M25 and the clank of ongoing construction is never far away, in certain glades the human din is now overwhelmed by birdsong and insect hum.

“We didn’t have this harmony last year and all of a sudden it’s never silent,” said Craner. “This is our hidden gem.”

This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said that the image of the damselfly was a dragonfly.
