Things are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots?

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 11:00:38 GMT

Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat

Another day, another apocalyptic warning about the likelihood that rampantly uncontrollable artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, including the problem of being alive.

Hot on the heels of disgruntled Anthropic researchers announcing the end of civilisation by 2030, we’ve now had the portentously named Hugging Face incident, as well as the Australian government’s grim discovery of a rogue AI’s attack on its Medicare website. Swarms of experts are now falling over each other to warn us that much, much worse is on the way.

Thank God, then, that PM Uncle Andy has thrust Britain on to the bleeding edge of the fight against the rise of the self-improving machines. Except he hasn’t. Not really.

Yes, Burnham went to the United Nations and risked enraging the Orange One with talk of Britain’s prospects of leading the drawing-up of international rules for AI. Slightly awkwardly, however, one of Burnham’s first acts after sweeping into office was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), the very department that had been leading work on AI safety. It’s a move that the Institute for Government warns will cause “real harm” and which former government AI adviser Matt Clifford has said “wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance”.

Isn’t there something gloriously British about all this? Having failed thus far to regulate the technology effectively at home, we are going to world-beatingly coordinate its regulation everywhere else. Whatever it is, it doesn’t quite feel like the response of a state gripped by existential urgency.

But perhaps that is because all of us – government ministers included – have already become desensitised to the risk of AImageddon. You can get used to anything. Sure, if one industry insider inadvertently leaks the news that scientists building a new technology believe it might kill everyone, a spot of existential panic is to be expected. But if you ram these tidings down our collective throat every couple of weeks, eventually the prospect of mass extinction acquires the urgency of that bowel cancer screening kit you’ve been meaning to send back to the doctor.

Civil servants understand this aspect of human nature only too well. Like the prospect of the galloping climate crisis, we too are simultaneously terrified by AI and utterly bored by it. The extraordinary becomes familiar; the familiar becomes an item on a civil service risk register, after which the real fear is that someone will arrange a Teams call to talk about it.

The median age of civil servants, remember, is 43 years, so many have already witnessed enough technological revolutions to choke a chatbot. Which means that, like me, there’s a large faction of the workforce that remembers the replacement of fax machines by email, and their first introduction to Clippy, that damnably moronic AI ancestor office assistant whose principal stab at sentience was appearing uninvited to chirp: “It looks like you’re writing a letter. Would you like help?”

So it’s entirely possible that civil servants of my vintage might not yet have been compassionately euthanised by the time government departments such as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) or HMRC contain more AI agents than carbon-based officials.

It may sound melodramatic, but that’s where we are headed. Ministers – convinced that harnessing AI will help keep Reform at bay by offering the tantalising possibility of slashing civil service jobs – have calmly and robotically emoted their concerns about the machines jumping their guardrails, while enthusiastically searching for things to give them. That’s amid civil service union concerns that the government is moving too quickly, citing the Fabian Society’s research finding that only 29% of those surveyed said they had been consulted about AI tools in their workplace.

They’re right to be worried. Before DSIT was deleted, its permanent secretary, Emran Mian, reportedly had plans for AI to eventually replace almost every departing civil servant in his department rather than replacing them with humans. Elsewhere, the DWP has been busily experimenting with AI across the welfare state, directing its machine-learning systems to identify supposedly high-risk universal credit claims. And in response to “serious concerns” about transparency and the handling of personal data, the DWP has been careful to insist that humans retain the final decision and that AI does not determine entitlement.

Is this just practical common sense, or the kind of world-beating complacency that some have pointed out is an echo of the government’s response to the climate emergency? Either way, the reassurances given by AI minister Kanishka Narayan to the parliamentary business and trade committee sound increasingly hollow after the spate of recent AI rampages.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Civil servants – especially those in public-facing government departments – are acutely aware that saying “a human remains in the loop” is not the same thing as saying “a human remains in charge”.

This really, truly, matters, because the commodity on which every government ultimately runs is not data, or productivity, or even money. It is trust, including the trust that – while below the OECD average – the British public still has in the civil service, and which, according to the public accounts committee, is being jeopardised by inadequate transparency and weak standards on AI.

We already have a national catchphrase for what happens when human discretion – and the accountability that comes with it – disappears. Little Britain’s “computer says no” still resonates – thanks in part to the haunting legacy of the Post Office’s Horizon scandal. Everyone recognises the terror of the human being behind the desk surrendering responsibility to a system whose conclusion can’t be questioned because nobody in the room understands how the hell it got there.

And that may be the real warning from Whitehall. Not that killer robots are about to lock the doors and announce the abolition of humanity. But that long before then, governments might quietly surrender thousands of small human judgments to a swarm of digital bureaucrats because doing so is cheaper, quicker and can be passed off in a ministerial speech as “transformation”. It will not feel like that to the public.

The author works for the UK civil service

Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 10:00:24 GMT

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt. com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje. com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Bill Gates thinks AI could kill a billion people – but can we trust his judgment after Epstein?

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 10:00:23 GMT

He knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was?

The Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein, Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with a dire warning about AI. If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday.

Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being used to kill people today. Gates may not be directly involved in Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks about the company’s role in the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza.

Another thing I’d like to hear Gates explain is why he reckons anyone should trust his judgment about anything, considering he met with Epstein on several occasions after being introduced to him in 2011. To be clear: that’s three years after the financier pleaded guilty to charges including solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, has said he recalled “being aware that Epstein had faced prior legal issues”, but didn’t understand the extent of them. Two minutes of Googling (or Binging) could have made it clear the man was bad news.

The oversight is particularly strange because Gates is obsessed with his public image. His team have a custom-size mannequin on which they test his outfits. The goal, per the Wall Street Journal, is “to depict someone calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers”. Not someone who cavorts with a sex offender.

Ignorance isn’t Gates’ only excuse. He has also said that Epstein “knew a lot of very rich people and [claimed he] could get them to give money to global health”. It seems the 17th richest man in the world didn’t know any wealthy people he could hit up for donations himself and, for the sake of the world’s health, had to lean on a dodgy financier whose funds were obtained in mysterious ways.

I’m not accusing Gates of anything nefarious. But, if we are to take his Epstein excuses at face value, I’m accusing him of being a fool. If we can’t trust his judgment about a man like Epstein, I’m not sure we should trust his proclamations about the future of humanity.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments

The Guardian Wed, 30 Sep 2026 07:00:14 GMT

The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed

As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.

But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.

When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.

These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himself eventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.

Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.

The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activist Ali Milani – who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.

Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.

But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form of Great British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.

The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to a subsidy for energy bills worth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunak being forced to bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and founded Great British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.

But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he has already backtracked on a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.

Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.

While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.

Consider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.

A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.

Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

Christa Pike tortured and murdered a classmate in 1995. She had been set to die on Wednesday, the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.

By Emily Cochrane

Reporting from Nashville

A federal court on Wednesday ordered a pause on the execution of Christa Pike, convicted of the murder of a classmate in 1995, just hours before she was set to die by lethal injection in Nashville.

Ms. Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. But her lawyers mounted a fierce last-ditch campaign to stop the execution, arguing that her defense at her initial trial had failed to consider her history of child sexual abuse and neglect.

The ruling came after the Supreme Court on Tuesday had declined to intervene in the execution. Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, also denied a request to allow Ms. Pike to serve out the remainder of her life in prison.

The office of Jonathan Skrmetti, Tennessee’s attorney general, quickly appealed directly to the U. S. Supreme Court after Wednesday’s ruling, calling it a “technical issue” and vowing to “advocate for the lawfully-imposed sentence.”

Tennessee’s “strong interest in finality and the surviving victims’ right to closure require rejection,” the state wrote in its filing.

The execution had been scheduled for 10 a. m. in Nashville.

Reporters and witnesses had gathered Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. There were white and purple mums on display outside, near large posters of Colleen Slemmer, the 19-year-old student Ms. Pike and two others tortured and killed in 1995. Ms. Slemmer’s family, steadfast in their support of the execution over three decades, had cobbled together the money needed to drive from their Florida home.

But on Wednesday, a divided panel of the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit said the pause was necessary to consider the new arguments from Ms. Pike’s legal team and the state’s response.

“The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments,” Judge Jane B. Stranch wrote, joined by Judge Karen Moore.

The court’s order amounted to at least a brief reprieve for Ms. Pike while litigation continues.

It was the latest twist in a decades-long legal battle over the case. The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Ms. Pike has expressed remorse for her crime. She was diagnosed and treated while in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, which her lawyers said had contributed to her violence. Women who were incarcerated alongside Ms. Pike said she was a supportive and kind presence.

But May Martinez, Ms. Slemmer’s mother, remained adamant that Ms. Pike could not atone for the death of her daughter and should be executed.

“Christa Pike’s case has galvanized public opinion like few cases we have seen in recent years,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. She added that the last-minute stay “is a kind of high-wire balancing act, when the risks and stakes are at their most extreme.”

In the grassy fields outside the prison, where protesters gathered both in favor and against the death penalty, there was confusion and disbelief over the last-minute intervention. Some people walked away, frustrated that another legal hurdle had temporarily delayed the execution.

“I’m really sort of torn,” said Michelle van Allen, 48, who drove in from Kentucky and stood on the side marked off for supporters of Ms. Pike’s execution and the death penalty. The last-minute stay, she said, was “messing with people’s emotions.”

Across the fence separating the two sides, Veronica Stokes, 42, wiped away tears, emotional as she spoke about Ms. Pike and her opposition to the execution.

The pause, she said, “gives us more time to pray.”

Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting. Seamus Hughes contributed research.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

By Matthew Cullen

A morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a scene of chaos and terror after one pilot stabbed another, causing the plane to plunge more than 17,000 feet. Passengers and crew charged the cockpit and subdued the attacker, allowing two off-duty pilots to make a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Much is still unknown about the incident, including what caused the violent altercation. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said the pilot-assailant seemed to be attempting to crash the plane, which was carrying at least 160 passengers.

The pilot and co-pilot were hospitalized in Saudi Arabia, while all of the passengers arrived safely in Israel. Once on the ground, witnesses shared harrowing stories: Screams came from the cockpit, overhead bins swung open, parents clung to their children, passengers prayed and several worried they were living through their final moments.

“In my head, I said, ‘I’m so screwed, I’m so screwed. I don’t deserve to die like this,’” said Peleg Itali, 16, a high school student. A dentist, Shota Musev, said he was one of the first to reach the cockpit after the attack, finding the injured pilot thrown to the ground and treating him for severe wounds in midair.

U. K. Believes Iran Was Involved in Incident at Air Base, Burnham Says

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Incident at U. K. Air Base

Advertisement

Supported by

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the events at R. A. F. Fairford on Sunday, without providing details why.

By Michael D. Shear

Reporting from London

Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain said Wednesday that his government believes Iran “played a part” in the incident on Sunday at an air base used by American bombers in the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran.

“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at R. A. F. Fairford,” Mr. Burnham told the BBC in an interview, referring to the British base about 90 miles outside of London. He added, “It remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America.”

The arrests of five men early Sunday morning near the base on suspicion of explosives violations and terrorism triggered more than two days of anxiety as the police and military used a bomb disposal robot to examine three white vans used by the men and evacuated more than 85 nearby homes.

In the hours after the men were arrested, Mr. Burnham had publicly urged people not to speculate about their motive or connections to other countries. The five men, who are British citizens, were released on bail on Monday. The authorities said on Tuesday that they had found no explosives in the vans, only an unspecified quantity of gasoline.

In the BBC interview, the prime minister refused to say why the government believes that Iran was connected to the incident. “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he said, adding: “Obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”

The Iranian Embassy in Britain on Monday issued a statement rejecting any suggestion that its government was involved in the events at the British base.

Exactly what happened in the area around R. A. F. Fairford on Sunday remains murky. A local resident contacted police at around 1:36 a. m. after seeing a group of suspicious men in masks around three parked white vans. But police said they first received a call almost 50 minutes earlier, from someone who reported that three suspicious vehicles were heading toward the base.

The Times of London, the BBC and other British news organizations reported Tuesday that the police believe the first call came from one of the five men who was later arrested.

Mr. Burnham said that the British authorities have been in contact with their counterparts in the United States as the investigation into the incident continues.

“We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done,” he said. “I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”

On Monday, the U. S. secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said publicly that the incident at the British base was connected to a foreign country. He did not say which one, but added that “in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally, we’re going to always take that very seriously.”

Michael D. Shear is the chief U. K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Republican Senator Sues Over Jack Smith’s Subpoena During Trump Inquiry

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The lawsuit, brought by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, tests the reach of the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause.

By Charlie Savage

Reporting from Washington

A Republican senator on Wednesday sued the former special counsel Jack Smith and the Justice Department, arguing that a subpoena for her phone records during an investigation into Donald J. Trump violated the Constitution.

The complaint, filed by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee in her state’s Middle District, could put before the courts a novel and contested constitutional issue on a matter that has become a Republican talking point: whether the so-called speech or debate clause bars subpoenas to phone companies for data about lawmakers’ communications.

Ms. Blackburn was among several lawmakers who apparently interacted with Mr. Trump while he was president, or with his proxies, during a period of days around the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol. The lawsuit seeks a declaration that Mr. Smith conspired to violate her rights, $1 in symbolic damages from the former special counsel, and an order that the Justice Department destroy her records.

When Mr. Smith oversaw an investigation into Mr. Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election, he signed off on subpoenas to phone companies for lawmakers’ toll records, or logs showing when calls took place, but not their contents. The subpoenas were accompanied by nondisclosure orders to the phone companies, but came to light last year.

Republicans have portrayed themselves as having been unfairly targeted, and have framed the subpoenas for their call records as violating the speech or debate clause. In her lawsuit, Ms. Blackburn’s lawyers said she sought to hold Mr. Smith “accountable for his gross abuse of power and his disregard for the Constitution’s separation of powers, the speech or debate clause,” and for other allegations.

Mr. Smith faced similar accusations on Tuesday when he appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Ms. Blackburn is a member of the panel but did not attend the hearing.

In his testimony, Mr. Smith said that the lawmakers were not the targets of the investigation. He added that the intent of seeking the data was to gather corroborating evidence about calls by Mr. Trump or his proxies to members of Congress seeking to get them to delay the Electoral College certification proceedings, which he said “added to the powerful evidence we had of Donald Trump’s guilt.”

Mr. Smith also noted that the public integrity section, which had been the Justice Department’s hub of legal expertise for issues involving criminal investigations and members of Congress until the Trump administration gutted it last year, signed off on the subpoenas as lawful.

“We took our obligations seriously under the speech or debate clause,” Mr. Smith said. “It’s, in my view, an important part of the separation of powers. I had members of my staff who were very familiar with the clause, having worked in the public integrity section for years. We also, when it was appropriate or required, consulted with the public integrity section regarding application of that clause.”

Ms. Blackburn’s complaint was full of political grievances. But beyond the bluster is a serious question of how far the speech or debate clause extends. The clause says that lawmakers “shall not be questioned in any other place” for their “speech or debate in either House.”

It is widely agreed that the clause bars both prosecuting lawmakers for their legislative acts and compelling them to testify about them. But appeals courts have disagreed about whether or how the clause may also protect the confidentiality of legislative material in circumstances in which lawmakers are not being forced to divulge information and the data is relevant evidence for investigations targeting other people.

To date, no court has held that the clause extends to barring subpoenas to phone companies. But lawmakers have also rarely had an opportunity to contest them in court, because investigators typically also obtain nondisclosure orders from a judge barring the phone companies from notifying their customers.

The applications for nondisclosure orders by Mr. Smith’s team did not tell the court that the phone numbers belonged to lawmakers, as material unsealed this summer at the request of The New York Times confirmed. Department policy at the time did not require such notice to the judges being asked to issue the gag orders, but was later changed to do so.

Charlie Savage writes about national security and legal policy for The Times.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

100 Zeros, a collaboration between Google and Range Media Partners, aims to give the tech giant a foothold in movies, TV and emerging forms of entertainment.

Jonathan Zepp, left, Google’s head of entertainment content and platforms, and Peter Micelli, chief executive of Range Media Partners, at Google offices in Los Angeles. Credit... Michelle Groskopf for The New York Times

Supported by

By Brooks Barnes

Reporting from Los Angeles

More and more, Hollywood depicts technology as a countdown to catastrophe.

Google would like Hollywood to consider another possibility: What if the technological future isn’t terrifying at all?

Consider “Sweetwater,” a short film starring Kyra Sedgwick that has been playing at festivals. It depicts artificial intelligence as a source of comfort and connection: Ms. Sedgwick plays the A. I. hologram of a dead movie star who appears to her grieving son. Google commissioned the film with Range Media Partners, and A. I. researchers at Google advised on how the digital ghost might plausibly function.

“Sweetwater” is part of 100 Zeros, a new partnership between Google and Range that gives the tech giant a foothold in Hollywood’s artistic ranks. The venture, which operates separately from Google-owned YouTube, has three ambitions: Shape how technology — particularly Google technology — appears onscreen; experiment with emerging forms of entertainment; and build relationships with talent.

An ambitious slate of microdramas is designed to do all three. Made for phones and unfolding in short, serialized episodes, the shows will begin rolling out on the Google TV streaming app in December. They’re a testing ground for A. I. production tools and other Google technology. And the microdramas put Google in business with marquee producers and actors, relationships that it hopes will extend well beyond the shows themselves.

One of the 30-episode series — “Dateable,” from Mike Fleiss, the creator of “The Bachelor” — is a reality show about a woman racing to find love before she turns 30. She’ll record herself on an Android phone. (Naturally.)

“Oftentimes, you’ve seen technology represented onscreen in a way that is intentionally making a point that may just be a bit misinformed,” said Jonathan Zepp, Google’s head of entertainment content and platforms.

“The world is changing quickly,” Mr. Zepp continued. “Technology is enabling that change, and it’s in all our interests, I think, from a societal perspective, for that story to be told accurately, authentically.”

100 Zeros is microscopic compared with Apple and Amazon’s Hollywood operations. But it is another example of technology giants extending their enormous reach into Hollywood — and, increasingly, into the stories that popular culture tells about technology itself. This sort of soft power can show up in different ways, like Amazon MGM Studios’s recent decision not to release “Artificial,” a barbed dramatization of OpenAI, a company in which Amazon has invested $50 billion.

Hollywood has increasingly imagined technology in dystopian terms. Examples from this year include “The Audacity” on AMC, the coming CBS drama “Cupertino” and the films “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die” and “Mercy.” All depict technology and the people behind it as variously venal, reckless and dangerous.

Researchers have found that science fiction can shape public attitudes toward emerging technologies. It may even rub off on the technology itself: Anthropic, the Google-backed A. I. company, disclosed in May that versions of its Claude chatbot appeared to have learned from science fiction stories in which A. I. is evil and intent on self-preservation. In simulated tests, the models sometimes behaved accordingly — including by blackmailing engineers.

Google can push only so hard. Filmmakers and showrunners can bristle at the slightest whiff of creative meddling, and audiences can tune out when they sense a corporate agenda.

Even some of the artists who have participated in 100 Zeros projects have conflicting feelings. “It’s self-serving, for sure,” Ms. Sedgwick said of Google’s involvement in “Sweetwater,” which also features Michael Keaton, who directed it. “There’s no question about that.”

She added: “Tech companies are definitely trying to portray A. I. as kind and loving and slightly human. I think it’s problematic and questionable.”

But Ms. Sedgwick also welcomed Google’s expanding role in film production. “They have a lot of money and resources, and if they want to be part of telling stories — giving filmmakers and writers, directors money to make actual movies instead of some A. I. version of a movie — then I’m all for it,” she said. “Ultimately, I think that they respect the craft and want it to continue.”

Getting Hollywood to listen is where Range comes in.

A talent management and production company, founded in 2020, Range represents prominent actors, writers and directors, including Bradley Cooper, Johnny Depp, Gabrielle Union, Damon Lindelof and Halle Berry. Range helped produce “A Complete Unknown,” the recent Bob Dylan biopic starring Timothée Chalamet. Its other film credits include “Primetime,” an A24 drama starring Robert Pattinson that took in an estimated $19 million over the weekend. Range also operates in music, sports, publishing and online media.

100 Zeros gives Range a calling card to appeal to clients: access to Google when technology is rapidly changing how entertainment is made and consumed.

“Google has the most remarkable toolbox,” said Peter Micelli, a co-founder of Range and its chief executive. Google tools include Android XR, an operating system for smart glasses, and Flow, A. I. filmmaking software that can generate and edit video.

Mr. Micelli cited 100 Zeros as one reason that resistance to A. I. among Range clients was easing.

“The tide is shifting in a big way, and I think we’ve had a healthy role in that — in explaining to people that there are positives,” he said. “We live too much in this dystopian ‘Oh, it’s going to be terrible.’”

Mr. Zepp and Mr. Micelli declined to say how much money Google and Range had committed to 100 Zeros. People who have done business with 100 Zeros say it’s millions of dollars. The year-old venture is structured as a rotating fund, with revenue from its projects going toward financing new ones.

What Google gets in return varies.

With some projects, 100 Zeros is chiefly trying to bring ascendant filmmakers and established stars into the Google orbit. 100 Zeros, for instance, has backed Neon films like Joachim Trier’s “Sentimental Value” and Tilman Singer’s “Cuckoo.” 100 Zeros was also a financier of the recent stoner comedy “The Wrong Girls,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat. Coming up is “Family Movie,” a horror comedy that Ms. Sedgwick directed with her husband, Kevin Bacon.

“The Wrong Girls” and “Family Movie” also feature characters using Google devices. Google has long pursued traditional product placement through United Talent Agency. 100 Zeros is meant to expand that effort by getting involved much earlier — helping develop, finance or produce entertainment that incorporates technology, either as products or as a core part of the story.

Google and Range are also using 100 Zeros to experiment with what entertainment itself might become.

There has yet to be a breakout microdrama in the United States, where an earlier experiment with quick-bite entertainment, Quibi, famously flopped. But the format, which originated in China, is expected to generate roughly $14 billion worldwide this year, a 27 percent increase from 2025, according to Omdia, a research firm. Beyond “Dateable,” 100 Zeros has microshows coming from Kenan Thompson of “Saturday Night Live,” the “American Idol” creator Simon Fuller and the “Charlie’s Angels” director McG.

Mr. Fleiss said the micro format, cheap to produce and unburdened by decades of convention, offered a chance to rethink reality television.

“I wanted to eliminate the manipulation and artificial qualities that come from an overproduced reality show,” he said of “Dateable.” At a time when launching a show is increasingly difficult, “Google can also generate huge awareness,” Mr. Fleiss added.

Google TV, where the microdramas will debut, has an estimated 50 million monthly active users worldwide, up 9 percent from a year ago, according to Sensor Tower, an app analytics firm. Afterward, 100 Zeros plans to syndicate the shows to other platforms.

Other 100 Zeros experiments depart more radically from conventional television. At the Venice Film Festival this month, 100 Zeros backed several projects for smart glasses that use Android XR, Google’s operating system for virtual- and augmented-reality devices. “Nevatars,” an animated story from Andy Serkis, allows viewers to converse with A. I. characters. “Galápagos: The Last Eden,” a nature documentary narrated by Margot Robbie, allows viewers to interact with a digital Charles Darwin.

100 Zeros is also a partner in the Future Vision XPrize, a new $3.5 million competition for short films and trailers depicting hopeful, technology-enabled futures. On Friday, “The Gifted,” about a boy who uses A. I. to rebuild his dead mother from her texts, voice and diary, was named the winner. Google and Range, through 100 Zeros, will develop and help finance a feature film based on the winning short.

“This competition creates space for a different, equally essential kind of storytelling — one that explores the complex optimism of a world in transition,” said Peter Diamandis, who founded the contest.

Google’s Hollywood ambitions extend beyond 100 Zeros. Over the summer, the company’s DeepMind laboratory announced a partnership with A24, the independent studio known for its fiercely loyal following, to develop A. I. tools for filmmakers. Google also invested roughly $75 million in the company, prompting a backlash among cinephiles worried about A. I.’s encroachment on filmmaking.

The response to the A24 deal showed the distrust Google must overcome among the artists and film enthusiasts it hopes to court. Ms. Sedgwick, wary though she was, offered the kind of acceptance Google hopes to win.

“It’s a fine line,” Mr. Zepp said, “between dictating a narrative — tell a positive story — versus, hopefully, if you understand this, you’re actually going to want to tell a positive story.”

Brooks Barnes is the chief Hollywood correspondent for The Times. He has reported on the entertainment industry for 25 years.

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder, said internally that the super PAC, Leading the Future, had become a “distraction” for the A. I. company.

By Theodore Schleifer and Mike Isaac

The OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have pulled out of a $25 million donation that they had planned to give to a leading artificial intelligence advocacy group, a sign of how sensitive the company has become to the growing backlash to A. I.

The group, a super PAC called Leading the Future, said last summer and repeated in later comments that the Brockmans planned to donate a total of $50 million, with the first $25 million in 2025 and a second $25 million this year. That second commitment has since wilted away.

Mr. Brockman’s retrenchment was never announced publicly. But inside OpenAI, the 38-year-old executive shared in June that he had no plans to make additional donations beyond the first $25 million.

“I also want to say that I feel terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company and become so much of a distraction for people here,” Mr. Brockman wrote that month in a Slack message obtained by The New York Times. “I’ve been thinking hard about how to turn the ship on it. We’ve donated $25m so far, and have no plans to donate more at this time.”

OpenAI has drawn fire for a host of safety concerns and the A. I. industry’s lobbying effort has attracted scrutiny in recent months. Some in the industry view Leading the Future as too dismissive of calls for A. I. safety, just as OpenAI tries to stake out a middle ground of sorts. Several ideological allies of the super PAC have also had issues with the group’s at-times aggressive tactics against opponents, including a high-profile effort against a New York congressional candidate.

In June, 10 days before Mr. Brockman’s internal message, OpenAI published an unusual blog post distancing itself from the super PAC.

“OpenAI does not direct the activities of LTF, or have visibility into their operations,” the San Francisco company wrote, adding in bold: “We want to be explicit: No outside political group speaks for OpenAI or represents our company’s views.”

Mr. Brockman, who increasingly oversees day-to-day management at OpenAI, has aligned himself tightly with the Trump administration, and appeared on Tuesday at an A. I. policy meeting hosted by President Trump. He has said his donations to Leading the Future, along with another $25 million he and his wife gave last year to Mr. Trump’s super PAC, are in pursuit of backing “team humanity.”

“There’s a small number of politicians who I think — despite realizing it’s not the most popular thing — are really putting themselves out there to say, actually, we think [A. I.] is important for the country,” Mr. Brockman told Wired earlier this year. “Anything I can do to support this technology benefiting everyone is a thing that I will do. In this sense, maybe supporting the team is bigger than the people that I happen to be employed with. It’s really team humanity.”

Mr. Brockman’s support for Leading the Future has been divisive inside OpenAI, The New York Times reported in June, with top policy executives trying to distance themselves from the super PAC.

The super PAC told The Times in February that the Brockmans’s second $25 million donation would come in the first quarter of 2026. It did not, nor did it come in the second quarter. The third quarter ends Wednesday.

A representative for Mr. and Ms. Brockman declined to comment. Leading the Future declined to comment.

Leading the Future is not hurting for cash. It accepted $50 million from the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, which has invested in A. I. companies, and Leading the Future’s groups had about $43 million on hand as of June 30. After spending tens of millions of dollars on the primary season, the super PAC network has not done much spending ahead of the general election. The group’s allied nonprofit is focusing its spending on promoting data centers in a few key states.

(The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Another Day of Pounding Rain Raises Flooding Fears Across the Southwest

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Hurricane Season

Advertisement

Supported by

Texas had a dry summer, and rain on Wednesday could run off the arid ground like water on concrete.

Notes: Forecast from Sept. 30 at 8 p. m. Eastern to Oct. 5 at 8 p. m. Updated as of Sept. 30 at 5:25 p. m. Eastern. Values are shown only for the contiguous United States and are in inches of water or the equivalent amount of melted snow and ice. Source: National Weather Service. The New York Times

By Erin McCannJesus JiménezIshani Desai and Judson Jones

Rain from a hurricane that made landfall in Mexico was threatening on Wednesday to inundate drought-stricken parts of Texas that haven’t seen heavy rain, or any rain, in months. Other pockets of the Central United States, including parts of Colorado, Kansas and Iowa, also faced the threat of heavy rain, which could lead to flash flooding.

Precipitation intensity

Note: Times are Eastern. Source: National Weather Service. William B. Davis, Joel Eastwood and Bea Malsky/The New York Times

At a news conference this week, Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas said officials had positioned crews and equipment across the state ahead of moisture sent into the region from Hurricane Polo, which made landfall twice this week on Mexico’s western coast — about 500 miles from the parts of Texas expected to be hit by storms. Governor Abbott cautioned that heavy rain could lead to flooding and rising rivers.

“We’ll do everything possible so that we can make it through this very heavy rain event with no loss of life,” he said.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, where official weather records are taken, no rain fell from July 16 to Sept. 20, a 67-day stretch that tied for the second-longest period without measurable precipitation, according to the National Weather Service.

More than 43 percent of Dallas County is experiencing an exceptional drought, the highest category of drought conditions, according to the U. S. Drought Monitor.

The weather on Wednesday is a classic collision of colliding air masses colliding across the Central Plains, setting off storms and outbursts of rain in the afternoons and evenings. Those outbursts can also bring tornadoes, hail and damaging winds, a pattern that also occurs in late spring but occurs again as summer transitions to fall.

What makes this system more potent is an influx of moisture from the remnants of Polo, which will drift into Texas on Wednesday.

Over the next two days, the heaviest rainfall is expected in a band stretching across Central Texas from the Mexican border and into Oklahoma. The storms will begin in the west and slowly shift east.

Downpours could drop up to five inches of rain in a short period, creating a severe risk of flash flooding. When water hits the dry soil, it will run off as if the ground were concrete rather than soaking in, heightening the threat of floods.

Emergency managers were also concerned about the lingering rainfall over southeastern Colorado, where the ground was saturated from days of rain and could fuel more flooding.

The storm system is large enough that it is also spreading moisture into the Northern Plains, where a flood threat was also possible in the Corn Belt, which includes parts of Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas.

Before the latest rain, a flurry of flash flood and tornado warnings hit New Mexico and Texas on Tuesday as the weather system moved through the Southwest. There were no reports of widespread damage, but some of the warnings included pleas by the National Weather Service for people to pay attention to emergency officials’ messages as more than three inches of rain fell in some areas.

In New Mexico, the problem was not significant rainfall on drought-stricken land, but rather on areas that were already saturated from storms last week. Albuquerque International Sunport, the state’s biggest airport, has had 4.49 inches of rain this month so far, making it the wettest September since recordings started in 1891.

Tuesday’s storms caused concerns that three dams could fail in southern New Mexico, officials said, leading to evacuation orders for some residents.

The southern part of the state typically gets about eight inches of rain a year, said Tim Brice, a senior meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in El Paso.

But on Tuesday, an area near Las Cruces, N. M., received about one to three inches of rain, he said, prompting officials to worry that a dam could overrun and cause flooding across nearby small cities and agricultural land.

“This is not normal,” said Joah Franzoy, the chief financial officer for Elephant Butte Irrigation District.

Also in New Mexico, Doña Ana County issued evacuation orders for the cities of Rincon, Hatch, Salem and Garfield, each populated by fewer than 2,000 people, because of the weather.

Erin McCann is the deputy editor for The Times’s Weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

Jesus Jiménez is a Times reporter covering North Texas. He is based in Dallas.

Ishani Desai is a reporter covering breaking news and other topics, and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times who forecasts and covers extreme weather.

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Clash on Flight to Israel

Supported by

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said one pilot stabbed another and may have attempted to crash the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane landed in Saudi Arabia and all passengers were safe.

By Leo Sands

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said a pilot tried to seize control of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, stabbing the other pilot. Passengers and crew members charged the cockpit and subdued the assailant, with crew members making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

According to Mr. Netanyahu, one of the pilots attacked the other midair in a possible attempt to crash the plane, FlyDubai Flight 1073. He said a passenger and member of the crew broke into the cockpit to “neutralize” the pilot-assailant, while another crew member stabilized the plane. The flight suddenly plunged thousands of feet and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli officials said the plane was carrying between 160 and 180 passengers. FlyDubai said the passengers were all safe and accounted for. The flight’s pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, according to the airport in Tabuk. The Saudi authorities arrested the suspected assailant, Mr. Netanyahu said.

Much of what happened aboard the flight remained unclear, including the cause of the sudden altitude loss and any possible motive.

Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement that one of the pilots aboard the FlyDubai flight “stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane,” in what appears to have been a failed attempted hijacking. Other crew members and a passenger retook control of the cockpit and landed the plane in Tabuk, Mr. Netanyahu said.

FlyDubai Flight 1073 plunged dramatically as it was flying over Saudi Arabia near the border with Jordan at around 8:20 a. m. local time on Wednesday morning, according to testimony from passengers and data from FlightRadar24, a flight tracking service. The flight had taken off from Dubai a little over two hours earlier.

Officials have not publicly shared any information about the assailant’s possible motive. According to two Israeli security officials who spoke on condition of anonymity in accordance with government protocol, the Israeli authorities are investigating the possibility that the altercation was an attempted attack on Israelis, among other lines of inquiry.

Passengers described a scene of chaos in the cabin as the aircraft lost altitude, fearing that the plane, a Boeing 737 Max 8, could crash. The aircraft dropped by around 17,000 feet in two minutes, according to FlightRadar24.

According to accounts from passengers, the fight that broke out in the cockpit left at least one pilot seriously injured. Those aboard the flight said passengers intervened to subdue the assailant.

A graphic social media video verified by The New York Times showed three men tending to two injured men on the floor of the cabin, both of whom appeared to be bleeding, while another bloodied man asks for help. At least one of the injured men on the floor wore what appeared to be a FlyDubai pilot uniform.

FlyDubai said that crew members who were on duty on the flight secured the aircraft. According to the airport in Tabuk, the flight made an emergency landing at 9:45 a. m. local time.

The pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, the airport said, but it did not provide further details.

The airline said it had sent two replacement aircraft to Tabuk to collect the passengers and crew and take them to Tel Aviv.

Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.

Panic and Heroics on FlyDubai Flight: ‘We Felt That This Was It’

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Clash on Flight to Israel

Advertisement

Supported by

A routine flight turned terrifying when a violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit and the aircraft dropped 17,000 feet in two minutes. Passengers subdued a knife-wielding attacker.

By Karla AdamAaron Boxerman and Natan Odenheimer

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door.

What began as a routine flight turned terrifying when a violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit in midair. Passengers described a desperate scramble inside the cabin as travelers realized the plane was out of control. Several rushed into the cockpit and subdued an attacker before two off-duty pilots helped steer the aircraft to a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” one passenger, Miriam Ohayon, told Israel’s I24 News, a television channel. “We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood.”

She recalled reciting a Jewish prayer often said in times of distress as the plane jolted through the air.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said the attacker was one of the pilots, and Almog Itali, a passenger on the flight, told the BBC that there were two pilots in the cockpit and that “one stabbed the other.” He said that two off duty-pilots on the plane, one of whom was British, helped to land the aircraft after the altercation.

The incident began about two hours after takeoff when a passenger returning from the bathroom saw a struggle inside the cockpit and alerted passengers, Ms. Ohayon reported to her mother, Yasmin Ohayon-Abukasis.

Speaking to reporters at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, Ms. Ohayon-Abukasis said her daughter had told her that the pilot had yelled “help, help, help” and that he was being attacked by a man with a knife.

Ms. Ohayon-Abukasis said her daughter had said that passengers had subdued the attacker and that a nurse and doctor on board provided initial medical care to the pilot.

Hila Gaier, who was on the flight, said that when the plane dived passengers couldn’t move. “You were sucked downward,” she told Kan, Israel’s public broadcaster. She said she was flying with her partner and two daughters. “I embraced them, told them I loved them, and we tried to practice breathing exercises,” she said.

Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed Flight 1073 descended more than 17,000 feet in less than two minutes. “The plane kept stabilizing and then dropping again for several long seconds,” Mr. Itali told Channel 12. The plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and the pilots were taken to a hospital.

Adam Polovincik, 40, who was on the flight with his family, described it as an “extreme experience,” even as he tried to remain calm for his children.

Speaking by phone from Saudi Arabia, where Israel has no formal relations, Mr. Polovincik said the circumstances were surreal.

“They brought us food and drink, served us coffee,” Mr. Polovincik said. “Yes, there are a lot of soldiers here and government officials, but the atmosphere is very relaxed, pleasant and respectful.”

Leo Sands and Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Natan Odenheimer is a Times reporter in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Congress Set to Leave Washington for the Midterms With No A. I. Progress

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Senate Democrats blocked a measure that would encourage, but not require, states to protect consumers from power rate hikes tied to data center growth, and had no limits on A. I. use or deployment.

By Michael Gold and Cecilia Kang

Michael Gold, who covers Congress, reported from the Capitol. Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy.

Facing a growing backlash over the boom in data center construction and widespread concern over the safety of artificial intelligence, Congress is set to depart Washington this week ahead of the midterm elections having accomplished nothing to address either issue.

Eager to show they hear the public alarm over A. I. as they fight to keep their majority, Republicans in the Senate on Wednesday attempted to bring up a bill intended to insulate Americans from rising electricity costs tied to data centers. But Democrats blocked it, noting that the legislation was not enforceable and arguing it would do little to significantly curb energy prices.

The bill, sponsored by Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican in a difficult re-election battle, also would not impose any regulation on the use or deployment of artificial intelligence in the wake of several revelations that A. I. agents evaded safeguards meant to constrain them.

With widespread disagreement over the best path forward but lawmakers eager to show voters progress on the issue before facing them in November, members of both parties have in recent days released a barrage of legislation, letters and statements of concern about A. I. and held a Senate hearing on “Rogue A. I.” on Wednesday afternoon as they rushed for the exits.

“I remain an A. I. optimist. I am not an A. I. doomer,” Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is also up for re-election, said. “But we are at a moment in time, particularly over the last few weeks, where I think the whole world has recognized we’ve got to do something.”

It comes as President Trump has played down A. I. safety risks and lawmakers in both parties remain uncertain about how to proceed on the issue as major players in the industry are spending heavily to influence the midterms. Though Mr. Trump convened top technology executives at the White House on Tuesday, the group agreed only to voluntary safety agreements and to follow the president’s preference in rebranding A. I. as “super intelligence.”

Some Republican senators have argued there is a need for stronger oversight. Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, who has sponsored several pieces of legislation that would limit A. I., convened Wednesday’s hearing and said that companies should be subject to consequences when their technology is misused.

“It’s time to talk about what we’re going to do to hold the companies, the product makers accountable, rather than all of this talk about the end of the world,” Mr. Hawley said. None of the executives who joined the White House meeting attended; Mr. Hawley said that Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had declined his invitation to participate.

Still, Republicans also are facing blowback for having included tax breaks in their major tax and spending cut legislation last year that benefited data center developers. Mr. Hawley has introduced legislation that would bar data centers from taking advantage of the incentives.

It is unclear whether Congress’s lack of action on the issue will have political consequences in November. A poll conducted this month by The New York Times and Siena University found that neither party had a clear advantage with voters on A. I., even as voters broadly opposed the construction of data centers.

Still, Democrats have sought to make data centers a central issue in competitive races across the country, including Mr. Husted’s in Ohio.

Before he was appointed to the Senate last year, Mr. Husted, the state’s lieutenant governor, backed tax incentives for data centers. Democrats have spent millions on television advertisements labeling him as the “face of data centers.” In August, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm distributed a memo warning that the issue was threatening Mr. Husted’s re-election bid.

Wednesday’s vote was seen as a potential boon for his campaign.

The legislation, which passed the House overwhelmingly earlier this month, would order state utility regulators to consider adopting rules requiring the centers to cover higher costs associated with their power use. But it would not force state regulators to follow federal standards when they are setting electricity rates, and it would give them two years to weigh changes.

Mr. Husted argued that the bill was the best mechanism available for Congress to quickly address energy prices. He pointed to its bipartisan support in the House and said it was the only legislation ready to make it to the president’s desk.

“This is the only game in town,” Mr. Husted said. “This bill passing is the only way to get a chance to prove to the American people before the midterm elections whose side you’re on.”

Democrats have argued that Mr. Husted’s bill is little more than a symbolic gesture that will have little effect on electricity costs. Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, pronounced it “toothless” and called for more meaningful regulations.

“An optional guardrail isn’t a guardrail at all,” Mr. Schumer said. “At a time when Americans are calling out for real guardrails on A. I., Senate Republicans are trying to secure an ineffectual participation trophy before they skip town.”

Though four Democrats joined Republicans, they still fell short of the 60-vote threshold required to proceed.

Republicans accused Democrats of putting politics first while seeking to flip Mr. Husted’s seat. But Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, said he was frustrated that lawmakers had waited until the last minute to try to do something about data centers.

“That’s the sort of thing that I wish we’d started talking about a month or a month and a half ago and tried to work something out with the Democrats,” Mr. Kennedy said of Mr. Husted’s bill. Instead, he said, “we’re doing it at the last minute.”

Lawmakers from both parties have introduced a flurry of proposals hoping to slow the pace of A. I. development, impose guardrails and address the national security risks that could be posed by rogue A. I. agents. But their bills have largely gone nowhere in the face of deep disagreements both within the parties and between them.

Even lawmakers who are calling for swift regulation are being careful to say they do not want to stop A. I. development outright.

On Tuesday, three Democratic senators, including Mr. Warner, asked their colleagues to quickly take up and pass a bill that would establish a federal panel to oversee safety standards for A. I. models and to evaluate models before they were deployed.

But Mr. Warner framed the effort in part as a chance to stem the rising A. I. backlash.

“We should not miss the moment to put a safety protocol in place now,” Mr. Warner, whose state has benefited from data center growth, said. “If Congress goes out, God forbid we have an incident, A. I. is already suspect by most Americans. We could see the stop of innovation if an A. I. tool took over a hospital or water system.”

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, objected and blocked the legislation, saying that he feared giving the government too much authority over A. I.

He also accused his colleagues of moving too quickly.

“Congress must not legislate on the issue of artificial intelligence hastily or in a closed manner,” he said.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy for The Times from Washington. She has written about technology for over two decades.

A Hasidic Jew Protested Against an Israeli Flag. He May Be Deported.

The New York Times September 30, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Yehonatan Ovadia, who opposed the mounting of the flag in a small New York town, belongs to a Hasidic branch that is anti-Zionist. He is now in ICE custody.

By Luis Ferré-Sadurní

The Israeli flag hanging outside a New York town hall disappeared just weeks after it was raised in solidarity with the victims of the 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel. Shortly after, two men were accused of stealing the flag during an anti-Israel protest.

The suspects were anti-Zionist Hasidic Jews who oppose Israel. Under their interpretation of religious law, they believe that establishing a Jewish state before the Messiah’s arrival is forbidden. Both men were initially charged with hate crimes, but the case ended quietly after they paid a fine and pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of disorderly conduct in early 2024.

Now, one of those men is facing deportation.

Federal immigration officers in August detained Yehonatan Ovadia, a 35-year-old Israeli citizen, after revoking his legal status because of the flag incident. Mr. Ovadia — a religious teacher who says that he participated in the protest but did not tear down the flag — has been in the United States since 2022 on a visa for religious workers.

His lawyers, who filed a 27-page lawsuit in Manhattan Federal District Court on Aug. 29 requesting his release, argued that the Trump administration was retaliating against his protected religious and political speech. Federal immigration officials have targeted noncitizens who engage in behavior the government regards as antisemitic.

Though federal officials did not cite antisemitism in revoking Mr. Ovadia’s legal status, his lawyers have accused the Trump administration of conflating their client’s anti-Israel activism with antisemitism.

“He’s against the Israeli government and the existence of the state of Israel for religious reasons, but to claim that he’s an antisemite is the peak of absurdity,” Eric Lee, one of his lawyers, said.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested Mr. Ovadia after he had been summoned to immigration court in Manhattan on Aug. 28. He is being held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, a federal prison where ICE also holds some detainees.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said that Mr. Ovadia had “overstayed his welcome and refused to depart” after his legal status was revoked.

“It is a privilege to be granted a visa or green card to live in the United States of America,” the statement said. “The Trump administration acted well within its statutory and constitutional authority, as it does with any alien who advocates for violence, glorifies and supports terrorists, harasses Jews and steals property.”

Mr. Ovadia, a husband and father of five, is part of a large enclave of ultra-Orthodox Jewish people in Rockland County, about an hour north of New York City. The area is heavily populated by Hasidic groups who commit to a traditional, insular lifestyle, and has many yeshivas.

While there is significant support for Israel among Orthodox Jews, Mr. Ovadia belongs to an ultra-Orthodox Hasidic branch known as Satmar. It is the largest Hasidic group in New York and is opposed to Zionism and the state of Israel on theological, not political, grounds.

Mr. Ovadia appeared to belong to a smaller grouping of politically active Satmars who not only oppose Israel, but have aligned themselves with the Palestinian cause. Mr. Ovadia frequently attended anti-Israel marches with other Satmar Jews wearing black coats and hats, and often flew the Palestinian flag.

“We demonstrated for Gaza, for the liberation of Gaza, for the rights of the Palestinians and to show to the world that the Jews, real Judaism, want to have peace,” Mr. Ovadia said in a brief phone interview from detention.

The flag controversy began on Oct. 12, 2023, when the supervisor of Ramapo, a town in Rockland County, mounted a large Israeli flag on its town hall, five days after Hamas fighters killed an estimated 1,200 Israelis and took dozens of hostages.

“We have people in Ramapo who have friends and relatives in Israel, and we stand with them as well,” the supervisor, Michael Specht, a Democrat, told a crowd of about 60 people at the time. (Mr. Specht did not respond to a request for comment.)

About a month later, as Israel’s retaliatory strikes killed and displaced thousands in Gaza, residents who were opposed to the display of the Israeli flag on a government building held a demonstration.

Mr. Ovadia and other Satmar Jews saw the flag’s display as an endorsement by their town of a state “whose existence their religion holds to be forbidden,” his lawsuit said. A state law prohibits municipal buildings from displaying a foreign flag except under limited circumstances.

Mr. Ovadia said that he drove several people in his van to protest the flag on Nov. 13, 2023, helping gather about 20 Jewish people outside the town hall. Also present, Mr. Ovadia said, were people affiliated with the anti-Zionist Neturei Karta, a fringe, ultra-Orthodox organization whose political activism has been condemned by mainstream Satmars.

“We wanted to express our opinion legally, peacefully,” Mr. Ovadia said.

Surveillance cameras captured four or five men in traditional Hasidic clothing ripping the flag from the town hall before two men destroyed it with scissors, according to police records reviewed by The New York Times.

Mr. Ovadia said that a friend had torn down the flag, and that he had opposed the action and tried to leave the demonstration immediately, an account that he later shared in writing with the federal government.

Two days after observing Mr. Ovadia’s van on the surveillance footage, police officers pulled him over and questioned him. He told the officers that while he had driven people to the demonstration, he did not know where the flag was, according to police records.

Mr. Ovadia was arrested and charged with criminal mischief, petit larceny and conspiracy — all as hate crimes. He was released without bail.

The criminal complaint, which accused him of stealing the flag, said that Mr. Ovadia and others “were motivated to participate in this act because of their hatred of the existence of the Israeli state.” The police arrested a second Jewish man in connection with the episode.

The hate crime charges were dropped.

In February 2024, Mr. Ovadia pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, a violation under New York law, but not a crime. He paid a $200 fine and an additional $125, according to his lawsuit.

“I said, ‘You know, I don’t have power, I’m out of money, I have no time, I am a teacher, I need to teach students every day,’” he recalled. “‘Let’s end this with disorderly conduct.’”

The following year, President Trump returned to power and issued an executive order that instructed the Department of Homeland Security to target noncitizens who had participated in actions the administration deemed antisemitic. Several international students, including Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University graduate, were detained.

When Mr. Ovadia’s congregation applied for an extension of his religious worker visa in September 2025, U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services demanded police records and court documents related to the demonstration.

The agency issued a rare split decision in May that highlights the quirks of U. S. immigration law. It agreed that Mr. Ovadia was qualified to continue working in the country, but refused to let him remain in the United States to do so, a move that stripped his lawful status and left him vulnerable to arrest.

In its denial letter, the agency said that while it had found no “conviction or commission of a crime involving moral turpitude,” it had used its discretion to deny his stay after considering “adverse factors.” Those factors included the dropped charges; the disorderly conduct violation; and police records showing that Mr. Ovadia had declined to identify other participants in the demonstration.

The immigration agency’s letter does not mention Mr. Ovadia’s activism or Mr. Trump’s executive order on antisemitism.

Federal officials charged Mr. Ovadia with remaining in the country without legal status, summoned him to immigration court in Manhattan and arrested him there last month.

“He’s very, very devoted, and he is strong-minded,” said Rabbi Leibish Iliovits, who lives in the same neighborhood in Rockland County as Mr. Ovadia and helped him settle in the United States. “He would stand up for what he believe is right, and he wouldn’t back down, but he would not harm anyone.”

On Wednesday, dozens of supporters dressed in Hasidic garb showed up at an immigration courthouse in Manhattan ahead of a hearing on Mr. Ovadia’s case. An immigration judge refused to release him on bail.

Eliza Shapiro contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

Luis Ferré-Sadurní is an immigration reporter for The New York Times.
