Fraternity Says It Acted Quickly to Expel Cornell Members

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

The national organization of the Chi Phi fraternity at the center of a Cornell University sexual assault lawsuit explained publicly for the first time how it handled the episode.

By Alan Blinder

A Cornell University fraternity ousted members days after a woman told the authorities in 2024 about being sexually assaulted, a national executive of the organization said Wednesday.

Trey Robb, Chi Phi’s interim executive director, said in a statement that the Cornell chapter had unanimously voted to dismiss the men three days after the woman gave her account to the police. The national group quickly suspended the men, too, and later expelled them.

“These actions went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us,” said Mr. Robb, whose organization is based in metropolitan Atlanta.

Mr. Robb’s statement was Chi Phi’s most detailed response to the accusations of the woman, who filed a lawsuit this month saying she was sexually assaulted on the campus in Ithaca, N. Y. She has been identified in court documents only as Jane Doe.

Cornell, as well as Chi Phi’s local chapter and national governing body, are among the defendants. The woman contends the university and fraternity were negligent and failed to protect her.

A person familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because litigation was pending, said the Cornell chapter had swiftly removed four men. In her lawsuit, the woman accused seven Chi Phi members of wrongdoing, and a prosecutor’s summation of her statement at the time refers to seven men.

The lawsuit makes specific claims about the behavior of each man. But it was not clear on Wednesday which members the fraternity had removed and what exactly the group knew in November 2024 about the scope of potential misconduct.

Mr. Robb did not comment on the lawsuit but defended the fraternity’s initial response to the episode.

“As a private membership fraternity, Chi Phi acted within its own authority at both the chapter and national levels to remove men suspected of betraying the values of our brotherhood,” the statement said. “They failed to meet the standards we set for every brother, and accountability is how we will always respond to behavior that falls short of those standards.”

The fraternity, Mr. Robb said, “condemns sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in the strongest possible terms.”

“Neither,” he added, “has any place in our fraternity or on college campuses.”

According to the lawsuit Ms. Doe filed this month, she headed to the Chi Phi house late on Oct. 19, 2024, having had about 10 drinks over roughly three hours. Once there, according to the lawsuit, fraternity members gave her drugs and more alcohol and repeatedly assaulted her.

The district attorney for the area did not bring charges when the authorities first investigated in 2024 but has since reopened the inquiry. Still, the prosecutor, Matthew Van Houten, said this week that the woman’s sworn statement in 2024 “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped.”

Instead, Mr. Van Houten said, the statement had “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.”

Soon after the woman spoke with authorities, Cornell issued a crime alert saying a victim had been “sexually assaulted by several males and coerced into consuming ketamine and other drugs.”

The lawsuit and the revived inquiry have prompted intense scrutiny of fraternities and sororities, especially on Cornell’s campus.

Cornell has a long tradition of Greek life, especially compared with other Ivy League schools. About one-third of its undergraduates participate in fraternities and sororities. The Chi Phi chapter was a cornerstone, founded at Cornell quickly after the university admitted students in 1868.

Court records do not suggest that the chapter was a regular subject of litigation, but between 2018 and 2023 — the year before the reported assault — the chapter had faced repeated campus discipline.

Cornell’s published records say little about the details and circumstances of the violations. One case in 2018, for example, involved hazing and underage drinking. A 2020 matter concerned overcrowding and an insufficient number of so-called sober monitors. Another case focused on subjects like noise levels and trash, while one in 2023 referred to “prohibited conduct — public urination, garbage.”

The penalties for those violations included a written reprimand, social probation and mandatory trainings.

And in 2020, the chapter was honored “for outstanding support and contribution to the Cornell Interfraternity Council.”

In spring 2024, the semester before the episode at the center of the lawsuit, the chapter had 67 members, 21 of whom were new. Its cumulative grade point average was 3.5, a touch above the average for Cornell fraternities and sororities.

After the woman made her report to authorities, Cornell suspended the fraternity. In statements this month, the university has emphasized that the chapter remained barred. The university said it also eventually suspended or expelled some members.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

Trump’s Voluntary A. I. Policing Echoes What Biden Did. But Is It Enough Today?

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Trump’s plan to let A. I. companies police themselves comes amid mounting examples that they are failing to put safeguards on the technology.

By David E. Sanger

David E. Sanger is a White House correspondent who has covered the intersection of technology and geopolitics for The Times for four decades, and written a book on the emergence of cyberwarfare.

If there was something familiar about the voluntary safety guidelines that President Trump signed on Tuesday with the nation’s frontier artificial intelligence companies, this may be the reason: It closely echoed a previous agreement that President Joseph R. Biden Jr. struck with many of the same firms three years ago.

But the question now is whether the kind of voluntary framework that seemed plausible in 2023 is sufficient in 2026.

Back then, the central concept was the same: Since federal regulations could not keep up with the blistering pace of new A. I. models, the companies agreed to set up systems to monitor themselves, establishing layers of protection aimed at ensuring the technology would not be turned to nefarious purposes. The most commonly discussed scenario, for example, is that as A. I. enables biological breakthroughs, alarm bells will go off at the first whiff of evidence that the model is being hijacked to produce biological weapons.

“We must be cleareyed and vigilant about the threats emerging from emerging technologies that can pose — don’t have to, but can pose — to our democracy and our values,” Mr. Biden said in the Roosevelt Room at the White House in July 2023. “This is a serious responsibility.”

Mr. Trump essentially offered the same approach on Tuesday afternoon, after a luncheon with A. I. executives. “They’re really going to be policing each other,” he said outside the White House, as the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceX AI nodded in agreement.

After a summer of surprises — of A. I. agents escaping the “sandboxes” designed to contain them, hacking into other companies, and engaging in activities behind the backs of their creators — why would anyone think these protections are sufficient? The layered early-warning systems designed over the past few years have clearly failed, by the accounting of the companies themselves. New cases of A. I. agents behaving badly, or at least unpredictably, emerge on nearly a daily basis. Virtually all are after-the-fact discoveries, like the Louvre guards who woke up eight minutes too late to a brilliantly executed heist last year.

“We recognized in 2023 that voluntary pledges alone would not be enough, which is why President Biden followed up with an executive order,” one that Mr. Trump overrode after coming to office, noted Ben Buchanan, a Johns Hopkins professor who was one of the authors of the 2023 pledge.

“Given how fast A. I. capabilities have advanced, it’s even clearer now the federal government will need to act once again,” added Mr. Buchanan, who has consulted for Anthropic and other firms and is about to publish a book on the efforts to rein in A. I.

Mr. Biden’s order created a small unit inside the Commerce Department, called the U. S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute, to create standards for new A. I. models and to test the models before they are released. The institute has been renamed and has been a bit player in the current A. I. debates; Britain, for example, has a far larger and more powerful institution playing that role.

It is hard to find another industry with so much potential to do harm as well as good that the government believes can regulate itself. After all, pharmaceutical companies are not permitted to approve their own drugs — that is why there is a Food and Drug Administration. Boeing cannot certify its own planes as flight-ready. And when OpenAI and Anthropic want to build new data centers — suddenly one of the most contentious issues of the midterm elections — they need to get more government approvals than they do for the new A. I. models that the centers’ computing power will be helping create.

In one respect, the Trump accord goes beyond the Biden one: The companies committed to embedding outside experts in their development process, with the power to blow the whistle if they see something going awry.

The idea is based on the International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors who visit nuclear sites, though those inspectors are chosen from countries around the world. It is a concept that has been around for a while, and was included in the essay Dario Amodei, one of the founders of Anthropic, wrote in recent weeks as he argued for slowing the pace of development until the industry had rogue A. I. agents under control.

As Anthropic heads toward an initial public offering that many on Wall Street expect to value the company in excess of $2 trillion — approaching the G. D. P. of Canada — the Trump administration is doubling down on the argument that regulation is simply an invitation for China to exceed the United States.

Advocates for shaping this surging technology with a light government hand celebrated the White House accord on Tuesday.

David Sacks, who was Mr. Trump’s A. I. czar until he left the White House early this year, ranked among the most enthusiastic.

“Only President Trump could convene all the leaders of the top companies developing chips, data centers and frontier models for Super Intelligence,” Mr. Sacks wrote later on social media, adopting Mr. Trump’s term for the technology, an attempt to rebrand it to sound more powerful, yet more under human control.

Mr. Sacks, who was sitting close to the center of the table for the luncheon that the president hosted for the A. I. leaders, said the agreement came down to one concept: that the frontier firms are “accepting responsibility for the safe development of their products and imposing new internal controls and external audits. This is far better than waiting years for some international agreement that would probably never happen.”

It is not yet clear that the firms are truly accepting responsibility for A. I. agents that go rogue, hacking into systems or sending misleading messages. But OpenAI did terminate work in recent days on a new model — called GPT-6.1 Astra — when it showed high levels of what the company labels as deception, covering up its actions.

“For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade-off,” Saachi Jain, the head of safety systems at OpenAI, said when the decision was announced.

OpenAI decided to take the cautious route. Presumably, every one of its competitors is struggling with the same issue.

On his second point — about how long it would take to secure international agreements — Mr. Sacks is undoubtedly right. When President Xi Jinping of China was in Washington last week for a state visit, the only concrete agreement on A. I. that emerged was a plan to convene experts from both countries — the two that dominate the field — to begin a conversation on mutual safety steps.

That decision also had its roots in the Biden White House, which took about 18 months to get Beijing to agree on what seems like a pretty obvious baby step: a single sentence declaring that any decision to employ nuclear weapons should be made by humans, not by artificial intelligence.

Mr. Xi built on that statement at the White House last week. Speaking in the Grand Foyer, he said that it was critical to “develop and manage A. I. for good and ensure that the development of A. I. is always under human control.” Mr. Trump has often repeated the first part, but he leaves out “under human control,” which worries those who fear the Pentagon is quickly moving toward fully autonomous weapons with weakened human oversight.

Mr. Trump clearly does not want to talk about autonomous weapons, or dwell on the recent cases of A. I. gone wrong. Last week he was still calling revelations of miscreant A. I. agents a “HOAX” being exploited by his political opponents.

On Tuesday, he dwelled at length on his effort to mandate use of the term “Super Intelligence,” as if changing the term will ameliorate the problem.

“This is going to be all for the good, and we’re going to have it be nice and safe,” Mr. Trump said.

While the accord was voluntary, he insisted, “it’s morally binding.”

The executives who came to the lunch yesterday, many of whom are already taking the steps outlined in the voluntary accord, say they agree they have a moral responsibility to get this right. But as they have learned to their shock in recent months, the technology is not entirely under their control. Whether the accord is morally binding on the rogue A. I. agents is yet to be determined.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

Judge Rules in Favor of Deporting Muslim Leader in Wisconsin

The New York Times September 30, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Salah Sarsour, a vocal supporter of Palestinian rights who leads the state’s largest Islamic group, says the case is politically motivated and plans to appeal the decision.

By Jacey Fortin

For six months, Salah Sarsour, a legal U. S. resident and the president of Wisconsin’s largest Islamic organization, has been fighting the Trump administration’s efforts to deport him.

But on Tuesday night, a federal immigration judge in Chicago ruled in favor of his removal, which means he could be ordered to leave the country unless he secures asylum or another form of legal relief.

Mr. Sarsour, 53, who grew up in the West Bank and is a vocal supporter of Palestinian rights, leads the Islamic Society of Milwaukee and has lived in the United States for more than 30 years. He was detained by U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in March and held for about 80 days in Indiana before a judge ordered his release in June.

His lawyers plan to appeal the Tuesday court ruling, which means Mr. Sarsour will not be immediately deported.

The government’s case against him goes back decades and crosses international borders. It cites charges that were brought against Mr. Sarsour by Israel during a Palestinian uprising when he was a teenager living in the occupied West Bank. Those charges resulted in his imprisonment.

He and his lawyers have argued that his detention by immigration officials this year was politically motivated, and they have accused the Trump administration of targeting pro-Palestinian speech and violating Mr. Sarsour’s First Amendment rights.

In an interview on Tuesday, before the decision, Mr. Sarsour said that federal officials had targeted him and other community leaders and demonstrators who had supported the rights of Palestinians during the Israel-Hamas war and who opposed American aid to Israel.

“I was not hiding,” he said. “I was saying that clearly. I believe they want to stop us.”

In pursuing Mr. Sarsour’s deportation, the Trump administration asserted broad power under a Cold-War era statute that says that the secretary of state can deem noncitizens deportable if their presence “would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.”

Congress has since tried to limit the power of that 1952 statute, and its use has been successfully challenged in court. Still, the Trump administration has used the statute to argue for the deportation of foreign students who participated in pro-Palestinian protests, and to bring its case against Mr. Sarsour, according to his legal team. The U. S. secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said last year that his department had used its authority to cancel hundreds of student visas.

In a statement after Mr. Sarsour’s arrest, the Department of Homeland Security said that Mr. Sarsour had been convicted of throwing Molotov cocktails at the homes of members of the Israeli military before he moved to the United States, and of illegally attempting to possess weapons and ammunition.

Mr. Sarsour has denied committing the crimes that he was accused of in Israel.

In the interview on Tuesday, he said that he was first arrested when he was 15. At that time, expanding Israeli settlements in the West Bank had prompted frequent Palestinian uprisings there, including what is now known as the first intifada, which began in 1987.

Mr. Sarsour said he was tortured while in detention, and that he had signed documents he could not understand because they were in Hebrew. And in a statement on Wednesday after the judge’s ruling, Mr. Sarsour said that “a foreign country’s false information and unjust military courts were used to trample on my rights and ignore the truth.”

Patrick Taurel, a lawyer for Mr. Sarsour, said on Wednesday after the ruling that the government of Israel had no evidence for the crimes other than coerced confessions. “We know that Israeli military tribunals are not places where you receive anything resembling due process.”

D. H. S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday, and the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not respond to questions about Mr. Sarsour’s arrests in the 1980s and ’90s.

According to D. H. S., Mr. Sarsour entered the United States as a conditional resident in 1993 and obtained a green card in 1998.

In the United States, Mr. Sarsour became a business owner, a father of six and a grandfather of 10. ICE agents intercepted him while he was running an errand on March 30, and he was taken to a detention facility in Clay County, Ind.

There, Mr. Sarsour said, he encountered a filthy environment where he could not worship as he wanted to, did not receive adequate care for his Type 2 diabetes and did not see the sun for the entirety of his detention.

“Immediately it brought me these dark memories — what happened to me when I was a child in Palestine,” he said in the interview.

If Mr. Sarsour is eventually deported, it is not clear where he would go. The judge on this case, Jayme Salinardi, suggested that he would be sent to Jordan, an idea that Mr. Taurel challenged.

Mr. Sarsour said in his statement that he hoped to stay in the United States. “I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” he said.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.

She Says Vaccines Killed Her Twins. The Authorities Say She Did.

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Tony Luong for The New York Times

In Payette, Idaho, population 8,800, a young mother is accused of killing her 18-month-old twins.

She says childhood vaccinations killed them.

The mother has the support of an anti-vaccine group founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Her fate will be in the hands of a jury in a place where skepticism about vaccines runs deep.

Supported by

By Lisa Miller

Lisa Miller reported from Payette, Idaho

Andrea Shaw has spent most of the summer alone in a cell in Payette, Idaho, taking comfort from photos of her family, according to her lawyer. Her twins were 18 months old when they died, in May 2025, and her living daughter is three months old. She can talk to her husband, Nate, and the baby only by phone or video chat, which she does several times a day. As she waits for her lawyer to drive up from Boise, she reads inspirational books such as “Tuesdays With Morrie.”

Shaw, 23, is charged with the smothering murder of the twins — Tyson, a boy, and Dallas, a girl — in the middle of the night, in the bed that they shared. At trial, scheduled for January, evidence will show that “the only conceivable explanation” for their deaths is that she suffocated them, the Payette County prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in a court filing. Shaw has pleaded not guilty.

Joe Filicetti, Shaw’s lawyer, describes Shaw as “sweet.” In court, in her red-and-white striped uniform, she mostly comes across as young. The Shaw case, grim as it is, might have been a purely local story except for the extraordinary attention it has received from the captains of the nation’s vaccine-skeptical movement. Three days after their twins died, Andrea and Nate Shaw appeared on a video podcast produced by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Looking stricken, the couple told their version of events. The twins had been preemies, Shaw said, and had required intensive medical care. She inoculated them on the recommended schedule without ill effects. But in April 2025, after receiving the D-tap, flu and hepatitis A shots, the toddlers got sick, and when she sought help, clinicians repeatedly dismissed her concerns, she said.

“I wish I was anti-vaccine now,” Shaw concluded, with a wry chuckle.

Shaw was indicted by a grand jury more than a year after the deaths of her children. During that interval, in January, 2026, she became the lead plaintiff in a federal lawsuit filed by Children’s Health Defense against the American Academy of Pediatrics. (“I don’t understand where they come up with these plaintiffs,” said Richard Sauber, the attorney who represents the academy in this case, when reached for comment.) That suit claims that the nation’s pediatricians defrauded American families by colluding with pharmaceutical makers to spread misinformation about the safety of vaccines.

The Vaccine Safety Research Foundation, established in 2021 by Steve Kirsch, the Silicon Valley tech entrepreneur, to “tell the truth about vaccines,” as he put it in an interview, is working “in conjunction” with Children’s Health Defense to help support Shaw and her family. (Children’s Health Defense did not respond to a request for comment.) Documents in the court file make a terse reference to the law firm of Aaron Siri, a Kennedy ally and prominent vaccine critic. Siri wrote in an email, “We do not represent Ms. Shaw with regard to her criminal proceedings.”

Kirsch described his motivation. “When you hear of a case which is 100 percent consistent with a vaccine injury and is not at all consistent with a mother who is killing her kids, you have an ethical obligation to come to the mother’s aid,” he said. He added that if a single shred of evidence pointed to murder, he would “be out of there in a heartbeat.”

Filicetti began representing Shaw the day after the twins’ deaths. He doesn’t remember who first called him, he said, but in 2023, he had met some of the players in the vaccine-hesitant world at a Children’s Health Defense conference in Georgia. Filicetti has a solo practice in Boise, with a focus on defending Idaho police accused of crimes and misdeeds. In the Shaw case, he consults with the high profile advocacy groups. “They all want to give input,” Filicetti said in an interview. “I take any help I can get from anybody.”

Having received almost “every vaccine, including the shingles vaccine,” he said, he does not consider himself a vaccine denier. But during the Covid outbreak, he questioned the lethality of the novel virus and the efficacy of the new vaccine. He viewed government mandates as an overreach.

A believer in alternative therapies — in massage, dopamine patches, cold plunges and therapeutic ketamine for trauma — Filicetti declined the Covid shot. Instead, he treated his Covid symptoms with a 30-day water fast, as well as “ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, and I went to a naturopath who flooded me with ozone,” he told me. “I came out of that healthier than I’ve ever been in my life,” he said. Existing as he does at the nexus of libertarian politics and the crunchy lifestyle of Boise, Filicetti gained a reputation for defending vaccine refusers.

In my conversations with him, Filicetti stressed Shaw’s vulnerability, portraying her as a young, naïve mother who is unjustly accused, has lost her twin toddlers and is separated from her newborn. His sole focus, he told me, is to “keep my client from being wrongly convicted and then receiving the death penalty for something she did not do.” At trial, his only burden will be to show that the state did not prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and in this case, “vaccines were a factor,” he said. In Payette, the “number of people who did not get vaccinated or are vaccine hesitant is high,” and those skeptics will be in the jury pool.

Filicetti is not out to set vaccine policy, he said. But he does have strong views about the way vaccines are debated in the public sphere. The pro-vaccine faithful are too absolutist, Filicetti told me. “When science becomes unquestionable, it becomes a religion,” he said. “They’re just saying, ‘Fall in line.’”

Filicetti sent Shaw “Tuesdays With Morrie” and other uplifting books. He also arranges frequent sessions for her with a trauma therapist specializing in E. M. D. R., or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, which can be conducted through a glass barrier.

The next hearing is scheduled for Oct. 15. “It’s super important for me to keep her emotionally and spiritually healthy,” he said.

Andrea Shaw made the 911 call on Thursday morning, May 1, 2025. At the time, she lived with Nate and the twins at the Northgate trailer park, at the edge of town. Northgate is known locally as the Stepford Wives trailer park because the 65 homes there all look the same, like whitewashed barracks. The dispatcher told her to wait outside.

The police arrived at around 11:30. The park’s manager, Kathy Killkenney, a sharp-eyed 82-year-old, sits in an office at the entrance collecting rent checks. That day, observing all the emergency vehicles, she decided to stay in her office, she told me when I stopped in to see her in September.

“Nobody asked you,” she said to herself that morning. “And the police are going to do an investigation. Just leave them alone.”

Instead, she called Nate at work, according to his account on the Children’s Health Defense podcast. “‘What’s going on?’” she asked him. “‘The police have taped up your trailer.’” Nate said he did not know. He repeatedly called Andrea, who did not answer, and when he called his mother, a police officer picked up the phone. The officer said, “‘Hey, I hate to inform you but your kids are dead,’” Nate recalled. “I was like, ‘You’re lying. You’re not telling me the truth. This isn’t happening.’”

Andrea described peeking in on the twins earlier that morning and thinking they were asleep. When she went to wake them up later, she said, she touched Tyson and he was cold.

“The way I saw them, they looked as if they had gone in their sleep. They were in their sleeping positions. I think it’s called rigor mortis,” she said on the podcast.

According to the prosecutor, Shaw changed her story several times under police questioning. Duke summarized Shaw’s interview at a July hearing: She had been out late with a friend the night before; first she said she had gotten up with the twins at around 8 that morning and fed them breakfast; later she said that wasn’t true. On the other hand, Nate’s account was consistent, Duke said: He had been sleeping the whole time. Duke did not respond to requests for comment.

For her part, Andrea said the police had gotten into her head and made her feel crazy. They said that “I had supposedly had a postpartum, overwhelming blackout and done it to my children,” she said on the podcast.

In the podcast interview, Andrea appeared stunned. Nate looked tense and chewed his lip. Encouraged by the interviewer, they recounted the events of the previous week. On April 23, Andrea and Wendy Shaw, Nate’s mother, had brought Dallas and Tyson to Snake River Pediatrics for their 18-month well-child checkup. Both women had expressed caution about the flu vaccine, Andrea recalled: Nate and other members of the Shaw family were reactive to it. The nurse practitioner was dismissive of these concerns, Andrea said, and Andrea consented to the shot. (Snake River Pediatrics did not return requests for comment.)

The following day, both children were passing a greenish diarrhea and had a blue cast to their lips, and they were lethargic, according to Andrea. Alarmed, she took them to the emergency room at St. Luke’s in Fruitland, Idaho, in the company of her mother-in-law. After assessing them and giving them Tylenol and ice pops, the doctor sent them home.

In medical records provided to The New York Times by Children’s Health Defense, the E. R. physician remarked that the children had not seemed to be in any danger. They were diagnosed with “post-immunization reaction,” and he noted, further, that Andrea “seemed satisfied with their visit.” According to Duke, postmortem tests had showed that one twin had a rotavirus infection, transmitted from feces to mouth and extremely contagious. Multiple physicians I spoke with explained that rotavirus is rarely fatal but can become so if children are not vaccinated against it in infancy, or if they are inadequately hydrated. (The children were making wet diapers, the hospital notes said. Whether they had been vaccinated is not known.)

According to Andrea, the toddlers continued to have “severe” diarrhea. On the morning of April 30, she called Snake River to see if she could get an appointment, but they were backed up. That was the final day of the twins’ lives. In the Children’s Health Defense interview Andrea said they had started to recover that day and were “great” — eating, talking and drinking from their sippy cups.

Angela Wulbrecht was in touch with the Shaws within days of the twins’ deaths. A nurse who worked for 17 years at a hospital in Marin County, Calif., caring for mothers and babies, Wulbrecht is on the board of Kirsch’s Vaccine Safety Research Foundation. For her whole career, she had been an avid vaccine proponent, she said in a joint interview with Kirsch. But she said she had suffered an adverse reaction to the Covid vaccine and over time became a skeptic. “I didn’t know, when I went and got my Covid shot and 12 minutes later I almost died, that there would be no help for me. There was no recourse, nobody to sue,” Wulbrecht said.

Now, helping families like the Shaws “is my passion,” Wulbrecht said. People harmed by vaccines are “distraught,” she said, “and they need guidance.” She wouldn’t speak about the Shaw case, but said she often meets families who post what happened to them on Facebook.

“All of a sudden I’ll get tagged,” she said. “People know me. So they’ll start saying, ‘Contact Angela.’” Wulbrecht estimates she has helped about 1,000 families since starting this work. Her Facebook page recently included selfies of her with Kennedy at public events.

In the time between the deaths of the twins and her arrest, Shaw became pregnant again. When Shaw worried that the fetus was too small, Wulbrecht reviewed her test results and reassured her by text. “I have a feeling everything is going to be just fine,” she wrote.

Shaw was charged with two counts of murder on June 29. Initially the judge set her bail at $2 million. But when Filicetti requested a bond reduction, citing the best interests of the mother and her newborn daughter, Duke responded with ferocity. His experts had considered explanations other than murder, he said. They had looked at poisoning and considered the temperature in the bedroom, which frequently surpassed 100 degrees. They had ruled out both possibilities.

A forensic pathologist excluded vaccines as the cause of death. “This is not a vaccine case,” Duke said in court.

According to the autopsy report, both children had pulmonary vascular congestion, or a buildup of blood and fluid in the blood vessels of the lungs, he wrote. Tyson had pulmonary edema, a more severe buildup, as well.

“According to our expert, these symptoms are consistent with being smothered. They occur when something blocks air from entering the airways, and as the diaphragm expands, it creates a low pressure condition in the lungs and airways,” he wrote. “This is the cause of death of the twins. It is also the only reasonable explanation for why both would die at the same time, on the same night, in the same room, in the same bed.”

While Shaw enjoys the presumption of innocence, Duke continued, he had to consider the risk presented to the defendant’s infant daughter. Judge Kiley Stuchlik agreed. Instead of reducing Shaw’s bond, she revoked it.

For Duke to prevail, a jury in Payette needs to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Andrea Shaw murdered her children. But in Idaho, doubt about doctors and medications, and especially vaccines, has long been a way of life.

Until the deaths of Tyson and Dallas, Andrea and Nate Shaw were not known for anything much. Andrea moved in with Nate’s family when she was 17, during Covid. She “has no criminal record of any kind — not even a speeding or parking ticket,” according to a filing by Filicetti. In high school, Nate liked working on engines and was an active member of FFA (formerly Future Farmers of America), his teacher Tyson Smith said in an interview. Tyson, the boy twin, was named after him.

In Payette, a town of 8,800, Shaw’s claim that vaccines harmed her children is seen as unremarkable. Childhood vaccination rates in Idaho are 68.9 percent, well below the state goal of 79.5, and declining. Bryon Hemphill, a family doctor I spoke to, said that in his rural clinic in Payette, “I don’t know that we are reaching 30” percent.

In a conversation in his office on a bright September day, Hemphill pondered the causes of this deep reluctance. In general, people don’t go to the doctor in Payette, he said. That’s in part because Idaho has fewer doctors per capita than most other states, and Payette has fewer than the Idaho average.

But neither conventional medicine nor the insurance companies have made wellness, or prevention, a priority. Patients drive to the doctors’ office only when they are ill. Since Covid, he said, they often arrive with their own theories about why.

In his practice, Hemphill confronts what he calls “an epistemological problem,” he said. As he experiences it, the vaccine debate boils down to warring truths, in which “truth is what you think it is. It’s your perception. There’s this element of, ‘It’s my truth.’”

Faced with such strong hesitancy, Hemphill knows better than to push too hard. Instead, he tries to engage his patients in a conversation about risk. The chance of dying from a vaccine is far smaller than that of dying from the disease it’s designed to prevent, he’ll explain. Symptoms after vaccination indicate that the vaccine is working, he’ll sometimes add.

But he doesn’t insist. It is not his role, he told me, to tell his patients what to do. “That can come across as judgmental.”

In July, days after Shaw’s arrest, Kirsch, the tech entrepreneur, sent the prosecutor’s office an email. Kirsch doesn’t usually delve into the nitty-gritty of individual vaccine-injury claims and said he has never been to Payette. But he spoke to Shaw after the deaths of her children, and he believes this case could change the national conversation. It could “break this acceptance of, ‘all vaccines are safe.’”

Kirsch wanted Duke to see a 2004 study, based on research from the 1980s, by a retired micropaleontologist that purported to show a correlation between childhood vaccination and respiratory distress and deaths otherwise attributed to SIDS or shaken baby syndrome.

“If a jury understands science, unless you have a witness to the suffocation (which you don’t have), this creates reasonable doubt,” he wrote to the prosecutor, using boldface type.

The prosecutor did not respond to his note, Kirsch told me. “They never do,” he said.

I was very affected by reporting this article. Any way you look at it, the story is so sad. But also, the country’s contentious views on vaccines are being played out in this one case. Everyone I spoke to had different, and strongly held, beliefs. Now, I’m curious to watch this unfold, in a vaccine hesitant place, as the trial approaches. The story isn't over yet.

Christina Jewett contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett, Alain Delaquérière, Georgia Gee, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Lisa Miller is a Times reporter who writes about the personal and cultural struggle to attain good health.

Fed’s Watchdog Finds No Misconduct or Illegal Activity in Costly Renovations

The New York Times September 30, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

A new report by the Federal Reserve’s independent inspector general concluded that a nearly $2.5 billion construction project was poorly managed but made no referrals to the U. S. attorney general.

By Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

The Federal Reserve’s internal watchdog found no evidence of illegal behavior or administrative misconduct associated with the central bank’s nearly $2.5 billion project to overhaul its headquarters in Washington, D. C., even as it concluded that the renovations were poorly managed and lacked sufficient budget constraints.

In a sweeping 120-page report, the Fed’s independent inspector general on Wednesday provided the most comprehensive overview to date of what caused extensive cost overruns on the project, which has been underway since 2022. It identified a range of missteps, including the Board of Governors’ failure to obtain a total cost estimate until the work was well underway or to establish a “guaranteed maximum price.”

The project last year became a major front in President Trump’s campaign to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates. Mr. Trump repeatedly criticized Jerome H. Powell, who served as Fed chair until May, for the cost overruns and frequently raised the question of whether he had committed fraud as he floated the idea of firing him.

The Federal Reserve Act stipulates that the president can remove a sitting Fed official only “for cause,” which has long been interpreted to mean gross negligence or a dereliction of duty. Mr. Trump’s attacks on Mr. Powell culminated in a criminal investigation led by the Justice Department over whether Mr. Powell misled Congress about the project.

The inspector general’s report undermined the Justice Department’s investigation, which was abandoned in April after a number of legal setbacks. The watchdog found no wrongdoing by Mr. Powell or his colleagues, and it affirmed that no referrals were made to the U. S. attorney general.

The report’s findings are significant given that Jeanine Pirro, U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia, had threatened to reopen the investigation at any point based on the inspector general’s findings. That possibility contributed to Mr. Powell’s decision to stay on as a governor after his term as chair expired, a position he can hold until January 2028. Kevin M. Warsh, whom Mr. Trump handpicked to replace Mr. Powell, took over in May.

In a social media post on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said that Mr. Powell should be “forced to resign” from the board in the wake of the report.

“He can’t manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn’t be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on “TRUMP!”),” the president wrote.

Mr. Trump added that he had asked Todd Blanche, the attorney general, to study the findings. If Mr. Powell does not resign, Mr. Trump said he “should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable.”

In a statement on Wednesday, a spokesman for Ms. Pirro said she was in the process of reviewing the report.

The watchdog’s report, which Mr. Powell commissioned in July 2025, was led by Michael Horowitz, who served as inspector general of the Justice Department before moving over to the Fed earlier that year. The document made clear that the Board of Governors, which has seven politically appointed, Senate-confirmed officials, was not engaged in the “day-to-day management of the renovation project.” Instead, those duties were delegated to staff members on the board’s Facility Services team.

The inspector general report found that the board did not obtain a project cost estimate until January 2026, three and half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in costs had been earmarked. A guaranteed maximum price was never set, meaning there was no cap on spending or built-in incentives to minimize costs.

One aspect of the construction project that received significant criticism was the inclusion of certain design features in a 2021 proposal such as new marble, a rooftop terrace and private dining rooms for top policymakers. When pressed at a congressional hearing in June 2025, Mr. Powell denied that many of those features were part of the latest proposal.

“There’s no V. I. P. dining room. There’s no new marble. We took down the old marble, we’re putting it back up. We’ll have to use new marble where some of the old marble broke. But there’s no special elevators. There’s just old elevators that have been there,” he said at the time.

The inspector general’s report corroborated Mr. Powell’s statement, concluding that its investigators “did not find that these design features materially contributed to the substantial construction cost increases.”

They acknowledged that some of the cost overruns were tied to inflation, which the Fed had flagged as a primary reason. But they also cited substantive design changes throughout the project, including the shift from an open-seating office plan to a closed-office arrangement, as well as the need for major mechanical, electrical and plumbing items that ran up the budget.

In a statement on Wednesday, Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, described the Fed’s cost overruns as “egregious” and said that “inflation does not change the Fed’s responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress.” He vowed that the Senate Banking Committee, which he leads, would “continue rigorous oversight to ensure the Fed is transparent and stays focused on its mission.”

His Democratic counterpart on the committee, Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, said in her own statement that the watchdog’s findings confirm that there is “no basis to restart the president’s witch hunt” against Mr. Powell.

In a letter to Mr. Horowitz on Tuesday, Mr. Warsh said he had retained the help of the General Services Administration, which is the agency responsible for managing federal work spaces, to work with the Fed “in the task of finally bringing the renovations to a speedy and successful completion.” He also said that the Fed would work with an independent auditor to examine the construction costs and, in keeping with the recommendations provided by the inspector general, that he would “promptly complete negotiations for a guaranteed maximum price for the project.” He also said staff would establish fixed metrics for the project’s budget and schedule.

Mr. Warsh’s arrival at the Fed has to some extent reset relations between the central bank and the White House, at least with top leadership. Mr. Trump has so far refrained from criticizing Mr. Warsh, even after the chairman voted with his colleagues to raise rates in September.

Mr. Trump directed his anger instead at other members of the Board of Governors, whom he accused of being “hostile” and “political.”

One of those governors, Lisa D. Cook, is involved in an extensive legal battle with Mr. Trump, who in August renewed his efforts to oust her after the Supreme Court ruled against the administration’s earlier attempts. Michael S. Barr, a governor nominated by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., also appears to be under heightened scrutiny for the implosion of Silicon Valley Bank, which happened under his watch in 2023 when he was serving as vice chair for supervision.

An external report on the bank’s failure released this month, which was commissioned by the current vice chair for supervision, Michelle W. Bowman, concluded that the central bank’s regulators “knew, or should have known,” about the mounting vulnerabilities at the lender. Instead, they failed to intervene in a timely fashion because of a “fear of taking action that may later be viewed as mistaken and being held accountable for such,” the report said.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Justice Dept. Tries to Rebuke Federal Judges for Speaking to The Times

The New York Times September 30, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Judge Patrick J. Schiltz had warned that the administration’s actions “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” The attorney general accused him of “obvious bias.”

By Mattathias Schwartz and Devlin Barrett

Mattathias Schwartz reports on the federal judiciary. Devlin Barrett reports on the Justice Department.

The Justice Department on Wednesday accused two of Minnesota’s federal judges of engaging in misconduct for comments made to The New York Times about how their court handled the administration’s immigration surge in Minneapolis this winter.

In a six-page complaint filed with the Judicial Council of the Eighth Circuit, which includes the Minnesota district, the department alleged that the judges’ comments violated ethics rules that limit what judges are allowed to say publicly, particularly on pending cases. It singles out Judge Patrick J. Schiltz and Judge John R. Tunheim, both of whom were quoted in the Times article.

At a news conference on Wednesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche accused the judges of “obvious bias” for giving interviews to The Times about the Trump administration’s immigration surge in Minnesota this winter. Judge Schiltz told The Times that the administration’s actions had “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” Mr. Blanche called those comments “overtly political.”

The article, which appeared on Sept. 17, drew on interviews that took place the previous month with all but one of the judges who were active during the weeks when Operation Metro Surge put the Twin Cities, as well as the court, under tremendous pressure. The judges described the challenges they faced when their dockets were swamped with petitions from detainees, criminal cases against protesters and civil cases challenging the administration’s entire approach.

The Justice Department urged a judicial investigation into four other federal judges in Minnesota who spoke to The Times. The department requested that Judge Schiltz and Judge Tunheim be ordered to recuse themselves from matters involving the Department of Homeland Security.

In a statement on Wednesday, Judge Schiltz, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, said he was “acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times.” He cited an opinion issued this year by a judicial committee, advising that judges are allowed to speak and write on “core judiciary matters,” including the rule of law and judicial independence.

“That is exactly what I did,” he said.

Judge Tunheim, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton, declined to comment.

Complaints about judicial misconduct are considered by other judges. The circuit’s chief judge can choose to dismiss the complaint or appoint a committee to investigate further. If an investigative committee is formed, that group can recommend that a judge be censured or impose other punishments.

In cases of extreme misconduct, the Judicial Council, the judiciary’s internal governing body, can refer a judge to Congress for impeachment. Ultimately, federal judges are appointed for life and can be ousted only by Congress.

Jeremy Fogel, a retired federal judge who consults with judges on ethics questions, said he did not believe the judges had engaged in misconduct. The judges’ comments in the article, he added, “described breaches of professional obligations by government lawyers” and “appear to have been directed to matters within their purview as judges rather than broader policy questions.”

A spokesman for The Times said, “Reporting by The New York Times on concerns among federal judges about the conduct of the Justice Department highlights the importance of public officials stepping up to shed light on governmental actions.”

“Seeking to punish or silence those who speak up to journalists about any administration’s agenda undercuts democratic accountability and the public’s right to know,” added the spokesman, Charlie Stadtlander.

The complaint escalates the long-simmering clash between the Trump administration and the district’s bench, which began when federal immigration agents poured into the Twin Cities last winter. It was aggravated by the killing of two Americans by federal agents, and pressure from the Justice Department to issue a warrant for the arrest of Don Lemon, the former cable news anchor.

In January, Judge Schiltz compiled a list of nearly 100 court orders that he said the Trump administration had violated in its effort to sweep up and deport hundreds of undocumented immigrants, including some who had lived in the United States for years. The Minnesota court was inundated with petitions from detainees asking the court to review the legality of their detention. During the first three months of 2025, the court fielded two of those petitions. Over the same period in 2026, it received 1,116 of them.

The Eighth Circuit was one of the few appeals courts to eventually rule in favor of the administration on the legality of its indefinite detention policy. That ruling has been appealed to the Supreme Court.

This is not the first time that the administration has tried to wield the judiciary’s internal disciplinary process against judges who have issued unfavorable rulings. The Justice Department also filed an ethics complaint against Judge James E. Boasberg over comments it claimed he made at a private meeting of judges. That complaint was dismissed earlier this year.

On Wednesday, Mr. Blanche drew a distinction between the criticism leveled against his department by judges and the public criticism he has leveled against them. He noted that he is not a judge and not bound by judicial ethics.

He then seemed to acknowledge the Justice Department had in fact violated orders from the Minnesota judges but said the orders should not have been issued in the first place.

“I’m allowed to get really fired up when, for example, judges in Minnesota complain about us violating court orders but the reason why, that we are, quote, violating court orders is because these judges are violating Supreme Court law, OK, in allowing these cases to be filed,” he said, apparently referring to a case that clarifies which courts have jurisdiction to hear detention challenges.

After sharply criticizing the Minnesota judges on Wednesday, Mr. Blanche added that the department has “total respect for the judiciary. There’s not a prosecutor in this country that should ever, ever violate a court order.”

Last year, Mr. Blanche railed against what he called “rogue judges” who were unfair to the administration.

“It’s a war, man,” Mr. Blanche said at a public event with conservative lawyers. “They have a robe on, but they are more political or certainly as political as the most liberal governor,” he said, adding, “There’s a group of judges that are repeat players, and that’s obviously not by happenstance, that’s intentional.”

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

I Thought Things Had Gotten Better. The Cornell Case Breaks My Heart.

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Jennifer Weiner

Ms. Weiner, a novelist, writes frequently about gender and culture.

Four weeks ago, I dropped off my younger daughter to start her freshman year at college. Parents of incoming freshmen at every school get versions of the same emails: about scheduling your kid’s move-in time and filling out forms for the health center and making sure to buy the extra-long sheets.

Parents of daughters get an extra assignment. It isn’t written down, but we all know what it is. In between buying shower caddies and LED lights, we have to give our girls a refresher course on Rape Prevention 101. Don’t leave your drink unattended at a party. Don’t walk home late at night by yourself. Make sure someone knows where you are. Watch out for your friends.

On move-in day, student volunteers wearing T-shirts in the school colors helpfully whisked my daughter’s suitcases, the single stuffed animal she brought to keep her company and her straining-at-the-seams IKEA bags up to her dorm room. Her father and I made her bed, unboxed her fan, helped her put her clothes in the drawers. We all went to lunch. She went to a meeting with her resident adviser group. Then it was time to say goodbye.

“Make good choices!” I called. I drove home, a little sad, mostly proud, thinking: My work here is done. I knew it wasn’t really true — she’ll still come home on breaks, and she’ll still need me — but it was a milestone. My kind, smart, big-hearted daughter was ready to spread her wings, ready to meet all the people and do all the things.

Twelve days later, news broke that a former Cornell student was suing the university and others, alleging that seven fraternity members had drugged and raped her at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, when she was 20. She said the university had failed to protect her or to adequately punish the participants, one of whom had sent an unprintable message to the fraternity’s Snapchat group alerting its dozens of members, in vulgar shorthand, that a woman’s body was available for the taking.

Hearing about it, I was incandescent with rage, as were a great many others. The immediate public outcry focused on the Snapchat message, the lack of any criminal charges, the apparent failure of anyone in the fraternity to intervene. Only two of the seven alleged assailants were expelled, and some of the discipline Cornell meted out included having the men write essays. I am so angry right now, I saw women posting on social media. We need to raise better men.

For women who’d gone to college decades ago, the ones who’d spent their undergraduate years marching and protesting and signing petitions and occupying buildings — the ones, that is, like me — the fury was laced with a kind of bewildered exhaustion. How is this still happening? Shouldn’t things be better by now? How could all of our activism have brought about so little change?

I started college in the fall of 1987. Back then, the idea of boys forcing themselves on girls, even girls who were passed out drunk, was still the stuff of punchlines in teen movies. The term “rape culture” wasn’t in wide circulation, but we could see it all around us — in what happened on weekends in the basements of the local social institutions, in the way some men talked about women. At a Take Back the Night march, where students walked through campus, stopping so that women could tell agonizing personal stories, a heckler held up a sign that said “We can rape anyone we want.”

Under pressure, the university hired a counselor to handle sexual assault cases — a start, but far less than was needed to address the problem. Back then, however, many universities were reluctant to address sexual assault head-on, lest their actions attract negative attention from alumni, donors or potential applicants.

In 2011, the feds stepped in. Under the Obama administration, the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights sent colleges strict new guidelines for how to handle sexual harassment and sexual assault cases. In part, the rules were intended to make it easier for victims to prove their case, including by lowering the standard of evidence. To me and the people I had marched with all those years ago, it was a victory — too late for us, perhaps, but maybe not too late to help our children. But then a different population felt outraged. Opponents of the new guidance said it went too far, skewing unfairly in favor of accusers at the expense of the rights of the accused.

When President Trump took office, the pendulum swung back, hard. Now campus sexual assault accusations can be held to a far higher standard of evidence, and people accused of sexual assault can in some circumstances cross-examine their accusers, a terrifying prospect for survivors of trauma. Just this week, the Trump administration weakened the rules yet again, rescinding Biden-era protections for gender identity and sexual orientation.

The facts of the Cornell case are still coming into view. Prosecutors say the woman, who has not been publicly identified, did not make it clear in her initial report to campus police that she was the victim of nonconsensual sex. (What then did she report, and why? The authorities did not say.) Cornell has disputed some accounts of the punishments it handed out to the fraternity members in question, though it has declined to say what actions it took. A lawyer for one of the young men is now making the media rounds, saying that his client is an innocent victim and that the woman’s lawsuit is a “money grab.”

New York State sets a high bar for proving rape allegations. A person who has willingly consumed drugs or alcohol is not assumed to be incapacitated unless she or he is unconscious.

No one, however, is disputing that Snapchat message. The one showing that the fraternity brothers felt comfortable enough with their actions that night to advertise them. At some point in the evening, one of the brothers reportedly checked in to see if the activity was still underway. “Shop still open?” he posted. “Yea,” someone replied.

I keep thinking about the woman whose body they were referring to. I think about her mother, who, not too many Septembers ago, might have unpacked bags and hung up posters, feeling just as proud as I’d felt. And I keep thinking about my daughter and her female classmates.

Would some student on their campus be capable of sending a text that offered up a woman like a used futon on Facebook Marketplace? And if so, would the university allow him or some of those who participated to continue their studies?

I wanted to think the world had changed, that all those years of marching and making demands by students at colleges all over the country had resulted in more effective systems. That colleges had better ways of handling sexual assault. That we’d educated boys and girls about rape culture. That young men see their female classmates as people. That all our work meant something.

Looking at the screenshots the Chi Phi brothers sent that night, I think maybe all that’s changed since 1987 is the technology.

All I can do is hope that in another few decades, when one of my daughters is dropping off her daughters on campus somewhere, things will finally be better. Until then, we’ll have to keep giving our girls the talk, and hoping, truly hoping, that it’s enough.

Jennifer Weiner, a novelist, writes frequently about gender and culture. Her latest novel is “The Griffin Sisters’ Greatest Hits.”

Democrats Block Stock-Trading Bill, Denying the G. O. P. a Pre-Midterm Win

The New York Times September 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A Republican measure to limit, but not bar, congressional stock trading faltered in the Senate as Democrats thwarted a G. O. P. bid to show progress on an issue that has rankled voters.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from the Capitol

Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation that would limit the ability of members of Congress to trade stock, dismissing it as an empty G. O. P. effort to appeal to widespread voter distrust of public officials ahead of the November elections without actually addressing it.

The Stop Insider Trading Act, which the House passed in July, would bar lawmakers and their spouses and family members from buying individual stocks but allow members of Congress who already own them to keep trading with new notice requirements. It places no restrictions on the president or the vice president.

The measure, which needed 60 votes to pass, was blocked on a party-line vote of 53 to 47, its failure predetermined after Republicans attached sweeping voter ID restrictions opposed by Democrats and some G. O. P. lawmakers that have already been rejected by the Senate six times.

But Democrats said they would have opposed the bill even without the voter ID measure, because it fails to do what voters have been clamoring for: impose an outright ban on congressional stock trading. They accused Republicans of bringing it up in an effort to appear as if they were addressing the issue, which has become politically toxic for both parties.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, called it a “toothless” bill that was as “ineffective as a screen door on a submarine.” He noted that it would do nothing to stop President Trump, who he said has made 30,000 stock trades in the past year, from continuing such transactions.

Mr. Schumer called the bill a “last-ditch effort to save face” with voters, but said that “Americans don’t buy it.”

The Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal organization, also urged Congress to reject the measure because it “does not actually ban congressional stock trading, and it will thus not remove the cloud of distrust that hangs over lawmakers’ suspicious stock sales.”

The bill was brought to the floor as part of a final sprint of legislative moves before the midterm elections by Senate Republicans. They are facing a bleak political landscape with just weeks to go before the balloting, aimed at showing they were responsive to voters’ concerns.

“It would ensure transparency when it comes to stock sales to provide that members of Congress and their families provide public notice of any stock sale,” Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on the Senate floor. He called it a “simple” but important way “to ensure that members of Congress are held to the standards that Americans should be able to expect of their representatives.”

Senator Pete Ricketts, Republican of Nebraska, said passage was necessary to “restore the faith of the American people in the House and in the Senate.”

For House Republicans who voted for an identical measure earlier this year, the bill has provided them with a talking point to appeal to voters on the issue.

In Iowa, for example, an outside group supporting Representative Zach Nunn, a vulnerable Republican, has spent almost $400,000 on an ad highlighting his support for the bill, exaggerating what it does.

“While honest, hard-working Americans struggle at home, fat cat politicians in Washington are getting rich on inside information,” the ad states. Mr. Nunn’s support for the bill, it claims inaccurately, means that “those fat cat lawmakers and their families are prohibited from buying stocks, putting an end to their greed and corruption, and leveling the playing field for hard-working Americans.”

A public backlash against perceived corruption in Washington has shaped the battle for control of Congress, with Democrats and Republicans alike seizing on congressional stock trading and putting it at the forefront of ads in some of the most competitive races in the country.

Candidates in both parties have cited congressional stock trading as a way to portray their opponents as corrupt and out of touch with the financial realities of working-class Americans.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks during this congressional session, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

This year, candidates and outside groups have spent an estimated $162 million on advertisements highlighting the issue, according to an analysis by AdImpact.

In competitive House districts, Republicans are targeting Democrats on the issue with television ads in Florida, Virginia, Texas and Ohio.

And Democratic candidates in some of the most competitive Senate races in the country, where they are hoping to flip seats, have all zeroed in on the topic as they make their appeals to voters.

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has been campaigning on a ban, attacking Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, for being one of the most prolific stock traders in Congress.

“He’s ballooned his net worth, reporting nearly 100 stock trades while serving in office,” she said at an event in July.

In North Carolina, the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, has said that the first thing he would support in Congress would be a stock trading ban. He also challenged his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, to sell his stock.

In Iowa, State Representative Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has been attacking Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, in paid advertisements for increasing her net worth up to $8 million since she went to Congress. (Ms. Hinson, in paid ads, also says that she is “fighting to ban stock trading in Congress.”)

And in Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, tells voters in an ad that “last year, members of Congress made more than $635 million in stock trades.” He adds: “The fact is, we’ve come to expect that kind of thing from Washington. But you shouldn’t, and I never will.”

Senate Democrats have made their own attempts at addressing the issue, all of which have been blocked by Republicans. In June, Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat of Georgia, sought to bar senators from trading stocks and cryptocurrency.

“This may be one of the most unifying issues in our deeply divided country,” he said at the time. A Republican, Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, objected.

In July, Senator Alex Padilla, Democrat of California, tried twice to offer a bipartisan bill that would bar members of Congress and their family members, as well as the president and vice president, from trading stocks.

Republicans moved to block it both times.

An earlier version of this article misstated a provision of proposed legislation to limit stock trading by members of Congress. The Stop Insider Trading Act would restrict trading by the spouses and family of members of Congress; it would not allow them to trade freely on a lawmaker’s behalf.

Legal Immigrants Lose Medicaid Coverage Under Trump’s Bill

The New York Times September 30, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Many immigrants without green cards will no longer be eligible for the health insurance program for low-income people.

By Madeleine Ngo

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration policy and the Department of Homeland Security.

Thousands of refugees and other legal immigrants across the country are set to lose access to Medicaid starting Thursday as Republican-led cuts to the health insurance program for low-income people take effect.

Some of those immigrants who depend on Medicaid said in interviews that they were not sure how they would afford to treat their conditions, such as kidney failure, multiple sclerosis and bipolar disorder. Several said they applied for permanent residency more than a year ago, a status that would allow them to keep their coverage. But they said they have yet to hear back from U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services amid slowdowns in green card processing.

States across the country have warned recently that the thousands who will lose coverage include refugees, people granted asylum, people granted parole and certain victims of domestic violence. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that the changes would lead to roughly 100,000 more people becoming uninsured. Immigrant advocates say many of those people would instead be forced to turn to emergency rooms for care.

The cuts represent a major shift for many legal immigrants who have had access to Medicaid for decades. The government has long recognized that refugees fleeing war, persecution and other dire situations often do not have many resources upon arrival, immigration policy experts said.

“Fundamentally, it’s a change in how we view people who come to the country and, specifically in this case, the humanitarian population,” said Valerie Lacarte, a senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank.

Medicaid, a program jointly funded by states and the federal government, provides free or low-cost health coverage to millions of poor families. The decision to make these immigrants ineligible for the program was approved by Congress last year as part of President Trump’s domestic policy bill, which enacted tax cuts and sweeping restrictions on immigrants’ use of safety net programs. Trump administration officials have targeted not only people in the country illegally but also immigrants who followed the steps to gain legal status.

Federal officials have said the cuts are necessary to reduce reliance on public benefits and prioritize American citizens. The domestic policy bill also imposed restrictions on legal immigrants’ use of food stamps, Medicare and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

“Aliens in the United States should be self-sufficient and should not depend on U. S. taxpayer resources to meet their needs, and the availability of public benefits should not be an incentive for immigration to the United States,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement this week.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that President Trump would “always put American citizens first.”

Some refugees said they had ailments that they informed the U. S. government about before they were granted status, while others developed them after arriving.

Farahzad Sediqi, 32, said she was set to lose Medicaid, which helps cover her treatment for multiple sclerosis, a disorder of the central nervous system that can cause paralysis and seizures. Because Ms. Sediqi is a paraplegic, nurses come to her house in Ohio daily to help her shower and change her clothes.

Ms. Sediqi fled Afghanistan and arrived in the United States as a refugee in May 2023, along with her brother and mother, Amina Safawi. Ms. Safawi, who also relies on Medicaid to treat back pain and diabetes, said she and her daughter each receive about $1,000 in federal disability payments each month. Ms. Safawi said her son works at Walmart, but their total income is only enough to cover rent and other basic necessities.

Ms. Safawi said she was unsure what would happen, as she cannot afford her daughter’s neurologist appointments, home care nurses or the treatment she needs to prevent seizures without insurance. Although they applied for green cards over a year ago, they are still waiting to hear back, she said.

“She’s my entire life and I can’t tolerate losing her,” Ms. Safawi said in Dari.

Danilo Zak, the policy director at Church World Service, a nonprofit group that aids refugees nationwide, said the organization was working with families to try to find alternatives to Medicaid but that options were limited. More immigrants will likely have to rely on emergency rooms and community health centers, he said.

“Access to basic health care and food assistance is part of those initial supports that are needed to get people to self-sufficiency,” Mr. Zak said.

Mr. Zak urged the federal government to speed up processing of green card applications, given that an approval could make them eligible for Medicaid again.

Although refugees can apply for permanent residency after living in the United States for a year, the Trump administration has slowed processing those applications, meaning many legal immigrants will be kicked off the program while they wait for their application decisions.

There are about 149,470 pending green card applications filed by refugees, according to data from U. S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. From October to the end of June, the agency completed reviewing only about 3,800 applications. It now takes about 18 months for the agency to process those applications, up from eight months at the end of 2024.

Esther Aguilar and her husband fled Nicaragua and later migrated to the United States as refugees in January 2024. Ms. Aguilar, a 39-year-old Ohio resident, said they submitted green card applications over a year ago, but they are waiting to hear back.

After arriving in the United States, Ms. Aguilar started swelling throughout her body and had difficulty breathing. Doctors later told her that her kidney was failing and she needed dialysis.

Ms. Aguilar said she now goes to a dialysis center three days a week. She recently joined a kidney transplant waiting list, she said, but her doctor told her that she will lose her spot on the list if she no longer has health insurance.

Ms. Aguilar said her medical expenses have been covered by Medicaid, including her nephrologist appointments, insulin and blood pressure medication. But she said she will not be able to afford treatment out of pocket.

Her husband makes $18 per hour working in construction and has asked his employer if he can get health insurance through his job. But they are not sure they will get coverage, and they depend on his wages to cover other basic expenses.

Ms. Aguilar said she feared she could die after losing Medicaid. “They are taking away my hope of moving forward,” she said in Spanish.

Cat Gossman, the health and wellness program manager at Community Refugee and Immigration Services, an Ohio nonprofit group, said she was reaching out to providers to ask about resources they might offer to lower-income individuals like Ms. Aguilar and Ms. Sediqi, but options were limited.

Drishti Pillai, the director of immigrant health policy at KFF, a health policy research group, said it was unclear if everyone subject to the change on Thursday would immediately lose coverage, given that it could take time for some states to reverify people’s immigration status. She added that pregnant women and immigrant children who are lawfully living in the country could continue to get coverage in many states.

The changes will likely result in more immigrants waiting until they become “horribly sick” before seeking treatment in emergency rooms, said Leighton Ku, the director of the Center for Health Policy Research at George Washington University. Hospitals are required to provide emergency care regardless of immigration status, which they can be reimbursed for through a provision known as emergency Medicaid.

“This will create additional strains for emergency rooms that could even have repercussions for citizens who are trying to get care,” Mr. Ku said.

Steven Camarota, the director of research at the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that favors lower immigration rates, praised the Trump administration’s efforts to curb immigrants’ use of welfare programs. But he said the move to revoke Medicaid for certain legal immigrants probably would not result in major savings for the federal government and added that he thought it would be more effective to focus on other efforts to reduce their use of public benefits.

“If you’re going to have humanitarian immigration, then it seems reasonable to say we’re going to give them this special eligibility,” Mr. Camarota said.

Ibrahim Daoud, a math teacher living in Southington, Conn., said he feared he could no longer afford the medication and psychiatrist appointments his sister needs to treat her bipolar disorder and schizoaffective disorder. He said her medications alone would cost more than $1,100 each month without Medicaid.

Mr. Daoud, 36, said they fled Syria amid its civil war and to find his sister better medical care in another country. The United States later accepted them as refugees, and they arrived nearly two years ago.

His sister, Ava Dawood, 29, said she worried that she would have trouble sleeping and more frequent thoughts of harming herself without medication. She also sees urologists to treat incontinence, the result of a fall she sustained from the fourth floor of a building in Syria.

Mr. Daoud said he did not want to abuse government benefits, but doctors have said his sister has limited ability to work because of her condition.

“I’m working here,” Mr. Daoud said. “I have no problem with that. But there are some people who really need help.”

Coral Murphy Marcos contributed reporting. Mehrnaz Ighani and Yasmin Alkashef contributed translation.

Madeleine Ngo covers immigration and economic policy for The Times.
